article_title: Renzulli Learning
citation: Renzulli Learning. (2024). Renzulli Learning program description. https://renzullilearning.com/en/Menus/21-technology
title: Differentiate instruction by focusing on individual student strengths and interests to foster engagement
description: The article describes Renzulli Learning as helping teachers differentiate instruction by "focusing on individual strengths and interests", with the aim of cultivating critical thinking, creativity, and 21st-century skills and supporting personalized learning and equitable opportunities for all students from Pre-K to 12th grade. The principle is to personalize learning around each student's strengths and interests as a route to engagement.
requirements: A platform or process for identifying individual student strengths and interests so instruction can be differentiated around them
constraints: The page presents this as the program's design rationale; the measured outcome in the supporting study was oral reading fluency growth
target_learners: All students from Pre-K to 12th grade
target_learning_goals: Student engagement
critical thinking
creativity
21st-century skills
equitable opportunities
examples: Renzulli Learning operationalizes this principle through an online platform that differentiates instruction around individual strengths and interests

article_title: Progress Learning – Math
citation: Progress Learning. (2024). Progress Learning — Evidence Rating. https://www.progresslearning.com
title: Use diagnostics and progress monitoring to identify students below grade level and assign targeted resources
description: The article describes Progress Learning's diagnostics and progress monitoring as the mechanism for catching students up: "Diagnostics and progress monitoring help educators understand which students are not performing at grade level so that they can provide the resources they need to catch up." District and school dashboards extend this by letting teachers monitor progress across subjects and grade levels and identify trends that may inform curriculum and teaching strategies.
requirements: Diagnostics and progress monitoring data available to educators
Dashboards for school- and district-level monitoring
target_learners: K-12 students, especially those not performing at grade level
target_learning_goals: Identifying and remediating below-grade-level performance
examples: The platform's diagnostics flag students not performing at grade level so teachers can assign catch-up resources
key_sources: Progress Learning. (2024). Progress Learning — Evidence Rating. https://www.progresslearning.com

article_title: Progress Learning – Reading
citation: Progress Learning. (2024). Progress Learning program evidence summary. https://www.progresslearning.com
title: Use diagnostics and progress monitoring to identify students below grade level and target remediation resources
description: The program embeds diagnostics and progress monitoring so educators can see which students are behind. As the summary states, "Diagnostics and progress monitoring help educators understand which students are not performing at grade level so that they can provide the resources they need to catch up." Dashboards extend this to school and district level, helping teams "better understand where students need remediation and identify trends that may inform curriculum and teaching strategies."
requirements: Teachers and administrators need access to the platform's dashboards and to the remediation resources the diagnostics point to.
constraints: The evidence summary does not report a study isolating the effect of the diagnostics or dashboards themselves; the measured outcomes concern overall program use.

target_learning_goals: Catching up students who are below grade level; informing curriculum and teaching strategies
examples: District and school dashboards allow teachers to monitor student progress across subjects and grade levels.

article_title: Lenses on Literature — Evidence for ESSA
citation: Lenses on Literature. (2013). Lenses on Literature. https://www.literacydesigncollaborative.org
title: Use a digital platform to deliver layered scaffolding, differentiation, and ongoing formative assessment with standards-aligned rubrics
description: Lenses is a hybrid program with print and digital components. The digital platform ensures that teachers can deliver layers of scaffolding and differentiation to meet varied learning needs, conduct ongoing formative assessment, and use standards-aligned rubrics to score periodic and summative performance tasks. The principle is that technology should serve differentiation and formative assessment within daily instruction.
requirements: A hybrid print and digital program structure with standards-aligned rubrics from the Stanford Center for Assessment, Learning, and Equity.
target_learning_goals: differentiated literacy instruction
formative assessment of reading and writing
examples: The program provides robust scaffolds for multilingual learners and embedded formative assessments using standards-aligned rubrics.

article_title: The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Kristin Hallgren. (2015). The Importance of a Teacher of Record: Definition and Roster Verification for High-Stakes Decision Making. Issue Brief, Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Allow district autonomy in implementing the ToR definition, provided it aligns with state priorities and high-stakes data use
description: The brief balances statewide consistency with local flexibility: districts may exercise autonomy in implementing the teacher of record definition as long as their approach aligns with the state's educational priorities and the state's use of the data for high-stakes decision making. This is paired with the recommendation that states provide guidance to districts on implementing the statewide definition.
requirements: A statewide ToR definition and stated state educational priorities must exist to bound district autonomy.
constraints: District autonomy is limited to approaches that align with the state's educational priorities and use of the data for high-stakes decision making.
target_learners: K-12 students in state accountability systems
target_learning_goals: Valid teacher-student data links for evaluation
examples: Key findings: 'Allow district autonomy, as long as it aligns with the state's educational priorities and use of the data for high-stakes decision making.'

article_title: School Instructional Program Coherence
citation: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Schoolwide coherence through coordinated adoption of a structured direct instruction program
description: Ackerman Elementary achieved the highest coherence ratings among the 11 field study schools by adopting a Direct Instruction program providing scripted lessons and matching assessments in mathematics and reading for grades one through six, supplemented by grade-level literacy leaders and classroom libraries. Teachers met in within-grade and across-grade teams, often twice weekly, to coordinate curriculum, instruction, and assessment. The report notes "The fully articulated instruction and assessment scheme provided by the Direct Instruction program, along with schoolwide implementation of the literacy/library supplement, were leading reasons for Ackerman's high rating on instructional program coherence."
requirements: A fully articulated instructional and assessment scheme
Ongoing whole-school staff development for implementing the program
Grade-level literacy leaders to support peers
constraints: Not every school would agree with Ackerman's decisions to adopt Direct Instruction and to focus its program so much on improved test scores
target_learners: Elementary school students in grades one through six in high-poverty urban schools
target_learning_goals: Raising reading and mathematics achievement through a common scripted instructional framework
examples: Ackerman staff decided after discussion to use Direct Instruction for grades one through six, and funded one teacher per grade as a literacy leader to assist peers with classroom libraries
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: Research Agenda 2026–30
citation: Porter, S., Ramirez Richter, R., de la Torre, M., & Allensworth, E.M. (2026). Research and Engagement for Systems Transformation: Building Knowledge, Capacity, and Coherence for Equitable Education Systems. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Democratize data and elevate community expertise through a distributed model of inquiry
description: The agenda commits to making data and research accessible to everyone through "a distributed model of inquiry—one that supports shared questioning, interpretation, and meaning-making across researchers, practitioners, families, and students." It works through accessible tools, synthesis, and engagement so evidence strengthens collective understanding and local capacity, treating data use as something communities participate in rather than receive. This principle underlies initiatives such as Evidence to Action, which convenes parent and community leaders to engage with rigorous evidence and their own lived expertise.
requirements: Accessible tools, synthesis, and engagement structures that support shared questioning and interpretation across researchers, practitioners, families, and students
constraints: The document notes limited tools and practices currently exist for democratizing data and research use
target_learners: Students and families in urban public school systems, particularly historically underserved communities
target_learning_goals: Building local capacity to interpret and act on school and student data
examples: The Evidence to Action initiative brings together Local School Council members, Bilingual Advisory Committees, Community Action Councils, Parent Advisory Councils, and elected school board members to make meaning of school improvement data.
key_sources: Porter, S., Ramirez Richter, R., de la Torre, M., & Allensworth, E.M. (2026). Research and Engagement for Systems Transformation: Building Knowledge, Capacity, and Coherence for Equitable Education Systems. UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices
citation: Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., and Torgesen, J. (2008). Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc
title: Provide direct and explicit comprehension strategy instruction with modeling, guided practice, and independent practice
description: The guide's second recommendation is direct and explicit teaching of comprehension strategies such as summarizing, questioning, paraphrasing, and finding the main idea. "Direct and explicit teaching involves a teacher modeling and providing explanations of the specific strategies students are learning, giving guided practice and feedback on the use of the strategies, and promoting independent practice to apply the strategies." Teachers should select appropriate texts, use a direct and explicit lesson plan, adjust guided practice to strategy difficulty, and talk about strategies while teaching them.
requirements: Use a direct and explicit instruction lesson plan for teaching comprehension strategies
Select texts appropriate to students' reading level and to the strategy being taught
Provide the appropriate amount of guided practice depending on strategy difficulty
Show students how to apply strategies to different texts
constraints: Studies compared strategies against business-as-usual controls, so no strategy can be ranked as more powerful than another
target_learners: Upper elementary, middle, and high school students, especially passive readers
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of narrative and content-area texts
examples: The panel rates the evidence strong based on five randomized experimental studies plus a single subject design study of main idea summarization.

article_title: Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings
citation: Luke Heinkel, Kristin Hallgren, Brian Gill, Megan Shoji. (2015). Making Effective Use of Postsecondary Data in K-12 Education Settings. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Disseminate postsecondary data to engage K-12 stakeholders
description: This principle addresses the communication side of postsecondary data use in K-12 settings. The brief's key findings state that "dissemination of postsecondary data is important for engaging stakeholders," and the brief's stated structure includes a section that discusses the importance of dissemination alongside its treatment of raw-data uses and sophisticated analyses. Dissemination is thus presented as a distinct, necessary component of effective data use, not merely an afterthought to analysis.
requirements: Postsecondary outcomes data that have been processed or analyzed for K-12 use
Channels for sharing findings with state, district, and school stakeholders
target_learners: K-12 state, district, and school officials
target_learning_goals: Engaging stakeholders through dissemination of postsecondary outcomes data
examples: The brief devotes one of its three stated parts to discussing the importance of dissemination of postsecondary data

article_title: Towards More Transparency in Learning Analytics: Sharing Information with University Students Increases Their Awareness of Data Collection Practices
citation: Stoo Sepp. (2025). Towards More Transparency in Learning Analytics: Sharing Information with University Students Increases their Awareness of Data Collection Practices. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 34–46. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8713
title: Disclose to students both what data is collected and who has access to it, including third-party vendors
description: The article recommends that educational institutions provide transparency about learning analytics data collection as a practical ethical step, stating "Educational organizations should thus work to provide more transparency around the details of what data is collected about students as well as who has access to it." Disclosure statements should cover not only what is collected but which parties have access, including listing the names and locations of third-party vendors, so that students can give informed consent and institutions build more trusting relationships.
requirements: Disclosure statements must be detailed rather than generic, since only non-generic disclosures increased understanding
Disclosure should name which parties have access to the data, including third-party vendors and private companies
constraints: Disclosure alone did not change acceptance of data collection or opinions on who should have access, so transparency by itself does not shift attitudes
target_learners: university students in online and technology-supported courses
target_learning_goals: awareness of learning analytics data collection practices
informed consent regarding educational data use
examples: Participants saw one of three disclosure formats from a fictional University of Australia: a generic vague statement, a detailed text statement, or an icon-based nutrition label mimicking mobile app store disclosures
key_sources: Stoo Sepp. (2025). Towards More Transparency in Learning Analytics: Sharing Information with University Students Increases their Awareness of Data Collection Practices. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(3), 34–46. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8713

article_title: 5Essentials Survey in CPS
citation: Title as printed. (2021). University of Chicago Consortium on School Research press release. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Districts should set and communicate priorities and provide supports so school climate survey data drive improvement
description: The article recommends that districts using school climate surveys pair them with a clear vision, priorities, and capacity-building supports. It states it "will be critical for CPS and other districts to set and communicate priorities and provide support to schools around using this data to ensure success." Without such strategy, interviews showed schools left data unused. The recommendation rests on the qualitative finding that absent district-wide guidance hampered data use and that coaching and team collaboration helped.

constraints: The article notes accountability incentives and pressures can overshadow the survey's improvement potential

target_learning_goals: using school climate survey data to guide school improvement
examples: CPS granted schools considerable autonomy in using survey data, but principals said the lack of district-wide strategy or guidance hampered use of the data for improvement

article_title: Practice-Driven Data
citation: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Disaggregate outcomes by students' prior achievement so cross-school comparisons highlight differences in practice, not population
description: This principle addresses a chronic failure mode of cross-school data discussions: comparing schools that serve very different populations, which invites defensive excuses. Effective data systems instead show comparisons of indicators and outcomes of similar students across schools, highlighting differences in practice rather than differences in population. The To&Through Online Tool operationalizes this by disaggregating freshman course performance by eighth-grade GPA and attendance — the most powerful predictors of ninth-grade performance — and by providing data on comparison schools whose ninth-graders had similar middle-grades performance. Focusing on students at a particular band of prior achievement allows more rational and fair comparisons, removes quick explanations, and supports a search for promising practices among schools achieving better results with similar students.
requirements: Data systems must be technically designed to disaggregate outcomes by indicators of prior performance and to identify comparison schools
Educators need dedicated time, space, trust, and safety for constructive cross-school conversations, with attention to objectives, norms, and facilitation
constraints: The paper notes school leaders may never fully separate learning from accountability contexts, and that lessons drawn from an outside partner perspective may vary from those of actors inside the system
target_learners: school leaders and educator teams comparing outcomes across schools
target_learning_goals: identifying relative strengths and weaknesses against similar schools
sharing promising practices across schools
examples: In Figure 4, only 41 percent of a sample school's high opportunity students — ninth-graders with strong eighth-grade course performance — earned a 3.0 GPA in freshman year, lower than high opportunity students citywide or at similar schools, prompting cross-school practice sharing
key_sources: Moeller, E., Seeskin, A., & Nagaoka, J. (2018). Practice-Driven Data: Lessons from Chicago's Approach to Research, Data, and Practice in Education. Chicago, IL: UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/practice-driven-data-lessons-chicagos-approach-research-data-and-practice-education

article_title: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Digital Promise's Competency-Based Assessment Framework: impact, equity, access, and language principles
description: Digital Promise's Competency-Based Assessment Framework guides the design of its micro-credentials and "emphasizes principles like impact, equity, access, and language to ensure inclusiveness and relevance". Each principle operates as an audit question: whether the competency supports all learners, whether demonstration options promote engagement with diverse learners, whether jargon is defined and resources freely accessible, and whether person-first, strength-based, gender-neutral language is used. The framework evolved from 2014 first principles and was iterated in 2021 after an internal content audit to exceed principles in inclusiveness, equity, and accessibility.
requirements: Micro-credentials are assessed against rubric criteria, with a three-part structure of competency overview, research and resources, and submission criteria plus scoring rubrics visible to learners in advance
constraints: The framework reflects continuous improvement and is specific to competency-based micro-credentials on the Digital Promise platform
target_learning_goals: Equitable, inclusive recognition of demonstrated skills
examples: The Carey Institute's Refugee Educator Academy found the template constraining in a good way, forcing clearer language and openly available research citations

citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Digital Promise Micro-credential Platform
description: The Digital Promise Micro-credential Platform is a competency-based assessment platform launched in 2015, first-to-market with a focus on K-12 educators. Learners "explore and select micro-credentials of their choice, review the requirements, prepare evidence showing their competency of the skill they are pursuing, and submit it", after which subject-matter expert assessors review submissions. The platform offers more than 800 competency-based micro-credentials developed with more than 100 issuing partners, has more than 40,000 registered users, and has awarded 24,000+ micro-credentials; almost 40% of earners have received 11 or more badges.

constraints: Digital Promise exclusively offers micro-credentials that verify the implementation of a practice, requiring a robust portfolio of implementation evidence
target_learners: Learners of all ages historically and systematically excluded

article_title: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Relationship between digital badges and micro-credentials: badges as representation, metadata as verification
description: The eBook distinguishes digital badges from micro-credentials: per Education Design Lab, a micro-credential is the "learning/earning experience" while a digital badge is the "technology used to display it". Digital badges are electronic images with embedded metadata and are not always connected to a micro-credential, since they also recognize participation, progress, or gamified achievements. Micro-credentials use Open Badges metadata — badge name, criteria, issuer, issue date, evidence URL, and more — to "connect evidence and criteria", conveying what the learner has demonstrated rather than only which program was completed.
requirements: To be an Open Badge, a digital badge must be portable, shareable, controllable, and verifiable by issuer and earner, adhering to the 1EdTech Open Badges standard
constraints: Digital badges and micro-credential are often used interchangeably in practice because badges often represent micro-credentials, but they are not always connected
target_learning_goals: Shareable, verifiable ownership of a learning record
examples: At Palm Beach State College's Institute of Excellence in Early Care and Education, learners complete pathways earning competency-based digital badges and then the micro-credential as a capstone
key_sources: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Dispositional competency: ability, sensitivity, and inclination as three interrelated aspects of a developed competency
description: Drawing on Project Zero, the report argues that for a competency to be dispositional, a learner must develop it within three interrelated aspects. Ability ('I can...') concerns capability to apply a skill; sensitivity ('I should...') is recognizing when a skill should be applied; inclination ('I will...') is being comfortable and motivated to choose to apply that skill. The report contends these must be 'developed and used together, repeatedly over time, and across multiple contexts' to become ingrained dispositions.
requirements: Sustained, consistent, cumulative, and complementary learning experiences across subjects and out-of-school contexts for competencies to become dispositional
constraints: Dispositional competency is harder to assess than academic or technical skill demonstration because it spans multiple dimensions, contexts, and abilities
target_learning_goals: cross-curricular skill transfer
adaptability
lifelong learning dispositions
examples: Author anecdote of high school geometry connected to theater set design building ability plus sensitivity and inclination, contrasted with trigonometry class that built ability only
key_sources: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244

article_title: English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students
citation: de la Torre, M., Blanchard, A., Franklin, K., Angeles, C., & Allensworth, E.M. (2024). English Learners in Chicago Public Schools: A Spotlight on High School Students. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Report English Learner outcomes by subgroup, because aggregate reporting obscures both successes and groups needing support
description: The report argues that districts should disaggregate outcome reporting for English Learners rather than reporting only on active English Learners as a whole. Aggregate statistics "obscures the possible variability in the skills and needs that English Learners bring with them to high school," hiding former English Learners' successes and the distinct needs of long-term and late-arriving English Learners. Disaggregated reporting allows identification of which specific groups need more support and which supports differ by group.
requirements: Administrative data systems that track English Learner classification history and exit status through high school and into college
constraints: The authors note there is a lack of information nationally because districts do not report outcome data for former English Learners separately
target_learners: English Learners in K-12 districts, especially high school students
target_learning_goals: Equitable identification of support needs for graduation and college access
examples: The report reported Freshman OnTrack, GPA, SAT, graduation, college enrollment, and persistence separately for four English Learner subgroups and an ever-English-Learner category

article_title: Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership over Their Learning with Formative Assessment
citation: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Divergent versus convergent perspectives in formative assessment
description: The brief distinguishes two assessment perspectives teachers bring to interpreting student evidence. A divergent perspective is based on events occurring in real time and oriented toward curiosity and openness toward students' sensemaking; it requires listening to student responses versus listening for how students are responding, and supports uncovering both assets and prior knowledge. A convergent perspective focuses on how closely student thinking corresponds with pre-determined learning expectations, such as end-of-year standards.
requirements: Teachers need to manage the dynamic between the divergent opportunities that unfold through classroom interactions and the opportunities they design to support student learning of predetermined goals, as Cowie states in the brief.
target_learners: Diverse students, including English learners from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Equitable formative assessment that maximizes opportunities for diverse students to demonstrate the breadth of their knowledge and abilities
examples: The brief cites Pryor & Crossouard's finding that when teachers took a divergent perspective, their feedback was exploratory, provisional or provocative, prompting further engagement rather than correcting mistakes.
key_sources: Barbara Jones, Molly Faulkner-Bond, and Jennifer Blitz. (2024). Accelerate English Learner Success: Students Take Ownership Over Their Learning With Formative Assessment. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673602

article_title: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom
citation: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials
title: Digital Promise system of educator micro-credentials for recognizing teacher competencies
description: The article describes a system Digital Promise is building "to provide professional educators a new way to identify competencies they are developing and gain recognition for the skills they learn throughout their careers." It addresses the gap that teachers "often don't have the opportunity to demonstrate the full breadth of what they have learned, including in informal contexts." The system moves professional learning toward a competency-based model with multiple ways to learn, demonstrations of competence, and desired outcomes, and is supported by a platform for earning the credentials.
requirements: Teachers demonstrate competencies through performance-based artifacts such as lesson plans, student work samples, reflections, observations, videos, and peer or self evaluations
constraints: Receipt of a micro-credential is not a guarantee of teacher quality — it is a signal of competency with a specific skill
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers and professional educators
target_learning_goals: demonstrating and gaining recognition for professional teaching competencies developed throughout a career
examples: Digital Promise launched a platform to support teachers in earning Deeper Learning micro-credentials
key_sources: Developing a System of Micro-credentials: Supporting Deeper Learning in the Classroom. (2014). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org/microcredentials

article_title: School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices
citation: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy
title: Districts and schools should create and enforce data privacy policies protecting teachers, students, and families
description: In the absence of other policies, the brief recommends local policies covering data collection, use, storage, breach handling, and opt-out rights. It states districts should "create and enforce policies to provide teachers, students, and families with reasonable protections from predatory practices," including limits on repurposing data (e.g., parent-communication data not used for teacher evaluation).
requirements: Policies must be specific about data, allow opt-out of specific data uses, and require understandable notification of policy changes
target_learning_goals: student and teacher data privacy and prevention of inequitable data use
examples: The brief warns that non-transparent algorithms used for teacher evaluation or student tracking can perpetuate inequities, likening the risk to police departments' profiling misuse of AI
key_sources: Jackson, T., Pakhira, D., Fusco, J., Ruiz, P., Lekshmi Narayanan, A. B., Glazer, K., Eaglin, P., & Eguchi, A. (2021). School Policies for Integrating AI in Classroom Practices. CIRCLS. https://circls.org/reports/ai-policy

article_title: Digital Fluency: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway
citation: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway: Digital Fluency. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Digital fluency framework with five components
description: The article presents a framework defining digital fluency as moving beyond knowing how to use technology toward knowing why and when to apply it. It states: "The digital fluency framework outlines five components of digital fluency" — curiosity, communication, creation, data, and innovation fluency. For each problem, learners must decide which tools to use, why, and how to create something new with them.
requirements: Learners must be able to answer which tools to use, why they should be used, and how to create something entirely new with them for each problem they are solving
target_learning_goals: applying technology to solve problems and create new knowledge
examples: The framework is used to organize digital fluency skills in culinary, skilled trades, and healthcare work examples
key_sources: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway: Digital Fluency. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/2574439a-3a90-422d-80b6-d31caa93636b

article_title: Digital Fluency: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway
citation: Integrating Future-Forward Skills Into Every Career Pathway: Digital Fluency. (2026). Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Teach digital fluency as a ubiquitous practice in career pathway programs
description: The article recommends that career pathway programs embed digital fluency throughout so learners emerge with future-forward skills, work-based learning experiences, and credentials. It states: "Teaching digital fluency needs to be a ubiquitous practice in career pathway programs to ensure learners emerge with future-forward skills." It frames digital fluency as a must-have for every career pathway.
requirements: Career pathway programs must integrate digital fluency across courses rather than treating it as an isolated topic
target_learners: K-12 and postsecondary learners in career pathway programs
target_learning_goals: future-forward workplace skills and credentials for quality jobs
examples: The article describes culinary, skilled trades, and healthcare workers employing data, AI, and cyber skills in day-to-day work

article_title: El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233
title: Marco de Evaluación Basado en Competencias de Digital Promise
description: El eBook describe el marco que fundamenta todas las micro-credenciales de Digital Promise. Sus primeros principios surgieron de profesionales de todo Estados Unidos: "construido sobre la base de destrezas demostrables, fundamentos basados en la investigación, múltiples formas de evidencia y evaluación y revisión transparentes y rigurosas". Tras una auditoría interna de contenidos en 2021, el marco se reiteró sobre principios de inclusión, equidad y accesibilidad, operacionalizados en cinco preguntas de revisión: impacto, equidad, acceso, lenguaje y el "Panorama General". El marco requiere que el estudiante presente evidencia de la aplicación de la destreza, evaluada por expertos objetivos contra rúbricas.
requirements: Los estudiantes presentan evidencia que demuestra su competencia y reciben una insignia digital si la evidencia cumple los criterios descritos en las rúbricas
constraints: El marco está destinado a reflejar la mejora continua y ha adquirido mayor especificidad según contextos de aprendizaje y tipos de destrezas
target_learners: Educadores K-12 y proveedores de desarrollo profesional que diseñan micro-credenciales
target_learning_goals: Evaluación rigurosa, equitativa e inclusiva de la aplicación de destrezas
examples: Julie Kasper describió la plantilla del marco como restrictiva en el buen sentido, obligando a su organización a reescribir lenguaje y citar investigaciones de libre acceso para su micro-credencial de educadores de refugiados
key_sources: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233

article_title: El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233
title: Estructura de tres componentes de una micro-credencial de Digital Promise
description: Cada micro-credencial de Digital Promise se desarrolla sobre el mismo marco con tres componentes principales. Según el eBook, "El primer componente está formado por tres partes: la Competencia, el Método Clave y los Componentes del Método", que ofrecen una visión general de las destrezas y cómo se demuestra la competencia. El segundo componente incluye la Investigación y los Recursos, con enlaces a estudios que respaldan la competencia y ayudas como publicaciones, vídeos y plantillas. El tercer componente comprende los Criterios de Presentación y las Rúbricas de Puntuación, que indican al estudiante qué responder y qué evidencia presentar, y sirven de guía anticipada y para los evaluadores.
requirements: La rúbrica de evaluación debe estar visible para el estudiante con anticipación
target_learners: Educadores y estudiantes adultos que obtienen micro-credenciales
target_learning_goals: Demostración de competencia mediante portafolios de evidencia
examples: La micro-credencial Live Coding pide un vídeo que capture cuándo se cometió un error y cómo se respondió, la verbalización del pensamiento y la oportunidad para estudiantes de predecir o plantear preguntas
key_sources: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233

article_title: El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233
title: Plataforma de Micro-credenciales de Digital Promise
description: La Digital Promise Micro-credential Platform es descrita como la biblioteca de micro-credenciales más completa y la mayor plataforma pública al servicio del ámbito educativo. Desde su lanzamiento en 2015, enfocada primero en educadores K-12, ha ofrecido más de 800 micro-credenciales basadas en competencias, desarrolladas con más de 100 socios proveedores; tiene más de 40,000 usuarios registrados y ha otorgado más de 24,000 micro-credenciales, con casi el 40% de los receptores habiendo obtenido 11 o más insignias. Las micro-credenciales se emiten como insignias digitales con metadatos seguros adheridos al estándar 1EdTech Open Badges.
requirements: Insignias digitales portátiles, compartibles, controlables y verificables según el estándar Open Badges
target_learners: Educadores K-12, estudiantes adultos y organizaciones proveedoras de desarrollo profesional
target_learning_goals: Certificación de competencias profesionales mediante evidencia de implementación
examples: Digital Promise ofrece más de 580 micro-credenciales desarrolladas, evaluadas y emitidas por más de 115 organizaciones asociadas, incluyendo pilas como la de Kentucky Valley Educational Cooperative y la de Refugee Educator
key_sources: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024). El Rol de las Micro-credenciales en el Aprendizaje y el Desarrollo a lo Largo de la Vida: Empoderando Estudiantes, Empoderando Organizaciones. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/233

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Differentiate initial EL classification procedures for Kindergarten and grade 1 students from later grades while monitoring classification accuracy
description: Several states assess only oral language domains for K-1 students, or assess all four domains but heavily underweight literacy (e.g., a composite that is 90% oral, 10% literacy), reflecting concern that young children's literacy reflects prior literacy experiences rather than English proficiency. The report cautions that students "classified as initially fluent English proficient based solely or largely on oral language skills may experience difficulty in developing foundational literacy skills", making this a tension point requiring ongoing monitoring and validation.
requirements: Ongoing monitoring and validation of classification procedures and decisions for early elementary language-minority students in particular
constraints: Determining the appropriate level of literacy assessment for young children is a tension point that should be approached carefully
target_learning_goals: Accurate initial EL classification and foundational literacy development
examples: States use composites weighted as much as 90% oral language and 10% literacy for early-grade classification decisions
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: California State Special Education Funding System Study, Part 2: Findings, Implications, and Considerations for Improving Special Education Funding in California
citation: Doutre, S. M., Willis, J., Barrett, T., Ripma, T., Caparas, R., & Krausen, K. (2021). California State Special Education Funding System Study, Part 2: Findings, Implications, and Considerations for Improving Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Distribute state special education funds to LEAs rather than exclusively to SELPAs to promote coordination and inclusive practices
description: The report recommends transitioning over time from distributing state special education funds exclusively to SELPAs to distributing them to LEAs, which could then contract with regional entities for regionalized services. Because most students with disabilities spend most of the day in general education, the authors argue "Such coordination could be optimized by distribution of AB 602 funds directly to LEAs," aligning funding with LCFF accountability for all students.
requirements: LEA authority to make decisions about how best to use funds for coordination purposes
Maintenance of effort and excess cost fiscal requirements under IDEA must continue to be met
constraints: The need for some regionalized services persists, especially for students in high-cost categories and small LEAs
The funding system alone cannot bring forth necessary changes, though it can communicate state intent
target_learners: Students with disabilities in California K-12 schools, including those in general education classrooms 80 percent or more of the day
target_learning_goals: Access to and progress in the general education curriculum; coordinated services across general and special education
examples: The report's near-term option distributes funds for low- and mid-cost disability categories directly to LEAs while routing high-cost category funds to regional entities
key_sources: Doutre, S. M., Willis, J., Barrett, T., Ripma, T., Caparas, R., & Krausen, K. (2021). California State Special Education Funding System Study, Part 2: Findings, Implications, and Considerations for Improving Special Education Funding in California. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED616106

article_title: Instructional Equity and Respect for Diversity in Schools: Staff Perceptions Vary by Race/Ethnicity and by Role
citation: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: Disaggregate staff climate perceptions by race/ethnicity and role rather than relying on aggregate staff perceptions
description: Because aggregate staff perceptions may primarily reflect the views of the largest and most positive-perceiving groups, schools should examine perceptions disaggregated by race/ethnicity and role. The brief states these findings "highlight the need to look beyond the aggregate perceptions of staff, which may primarily reflect the views of White respondents (60% of the sample) and teachers (68% of the sample)." Staff in less positive-perceiving groups may have unique insights into unwelcoming aspects of school climate.
requirements: Survey data capable of being disaggregated by staff race/ethnicity and role, such as the CSSS
constraints: The brief notes staff of different races may work in different roles within schools, which can affect perceptions of the school environment
target_learning_goals: identifying unwelcoming and inequitable aspects of school climate that aggregate perceptions mask
examples: The brief analyzed CSSS data disaggregated by six racial/ethnic groups and seven staff roles, finding consistent variation in both areas
key_sources: McCullough, S. N., Hashmi, S., Austin, G., & Cerna, R. (2022). Instructional equity and respect for diversity in schools: Staff perceptions vary by race/ethnicity and by role. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED621215

article_title: Teacher Shortages during the Pandemic: How California Districts Are Responding
citation: Carver-Thomas, D., Burns, D., Leung, M., & Ondrasek, N. (2022). Teacher shortages during the pandemic: How California districts are responding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/899.809
title: District strategy pattern: compensation increases, high-retention pathways, recruitment capacity, and added student-support staff
description: The report identifies a four-part pattern of district responses to shortages: "increasing teacher compensation, improving recruitment and hiring capacity, developing high-retention pathways into teaching within the district, and adding new staff to improve teaching and learning conditions." Districts used state and federal recovery funds for wage increases, stipends, and bonuses (especially for hard-to-fill positions and substitutes), Grow Your Own initiatives and teacher residencies, streamlined hiring such as open contracts and 24-hour offer turnaround, and new counselor, psychologist, social worker, and instructional coach positions intended to ease teacher workloads and support retention.
requirements: State or federal recovery funding to finance compensation increases, pathway development, and additional staffing
constraints: The report notes a rural district offered a $15,000 signing bonus and $3,000 moving stipend for high school mathematics and music positions but had not received any applicants, showing limits of compensation alone for hard-to-staff rural locales
target_learners: K-12 students in California districts facing teacher shortages
target_learning_goals: Stable staffing with fully prepared teachers; smaller class sizes; learning recovery and social-emotional support
examples: Chula Vista USD raised substitute daily pay from $122 to $200 and long-term substitute pay from $132 to $283; one district offered contracts within 24 hours of interview
key_sources: Carver-Thomas, D., Burns, D., Leung, M., & Ondrasek, N. (2022). Teacher shortages during the pandemic: How California districts are responding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/899.809

article_title: Supporting Students Experiencing Homelessness: District Approaches to Supports and Funding
citation: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894
title: District homeless programs provide a coordinated web of six support categories: essential items, transportation, academic services, health supports, specialized unaccompanied-youth support, and family supports
description: Across all five study districts, homeless program staff coordinated services provided by the district program, schools, and community-based organizations. The report enumerates the categories: "Essential items. District homeless programs in our study prioritized providing students and their families with basic necessities, including food, hygiene products, clothing, shoes, and school supplies." Transportation to and from school is required by the McKinney-Vento Act; academic services include tutoring, summer programs, and post–high school planning; health supports include physicals, screenings, counseling, and safety classes; unaccompanied youth receive shelter-embedded staff and prepaid cell phones; families receive linkages to child care, counseling, and emergency funding to prevent loss of housing.
requirements: McKinney-Vento-funded liaisons with dedicated time to provide and coordinate supports, plus partnerships with schools, shelters, food banks, medical providers, nonprofits, child welfare agencies, and housing authorities
constraints: Program staff consistently described transportation as a large cost for their programs, and emergency family funding was provided only when resources and need were known
target_learners: k–12 students experiencing homelessness, including unaccompanied youth and their families
target_learning_goals: educational engagement, attendance, and academic success for students in temporary housing
examples: Cincinnati's Project Connect offers an 8-week summer academic and enrichment course plus after-school tutoring; Santa Fe's Adelante Program provides school supplies, clothing, groceries, tutoring, mentorship, and case management in Spanish and English
key_sources: Levin, S., Espinoza, D., & Griffith, M. (2022). Supporting students experiencing homelessness: District approaches to supports and funding. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/557.894

article_title: Strategies to Foster Integration in Early Childhood Education
citation: Plasencia, S., & Melnick, H. (2024). Strategies to foster integration in early childhood education. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/639.507
title: Diversity by design schools combine innovative instructional models, transportation, and a controlled-choice lottery
description: The report describes San Antonio Independent School District's "diversity by design" schools, which enroll students from inside and outside district boundaries starting in preschool. These schools "have three main components to foster and maintain socioeconomic diversity: (1) innovative instructional models that attract diverse families, (2) transportation that allows children to attend schools outside of their neighborhood, and (3) a complex lottery that maintains socioeconomic and linguistic diversity." The pattern pairs a controlled choice enrollment mechanism with features that make the school attractive and accessible across segregated residential areas.
requirements: a complex lottery that maintains socioeconomic and linguistic diversity
transportation enabling attendance outside the neighborhood
instructional models with broad appeal to diverse families
constraints: the report presents this as one district's approach within a controlled choice system
target_learners: preschool-age children and students in a district's choice system
target_learning_goals: socioeconomic and linguistic diversity in classrooms
examples: San Antonio ISD uses a controlled choice approach in its diversity by design schools, enrolling students from inside and outside the district's boundaries, starting in preschool
key_sources: Plasencia, S., & Melnick, H. (2024). Strategies to foster integration in early childhood education. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/639.507

article_title: Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase?
citation: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://www.edtrust.org
title: Do not accept overall graduation-rate gains as evidence that all student groups are benefiting; examine disaggregated outcomes and be intentional about closing gaps
description: The report argues that institutions must be intentional about success for black students because aggregate improvement can mask stagnation or decline for subgroups. It states "we shouldn't accept wholesale that increases in overall graduation rates lead to gains for all student populations," noting that 31.5 percent of improving institutions showed no gains for black students. Institutions that disaggregated and acted — Buffalo, Ohio State, NC State, Rutgers — narrowed gaps, showing "demographics aren't destiny."
requirements: Institutional data systems that can track graduation rates by race/ethnicity over time
constraints: The report's analysis covers four-year public institutions with at least 30 first-time, full-time black and white students; HBCUs were excluded
target_learners: black students at four-year public colleges and universities
target_learning_goals: closing racial graduation-rate gaps and equitable degree completion
examples: The report urges paying closer attention to the 73 institutions that did not improve graduation rates for black students at all and to the 39 with both declining black rates and widening gaps
key_sources: Nichols, A. H., Eberle-Sudré, K., & Welch, M. (2016). Rising Tide II: Do Black Students Benefit as Grad Rates Increase? The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED566672

article_title: "...And They Cared": How to Create Better, Safer Learning Environments for Girls of Color
citation: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://nwlc.org
title: District-level reform pattern: data transparency, defiance-suspension bans, and restorative infrastructure
description: The guide identifies a reusable district-level pattern of policy changes: "Oakland has implemented a few practices that other districts across the country can adopt or adapt to improve schools for Latina and Black girls." The pattern includes making discipline data by race and gender publicly available, banning suspensions for willful defiance, prohibiting suspension or police referral for dress code violations, requiring community input, maintaining centrally supported restorative justice programs, providing professional development on classroom management, and investing in school-based health centers. Chicago implements a parallel set including student-led disciplinary proceedings and ending early-grade suspensions.
requirements: Central office support for restorative justice, including coordinators and counselors
Regular review of discipline data with action to address disparities
constraints: Implementation inconsistencies at the school level persisted in Oakland
Chicago kept a $33 million annual school police contract in 2020
target_learners: K–12 students, especially Black, Latina, and Native girls
target_learning_goals: Positive school climate
Equitable discipline
Reduced lost instructional time
examples: Oakland implemented 16 School-based Health Centers as part of a full-service community schools strategy available to nearly all secondary students
In 2020 Oakland’s board voted to eliminate its schools police department and reinvest $2.5 million in student support services
key_sources: “...and they cared”: How to create better, safer learning environments for girls of color. (2020). National Women’s Law Center & The Education Trust. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED607322

article_title: Leading Inclusive, Coherent, and Effective Assessment Systems: Closing Opportunity and Outcome Gaps for Students with Disabilities
citation: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Leaders should dismantle structural barriers separating assessment in special and general education contexts
description: The brief's second theme holds that the divide between general and special education creates "a fundamental crack in the foundation of many education systems," affecting assessment decisions. Experts recommended including special education expertise in all assessment-related decision-making, and establishing structures for collaborative data sharing, analysis, and use among general and special educators, administrators, support staff, students, and families.
requirements: Leaders establish expectations, structures, and routines that support inclusive and collaborative data sharing, analysis, and use
constraints: Without addressing structural divides, assessment data for students with disabilities cannot be used effectively to promote success in the general education curriculum
target_learners: students with disabilities, including multilingual learners with disabilities
target_learning_goals: use of assessment data to improve instruction and supports
examples: Leaders can audit whether intervention data are shared with all educators and whether general and special educators regularly review formative, interim, and summative results together.
key_sources: Arnold, J., Hayes, S., & Zagata, E. (2025). Leading inclusive, coherent, and effective assessment systems: Closing opportunity and outcome gaps for students with disabilities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673562

article_title: From automated scoring to learning diagnosis: a mechanism study of AI-supported formative assessment in English writing
citation: Yao X-C and Fan L (2026) From automated scoring to learning diagnosis: a mechanism study of AI-supported formative assessment in English writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1905455. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905455
title: The diagnostic-review mechanism: AI issue-level diagnosis passing through student interpretation, revision, teacher review, and reflection
description: The article proposes a classroom sequence in which AI diagnostic feedback becomes formative only through downstream activity. "The classroom sequence was task submission, AI diagnosis, student interpretation, independent revision, structured teacher review, reassessment, and reﬂection." The framework integrates formative assessment, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and teacher-feedback research, ordered by how diagnostic information moves through interpretation, revision, reassessment, and reflection. Teacher review comprises "conﬁrmation, correction, supplementation, and re-explanation of AI feedback", connecting automated evidence with situated writing judgment and making review workload observable.
requirements: Issue-level AI diagnosis that separates problem diagnosis from revision suggestions and does not rewrite the composition
Structured student interpretation before revision (restating problems, explaining effects, identifying uncertainties, specifying a revision plan)
Structured teacher review after revision, followed by reassessment and reflection
constraints: Evidence comes from two intact classes taught by one instructor, leaving class selection and instructor effects in the observed group contrast
Student time-on-task was not recorded, and the contrast may include additional interpretation, reflection, and revision time
Cycle order coincided with task type, and no delayed post-test was administered
target_learners: University EFL students in English writing courses
target_learning_goals: L2 writing quality and revision skill
Feedback literacy and self-assessment accuracy
Self-regulated revision behavior
examples: In the study, Diagnostic Review students completed an interpretation sheet requiring them to restate problems, explain their effects, identify uncertainties, and specify a revision plan before independent revision, while Control students received AI score/standard feedback with routine checking
key_sources: Yao X-C and Fan L (2026) From automated scoring to learning diagnosis: a mechanism study of AI-supported formative assessment in English writing. Front. Psychol. 17:1905455. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1905455

article_title: Bots and Blocks: Presenting a Project-Based Approach for Robotics Education
citation: Tobias Geger, Dominique Briechle and Andreas Rausch. (2026). Bots and Blocks: Presenting a project-based approach for robotics education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.14529
title: Digital Technologies project framework: semester-spanning agile Scrum projects as an integral third of a robotics-relevant CS curriculum
description: The article proposes a project-based learning framework in which students work in small teams on industry-relevant problems across multiple semesters. The bachelor's program comprises 180 ECTS points, of which 60 are project-based courses worth ten ECTS each, organized with the Scrum framework. The authors state that "the project team is not driven by consecutive tasks to develop a product but by the development of a minimum viable product (MVP)" defined by user stories. Projects are consecutive: early semesters teach project skills, later ones mix cohorts for interdisciplinary work.
requirements: A multi-semester study program structure so that application modules and skill refinement can span several projects rather than a single course
Scientific staff acting as Product Owner and a senior student acting as Scrum Master for each team
constraints: The framework is described for the undergraduate program of one applied computer science degree (Digital Technologies); the authors note transferability to other domains is future research
target_learners: undergraduate bachelor's students in applied computer science (Digital Technologies)
target_learning_goals: practical robotics and software engineering skills alongside theoretical knowledge
agile self-managed teamwork on industry-relevant problems

article_title: DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation
citation: Vishal Kumar, Shubhra Mishra, Rebecca Hao, Rizwaan Malik, David Broman, Dorottya Demszky. (2025). DiagramIR: An Automatic Pipeline for Educational Math Diagram Evaluation. NeurIPS 2025 Workshop: MATH-AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08283
title: DiagramIR back-translation pipeline with intermediate representation and rule-based checks
description: DiagramIR evaluates TikZ-generated diagrams by having an LLM translate the code into a schema-constrained intermediate representation, on which deterministic rule-based checks run (e.g., diagram fully in canvas, outlines closed). The article states that back-translating into an IR lets it "factor out surface form (code formatting, macro usage)", localize errors to explicit types, enable validators that run without a large model, and gain auditability, since checks explain precisely why a diagram passes or fails.
requirements: An LLM performs the semantic analysis (TikZ to IR), while rule-based checks perform the evaluation
constraints: The intermediate representation captures a restricted set of geometric primitives and relations; complex diagrams like multi-step constructions may require iterating on the schema and checks
Back-translation relies on LLMs for parsing TikZ into IRs, which introduced stochastic errors during IR generation
target_learners: K-12 mathematics educators and education-technology developers
target_learning_goals: Scalable automated evaluation of mathematical and spatial correctness of generated diagrams
examples: Rule-based checks include whether the diagram is fully in canvas, whether outlines are closed, and whether labels are associated with correct elements

description: The rubric assesses generated diagrams on two axes, mathematical correctness and spatial correctness, and was mirrored in the automated pipeline. citation: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040
title: Digital Portrait Three-Layer Framework for dynamic, multi-source learner assessment
description: The Digital Portrait Three-Layer Framework, by Zhang et al., argues that traditional test-score-based evaluation captures only a narrow slice of learner ability. It comprises "an indicator system layer that defines what to measure, a data practice layer that collects and fuses multi-source behavioral and academic data, and a digital portrait layer that constructs a dynamic, visualized learner profile for educational decision-making." The framework motivated ECNUClaw's five-dimension profile structure, which captures behaviors, emotional states, and metacognitive patterns beyond academic performance.
requirements: Effective learner modeling must capture multiple dimensions beyond academic performance, including learning behaviors, emotional states, and metacognitive patterns
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive, dynamic learner assessment for educational decision-making
examples: ECNUClaw's five-dimension profile—cognitive, behavioral, emotional, metacognitive, contextual—directly implements the framework's call for multi-dimensional profiling

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Discernment, empathy, and sense of self as three essential outcomes of AI-era education
description: The article identifies three objectives for educational practices in the modern era: "discernment: the abilities to ask and frame appropriate questions, validate and contextualize answers to these questions, and to act appropriately with the results"; empathy, which underpins communication and collaborative work; and sense of self, where students learn their roles, purposes, and belonging. It argues these practices support metacognition, ethics, and judgement, and underpin performance, engagement, and retention.
requirements: Educators must deliberately cultivate these outcomes, since instantaneous access to information and analyses makes discernment practices central
constraints: The article presents these as argued priorities rather than empirically tested outcomes

examples: The preamble frames these three objectives as particularly important because accessing information, calculations, and analyses has become nearly instantaneous with modern technologies

citation: Song, Y., Choi, S., Kim, J., Kim, Y., Weisberg, L., & Moon, J. (2026). A Guiding Framework for K-12 Teachers in Creating AI-powered Learning Technologies through Vibe Coding. https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383
title: Teacher-mentor-AI collaboration as a distributed expertise system in AI technology creation
description: The article conceptualizes workshop interactions among teachers, mentors, and AI as "a dynamically coordinated system of distributed expertise, grounded in distributed cognition theory". Evidence-based knowledge from mentors, practice-based knowledge from teachers, and generative knowledge from AI are integrated and reconfigured through interaction. AI is treated not merely as a tool but as a mediational artifact that shapes teachers' thinking, as teachers externalize tacit knowledge through prompt writing, prototype demonstration, and output review.

article_title: Ethics Training Agents: Facilitating Group-Based Ethics Education with Role-Playing and Discussion for Ethical Reflection and Exploration
citation: Seo, Y., Jang, S., Park, H., Gutierrez, R. S., Seering, J., & Lee, U. (2026). Ethics Training Agents: Facilitating Group-Based Ethics Education with Role-Playing and Discussion for Ethical Reflection and Exploration. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11529
title: Divergence-groan-convergence participatory decision-making structure for group ethics discussion
description: The system structures each discussion stage around a participatory decision-making model comprising "divergence (generating diverse ideas), groan (struggling with differences), and convergence (narrowing down to shared decisions)." Each stage cycles through Idea-gathering (90 seconds of free idea presentation), Deliberation and Questioning (alternating turn-based phases), and Wrap-up (key idea selection). This structure was adapted from Kaner et al. and applied to all stages except Write Reviews, where participants write individually.
requirements: A facilitator (human or LLM) to manage phase transitions, speaking turns through stacking, and time management
constraints: Some participants noted the stacking-based turn format limited opportunities for in-depth exploration of a single idea
target_learners: Undergraduate STEM students in group-based ethics education
target_learning_goals: Structured ethical deliberation covering diverse perspectives within limited time
examples: Each of the four Judgment Call stages (Identify Stakeholders, Write Reviews, Identify Problems, Find Solutions) was structured with the three-phase cycle except the individual review-writing stage

article_title: Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education
citation: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731
title: Coding scheme for observable Direction, Integration, and Evaluation in student–AI interaction traces
description: An exploratory multilabel coding scheme applied to student turns in AI-mediated conversations, with the student turn as coding unit interpreted in relation to its local sequence and the whole conversation. Direction is coded when "the learner exercises task-relevant control over the purpose, constraints, procedure, artifact, or trajectory of the activity"; Integration when a subsequent action connects to uptake, application, transformation, or reuse of a prior AI contribution; Evaluation when the learner participates in judging a contribution through inspection, comparison, testing, discrepancy detection, diagnosis, correction, or criterion-based judgment. Provenance is recorded separately for content, criteria, and judgments, and evidence is classified as explicit or conservatively inferable.
requirements: Development through iterative human-in-the-loop analysis of boundary cases, with the codebook, prompt, and output schema frozen before application to the analytical sample
constraints: The codes describe observable participation, not an additive measure of epistemic ownership; Integration and Evaluation require opportunities for learner re-entry, so short conversations provide few opportunities for these dimensions to appear
target_learners: higher-education students interacting with LLM chatbots on coursework
target_learning_goals: observable cognitive participation in AI-mediated tasks
examples: The protocol was developed on 40 heterogeneous conversations, reaching saturation after 23 cases, tested on a 14-conversation pilot, then applied to 150 conversations using GPT-5.6 Sol with Structured Outputs
key_sources: Jorge Fábrega. (2026). Same Performance, Different Process: Epistemic Ownership in AI-Mediated Education. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02731

article_title: Rethinking teachers’ diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis
citation: Hoppe T, Loibl K and Leuders T (2026). Rethinking teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment: from diagnosis to meta-diagnosis. Front. Educ. 11:1857661. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1857661
title: DiaCoM framework specified for AI-supported formative assessment
description: The DiaCoM framework (Loibl et al., 2020) conceptualizes teachers' diagnosing as information processing: 'when teachers assess students' prerequisites, they perceive and interpret cues (such as verbal explanations or written solutions) and form diagnostic judgments.' The article specifies it for AI-supported settings: situation characteristics now include AI-generated diagnostic inferences as an additional information source, diagnostic behavior includes accepting, rejecting, or modifying AI suggestions, and person characteristics include knowledge about AI systems' functioning and limitations. The AI-related specification of diagnostic thinking is conceptualized as meta-diagnosis.
requirements: The framework distinguishes internal processes (perceiving, interpreting, deciding) from observable external diagnostic behavior, both shaped by person characteristics and situation characteristics.
constraints: The article states the goal is 'not to prescribe how teachers should diagnose more effectively, but to better understand the cognitive processes underlying their diagnostic judgments in AI-supported contexts.'
target_learning_goals: understanding and developing teachers' diagnostic skills in AI-supported formative assessment
examples: The framework has been used in studies of judgments about task demands, interpretation of ambiguous student responses, and prediction of student errors.

article_title: Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot
citation: Syed Furqan Abbas Hashmi, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2025). Analyzing Undergraduate Problem-Solving in Physics Through Interaction With an AI Chatbot. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14778
title: Use complete AI-tutoring dialogue transcripts as fine-grained analytics linking help-seeking behavior to performance
description: The article argues that Socratic AI systems can serve instruction and research simultaneously by logging full interaction transcripts. The authors state that AI-driven Socratic dialogue "generates fine-grained analytics for physics education research, establishing a scalable dual-purpose tool for instruction and learning analytics." Transcript-based coding of question specificity linked help-seeking behavior to expected grades, a methodological gap the authors say existing studies leave open because they focus on aggregate performance metrics.
requirements: Full dialogue transcripts must be logged and student utterances coded (e.g., broad versus specific questions) for the analytics to be computed
constraints: The article states its binary broad/specific classification is coarse and overlooks nuances, and a finer-grained taxonomy is planned
target_learners: first-year STEM majors in large-enrollment introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: problem-solving progress and help-seeking behavior in physics
examples: The authors coded each student question in 150 transcripts as broad or specific and related the specificity fraction to self-reported expected course grade

citation: Youjie Chen, Xixi Shi, Xinyu Liu, Shuaiguo Wang, Tracy Xiao Liu, Dragan Gašević. (2026). Not All Students Engage Alike: Multi-Institution Patterns in GenAI Tutor Use. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.00447
title: Design and scale GenAI Tutors with discipline-sensitive embedding rather than as a one-size-fits-all solution
description: The article argues that productive engagement with GenAI Tutors at scale depends on how tools are embedded in discipline-specific instructional and assessment structures, not only on backend model generalizability. The authors conclude that "GenAI Tutors should not be viewed as a one-size-fits-all solution, but require discipline-sensitive design to support effective use at scale," since engagement patterns differed substantially between STEM and non-STEM courses.
requirements: Attention to disciplinary variation in instructional design and assessment structures when embedding the tutor in courses
constraints: Findings come from classes and institutions with high GenAI Tutor adoption and may not generalize to low-use settings
target_learners: post-secondary students across STEM and non-STEM disciplines
target_learning_goals: productive, learning-supportive engagement with GenAI tutoring tools
examples: STEM courses' weekly closed-ended problems were associated with brief, task-oriented tutor use, while non-STEM open-ended assignments and take-home projects were associated with more iterative, later-semester use
