article_title: Interpretable Knowledge Tracing
citation: Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Andrew Lan. (2026). Interpretable Difficulty-Aware Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01097
title: Interpretable difficulty-aware conversational knowledge tracing framework (knowledge estimator + difficulty estimator + IRT-based predictor)
description: A three-module framework for knowledge tracing in tutor-student dialogues: a knowledge estimator that encodes the original question and dialogue history to produce a scalar ability estimate from LLM logits over GOOD/BAD tokens; a difficulty estimator that jointly considers question text, dialogue context, and the next tutor-posed task to produce a difficulty estimate from HARD/EASY logits; and an IRT-based predictor applying a 1PL (Rasch) model, where "the probability of correctness increases as the positive difference between ability and difficulty grows." The design "aligns model predictions with cognitive theory and improves interpretability."
requirements: An LLM fine-tuned on dialogue-based tutoring data with observed correctness labels, optimized by minimizing binary cross-entropy loss through the IRT prediction layer
constraints: Experiments cover only math dialogues; a learnable vector discrimination parameter led to degraded performance, so a scalar sensitivity parameter is used
target_learners: students in one-on-one math tutoring dialogues
target_learning_goals: predicting student correctness on upcoming tutor-posed tasks and tracking evolving knowledge state during tutoring
examples: The framework was instantiated on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with LoRA fine-tuning and evaluated on QATD2k and MathDial against LLMKT and deep learning KT baselines
key_sources: Shuyan Huang, Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Andrew Lan. (2026). Interpretable Difficulty-Aware Knowledge Tracing in Tutor-Student Dialogues. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.01097

article_title: Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs
citation: Ashish Gurung, Ge Gao, Jordan Gutterman, Danielle R. Thomas, Shivang Gupta, Lee Branstetter, Emma Brunskill, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2026). Improving Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring by Differentiating Human Tutor Roles Based on Student Needs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11155
title: Differentiate human tutor roles by student need: tutors proactively initiate support for lower-performing students while higher-performing students receive reactive, on-demand support
description: This policy matches the intensity of human support to student needs in hybrid human-AI tutoring. Students below the within-grade median on prior performance receive tutor-initiated motivational and conceptual support, while higher-performing students work independently with on-demand access. The article proposes "a proactive-reactive tutoring policy that matches the intensity of human support to student needs," maximizing human support for students who need it most while maintaining the autonomy of students who benefit from working independently.

constraints: The dichotomous median split may oversimplify the relationship between student need and optimal tutoring intensity; students far below the median may need more intensive support than the 1:4 proactive ratio provided

target_learning_goals: Academic growth on standardized math tests
Engagement (time on task) and skill proficiency in AI-tutor practice
examples: 635 students in grades 5-8 were assigned by within-grade median prior state test scores to proactive (below median) or reactive (at or above median) tutoring during twice-weekly IXL math sessions with remote tutors on Zoom

article_title: Math Education Digital Shadows for facilitating learning with LLMs: Math performance, anxiety and confidence in simulated students and AIs
citation: Esposito, N., Tricarico, A., Porzio, L., Aghazadeh Ardebili, A., & Stella, M. (2026). Math Education Digital Shadows for Investigating Learning with GenAI: Mathematics Performance, Anxiety, and Confidence in LLMs. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.27618
title: Digital shadowing as a framework for recording LLM behaviour under controlled conditions
description: Digital shadowing is the article's organising methodological framework: unlike digital twins, shadows record system behaviour without feedback loops. The article states that "digital shadows record what a system does across controlled conditions without updating, simulating, or influencing external counterparts." A Math Education Digital Shadow is defined as a structured record of an LLM's mathematics-related psychological profile and problem-solving behaviour under specified constraints. Human shadows simulate synthetic individuals defined by sociodemographic and psychological attributes, while AI assistants respond as themselves.
requirements: A structured record combining persona attributes, prompting mode, and task outputs so latent human variables become experimentally manipulable
constraints: The article notes MEDS is systematically generated using only LLMs with no human input
target_learners: LLM-based synthetic respondents in education research
target_learning_goals: studying prompt-conditioned LLM behaviour in mathematics education
examples: Human shadows were assigned persona dictionaries with age, gender, education, and Big Five traits; AI-assistant mode set the persona field to null

title: Digital transformation in education as social innovation
description: The chapter proposes understanding digital transformation in education 'not only as technological modernisation or institutional reform, but also as a process of social innovation'. citation: Shahin Hossain, Sima Ahmadi, Leqi Li, Idowu David Awoyemi, Wei Huang, Chenxi Zhou, Jujia Li, Samaa Haniya, Shapla Khanam, Tasbirun Mashreka Subaha. (2026). Rethinking Generative AI Literacy: An Integrative, Developmental, and Dialectical Framework for K–12 Teacher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01705
title: Dialectical commitment: the same GenAI affordance can deepen or displace learning depending on teacher literacy
description: RAIL-Ed's dialectical commitment holds that generative AI affordances simultaneously enable and constrain learning. As the paper states, "It is also dialectical, acknowledging that generative AI affordances simultaneously enable and constrain learning: the same capabilities that support source discovery can produce fabricated information (the source discovery–fabrication paradox), and the efficiency gained through AI use can undermine the development of underlying skills." Outcomes therefore depend on the literacies users bring, making cultivation of that literacy, not tool adoption, the object of design. This commitment follows, in the authors' account, from combining Vygotskian mediation with Freirean attention to structures of power.
requirements: Treats risks and benefits as conditional outcomes of educator and learner capacity, which the framework specifies through its six pillars
constraints: Conceptual, drawn from affordance theory (Gibson, 1979) and the four theoretical traditions; not empirically validated in this paper
target_learning_goals: Judging when a generative affordance deepens versus displaces learning; cultivating literacies that determine outcomes of AI engagement
examples: The paper names the source discovery–fabrication paradox: the same capability that supports source discovery can produce fabricated information
key_sources: Shahin Hossain, Sima Ahmadi, Leqi Li, Idowu David Awoyemi, Wei Huang, Chenxi Zhou, Jujia Li, Samaa Haniya, Shapla Khanam, Tasbirun Mashreka Subaha. (2026). Rethinking Generative AI Literacy: An Integrative, Developmental, and Dialectical Framework for K–12 Teacher Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01705

article_title: Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models
citation: Ali Keramati, Jie Cao, Iman Mohammadi, Mark Warschauer, Yang Shi. (2026). Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14113
title: Diversity-alignment trade-off framework for LLM student-error simulation
description: The article proposes two dimensions, diversity and alignment, as central to the usefulness of LLMs as proxies for authentic student errors. Models strong in diversity (e.g., Gemini) often exhibit weaker alignment, and vice versa, with Claude Sonnet 4 described as "the most balanced option". The framework holds that model choice should be guided by analytic goals: diversity-oriented models explore the breadth of potential misconceptions, while alignment-oriented models approximate authentic error distributions. Struggling level acts as a moderator within this framework, raising diversity while lowering fidelity.
requirements: Evaluation must assess both diversity (e.g., pairwise AST edit distances) and alignment (nearest distance to authentic submissions) simultaneously
constraints: Even the most balanced model varied across tasks and prompts, so no single LLM is universally optimal
target_learning_goals: realistic simulation of novice logical errors for feedback design and misconception analysis
examples: Figure 5 plots the trade-off between alignment (fidelity) and diversity across the five evaluated models
key_sources: Ali Keramati, Jie Cao, Iman Mohammadi, Mark Warschauer, Yang Shi. (2026). Simulating Students' Java Programming Errors with Large Language Models. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14113

article_title: Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation
citation: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232
title: DIPSER multimodal classroom dataset for in-person student engagement and attention recognition
description: DIPSER (Dataset for In-Person Student Engagement Recognition in the Wild) synchronizes camera recordings with smartwatch sensor data to capture student attention and emotional states during scheduled educational activities without experimental staging. It provides RGB facial images at 640× 480 pixels at approximately 10 frames per second, wearable sensors (heart rate, linear acceleration, gyroscope, rotation vector, ambient light) at up to 100 Hz, per-second attention labels on a scale from 1 to 5, emotion annotations across 9 categories, and automatically inferred demographic metadata. "The dataset contains recordings from 57 subjects, organized into three groups of 16–21 students, and comprises 9 distinct educational scenarios, ranging from passive learning settings (lectures) to highly interactive activities (robotics experimentation)."
requirements: Synchronized multimodal recordings with per-second attention labels and demographic metadata for subgroup-aware modeling
constraints: Approximately 95% of subjects were classified as white (Caucasian), leading to the exclusion of race as a fairness axis due to this imbalance
Demographic attributes are automatically inferred rather than self-reported
The authors note its real-world setting, demographic imbalance, and the subjectivity of human annotations introduce realistic sources of bias
target_learners: classroom students across secondary and higher education age groups (13–44)
target_learning_goals: continuous estimation of student attention during passive and interactive learning activities
examples: Used in this study with subject-level splits (39 train, 9 validation, 9 test subjects), 10-second rolling windows, and inverse-frequency weighting for imbalanced attention labels
key_sources: Christoforos Fragkiadakis, Seyed Sahand Mohammadi Ziabari, and Ali Mohammed Mansoor Alsahag. (2026). Fairness-Aware Multimodal Transformer Modeling for Real-Time Student Attention Estimation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02232

article_title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: Discovery-synthesis split: system initiative over domain discovery, author initiative over narrative synthesis
description: The article's organizing design framework divides cognitive labor in AI-assisted writing: the system takes initiative only over domain discovery, where the Illusion of Explanatory Depth renders authors unable to act for themselves, while the author retains full initiative over narrative synthesis. The authors argue the cognitive work of transforming knowledge into one's own prose is itself the mechanism through which deeper understanding forms, grounding the framework in the knowledge-transforming model of written composition. They propose it generalizes to journalism and documentary filmmaking, with parameters such as cue aggressiveness and source traceability calibrated to each domain's epistemic conditions.
requirements: A domain where practitioners face blind spots they cannot self-diagnose and where voice, interpretation, and judgment constitute the output's core value
constraints: The authors state generalizing the split is not plug-and-play: a journalist on deadline has a narrower discovery window, and an academic in their own specialty faces a shallower IOED
target_learners: Creative writers and knowledge workers producing domain-specific work in unfamiliar domains
target_learning_goals: Knowledge-transforming: synthesizing unfamiliar specialized domain facts into authentic prose
examples: VeriForge implements the split by having the system monitor drafts and surface highlights while authors alone write and integrate narrative prose
key_sources: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698

article_title: Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning?
citation: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017
title: Definition and taxonomy of discovery-learning conditions (unassisted vs. enhanced)
description: The article defines discovery learning as occurring "whenever the learner is not provided with the target information or conceptual understanding and must find it independently and with only the provided materials." It organizes the heterogeneous literature into unassisted types (unassisted, invention, matched probes, simulation, work with a naive peer) and enhanced types (generation, elicited explanation, guided discovery), each coded as moderators in the two meta-analyses. This taxonomy underpins the central finding that guidance, not discovery per se, determines effectiveness.
requirements: Studies must provide useable statistical information and comparable conditions differing in type of instruction
constraints: The field lacks a precise definition; at times the discovery condition is defined more by the comparison method than by the learning methods themselves
target_learning_goals: domain learning across math, computer skills, science, problem solving, physical/motor, and verbal/social skills
examples: The meta-analyses coded 580 unassisted comparisons and 360 enhanced comparisons using this taxonomy, with inter-coder kappa of .87
key_sources: Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does Discovery-Based Instruction Enhance Learning? Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(1), 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0021017

article_title: Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators.
citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209
title: Discriminative contrast hypothesis of the interleaving effect
description: The discriminative contrast hypothesis (Kang & Pashler, 2012) holds that interleaving benefits inductive learning because juxtaposing items of different categories close together in time promotes "discriminative contrasts of subsequent items, which might benefit inductive learning." It is based on the observation that temporal spacing between items hinders inductive learning in interleaved conditions and has no advantage in blocked conditions. The meta-analysis coded temporal spacing between successive items to test this assumption.
requirements: Items of different categories must be juxtaposed closely in time for discriminative contrasts to arise
constraints: The hypothesis addresses temporal spacing, which the meta-analysis analyzed separately because only four studies fell in the spaced categories
target_learning_goals: inductive category learning and discrimination between categories
examples: The meta-analysis coded the time elapsed between presentations of successive items into three categories, with immediate succession as the reference category.
key_sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin. https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000209

article_title: A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy
citation: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis of the interleaving effect
description: Proposed by Kang and Pashler (2012), this account explains the interleaving benefit through "increased opportunities to compare and contrast exemplars if they are seen side by side or adjacent in a series". It explains why spacing items out can be harmful to interleaving — the review notes the two phenomena are not additive — and why interleaving unrelated items (e.g. science terms with vocabulary) is not beneficial. The review treats it as the leading candidate explanation alongside attentional accounts.
requirements: Materials must be related category exemplars such that juxtaposition creates meaningful contrast between categories
constraints: Spacing and interleaving are not additive; spacing items out can reduce or eliminate the interleaving benefit
target_learning_goals: inductive concept learning and categorisation
transfer to novel exemplars
examples: Zulkiply and Burt (2013a) went as far as to call interleaving 'the compare and contrast effect'
key_sources: Jonathan Firth, Ian Rivers and James Boyle. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/rev3.3266

article_title: A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation
citation: Jimmy de la Torre and Chia-Yi Chiu. (2016). A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation. Psychometrika, Volume 81, Issue 2, June 2016. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9467-8
title: Discrimination-index rationale for Q-matrix validation grounded in mathematical proofs of lemmas and a theorem
description: The article supplies the theoretical basis for using its discrimination index as the foundation of a Q-matrix validation method. The abstract states: "The rationale for using the index as the basis for a proposed validation method is provided in the form of mathematical proofs to several relevant lemmas and a theorem." The index is defined for CDMs subsumed by the generalized DINA model, so the framework is general rather than tied to one specific CDM.
requirements: Applicability to the class of CDMs subsumed by the generalized deterministic input, noisy “and” gate model
target_learners: Examinees assessed with cognitive diagnosis models
target_learning_goals: Fine-grained diagnostic assessment of multiple discrete skills or attributes
key_sources: Jimmy de la Torre and Chia-Yi Chiu. (2016). A General Method of Empirical Q-matrix Validation. Psychometrika, Volume 81, Issue 2, June 2016. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-015-9467-8

article_title: Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus
citation: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283
title: Direct a young child's behaviour only within a joint focus of attention to support vocabulary learning
description: The article concludes that adult directives can aid early word learning when they follow, rather than redirect, the child's current attention. As the abstract states, "given joint focus, directing a 13-month-old's behaviour can have beneficial effects on subsequent vocabulary development". Caregivers and educators should therefore embed behavioural directives in activities the child is already attending to, rather than pulling attention to new objects or activities.
requirements: The adult must establish or share the child's current focus of attention before issuing the directive
constraints: Evidence comes from a correlational study of twelve mother-child dyads observed at 1;1 with vocabulary measured at 1;10; the article does not establish causation
target_learning_goals: Productive early vocabulary
examples: The study distinguished FOLLOW-prescriptives, which followed the child's focus of attention, from LEADING-prescriptives, which changed it, and found only the FOLLOW type correlated with later vocabulary
key_sources: Nameera Akhtar, Frances Dunham and Philip J. Dunham. (1991). Directive interactions and early vocabulary development: the role of joint attentional focus. Journal of Child Language, Volume 18, Issue 1, pp. 41-49. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900013283

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis of the interleaving benefit
description: The article's central explanatory account: interleaving benefits inductive learning because it juxtaposes exemplars of different categories, which highlights the differences that separate categories and supports discrimination learning. The authors define it as the idea "that we refer to as the discriminative-contrast hypothesis", building on Kang and Pashler (2012) and Goldstone's observation that frequent alternation highlights features distinguishing categories. The three experiments test its strong predictions within interleaved conditions.
requirements: Applies to inductive category learning where the goal is classifying new exemplars into appropriate categories, so knowing what distinguishes categories is crucial
constraints: The authors note simultaneous presentation results may not extend to single presentations because simultaneous presentation places greater demands on working memory
target_learners: adult learners studying naturalistic visual categories
target_learning_goals: inductive concept and category learning
discrimination between similar categories
examples: Experiment 1 held total spacing constant and showed that only the condition interrupting between-category juxtaposition impaired performance
key_sources: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7

article_title: Effective differentiation Practices:A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education
citation: Deunk, M. I., Jacobse, A. E., de Boer, H., Doolaard, S., & Bosker, R. J. (2018). Effective differentiation Practices: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education. Educational Research Review, 24, 31-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.02.002
title: Taxonomy of differentiation practices in primary education by implementation form
description: The review organizes differentiation practices in primary education by implementation form, distinguishing computerized systems used as a differentiation tool, differentiation as part of a broader program or reform, and between- or within-class homogeneous ability grouping. The abstract states "This systematic review gives an overview of the effects of differentiation practices on language and math performance in primary education," synthesizing empirical studies since 1995 and extracting 78 effect sizes across these practice forms.
requirements: Practices must be classifiable by their implementation form (technology-based tool, embedded in broader program, or ability grouping) to be compared
constraints: Scope limited to cognitive effects on language and math performance in primary education
target_learning_goals: language performance
mathematics performance
key_sources: Deunk, M. I., Jacobse, A. E., de Boer, H., Doolaard, S., & Bosker, R. J. (2018). Effective differentiation Practices: A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies on the cognitive effects of differentiation practices in primary education. Educational Research Review, 24, 31-54. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2018.02.002

article_title: Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components
citation: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6
title: Use discipline-independent online SRL training coupled with mobile-app diaries to reach more students than face-to-face or discipline-dependent formats
description: The article recommends overcoming the reach limits of existing SRL training formats: "Face-to-face training, discipline-dependent training, and paper-and-pencil diaries are limited in the number of students they can reach." The study implemented discipline-independent online training together with novel mobile-app based diaries, and the combined condition improved more than other conditions, supporting this scalable delivery approach for improving SRL.
requirements: Online delivery of training plus a mobile-app based daily diary
target_learners: University students from mixed disciplines and study modes
target_learning_goals: Improved self-regulated learning
examples: The randomised control study implemented the discipline-independent online training and mobile-app diaries with 73 university students
key_sources: Broadbent, J., Panadero, E. & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, M. (2020). Effects of mobile-app learning diaries vs online training on specific self-regulated learning components. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09781-6

article_title: Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems
citation: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714
title: Develop students' evaluative expertise by providing direct authentic evaluative experience
description: The article argues that the evaluative capacities underlying self-monitoring — appreciating high quality, comparing one's work objectively with that standard, and holding tactics for modifying work — are learnable. It states: "It is argued that these skills can be developed by providing direct authentic evaluative experience for students." Instructional design should therefore build in opportunities for students to make and refine quality judgments themselves.
requirements: Instructional systems must make explicit provision for the acquisition of evaluative expertise
target_learners: students producing work judged against quality criteria
target_learning_goals: developing evaluative skill, appreciation of quality standards, and modification tactics
key_sources: Sadler, D. R. (1989). Formative assessment and the design of instructional systems. Instructional Science, 18, 119–144. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00117714

article_title: Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Liu S, Yu Q, Li Z, Cunha PM, Zhang Y, Kong Z, Lin W, Chen S and Cai Y (2020) Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis. Front. Psychol. 11:554915. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.554915
title: Diamond's three-factor model of executive functions (inhibitory control, working memory, cognitive flexibility)
description: The article adopts Diamond's three-factor model of executive functions as its organizing framework, under which "inhibitory control, working memo ry, and cognitive ﬂexibility are the three core executive funct ions (EF)". These three cognitive abilities are said to work together to influence higher-order executive functions such as reasoning, planning, and problem solving. The review restricts its analysis to these three components because longitudinal evidence linking physical activity to higher-level executive functions in children is scarce. Inhibitory control is defined as the ability to suppress irrelevant reactions, working memory as registering information and performing cognitive operations on it, and cognitive flexibility as the ability to move flexibly to a new situation.
requirements: Outcome measures must target at least one of the three core components: inhibitory control, working memory, or cognitive flexibility
constraints: The review excludes higher-order executive functions such as decision-making and reasoning due to limited longitudinal evidence in children and adolescents
target_learning_goals: inhibitory control
working memory
cognitive flexibility
examples: The meta-analysis pooled effects separately for each of the three EF components across 36 RCTs
key_sources: Liu S, Yu Q, Li Z, Cunha PM, Zhang Y, Kong Z, Lin W, Chen S and Cai Y (2020) Effects of Acute and Chronic Exercises on Executive Function in Children and Adolescents: A Systemic Review and Meta-Analysis. Front. Psychol. 11:554915. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.554915

article_title: How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children
citation: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x
title: Four-condition dichotic listening paradigm with mTRF speech-envelope reconstruction
description: A child-appropriate EEG paradigm in which participants attend to an English narrative in one ear while ignoring interference in the other across four conditions: Single talker (no interference), English–English, English–Latin, and English–Musical Rain. Backward mTRF decoding models reconstruct attended and unattended speech envelopes from 60-channel EEG, with reconstruction accuracy (Pearson's r) as the index of attentional encoding. The article notes the method "maps all available neural data simultaneously" and is suited to multi-channel EEG and natural speech.
requirements: A minimum threshold of five minutes of data per condition for input to the mTRF toolbox
Children old enough to perform selective attention tasks reliably; a minimum age of 6 is recommended in the literature the article cites
constraints: Epoch rejection removed 16.33% of data overall, varying by condition from 12.77% to 19.68%
target_learning_goals: measuring neural encoding of attended versus unattended speech
examples: Each target story was split into two 3.3-minute blocks with 10 comprehension questions per block; Musical Rain was generated from the target sentences' temporal envelopes filled with synthesized vowel fragments
key_sources: Jacqueline Phelps, Adam Attaheri & Mirjana Bozic. (2022). How bilingualism modulates selective attention in children. Scientific Reports 12:6381. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-09989-x

article_title: Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children
citation: Rouse, H. L., & Fantuzzo, J. W. (2006). Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children. School Psychology Review, 35(3), 341-355. http://dibels.uoregon.edu
title: Use brief fluency-based early literacy screeners such as the end-of-kindergarten DIBELS subtests to identify at-risk urban kindergartners and guide classroom intervention
description: The article recommends using the three end-of-kindergarten DIBELS subtests as a screening and progress-monitoring tool in urban districts, because the subtests demonstrated concurrent, convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity for a low-income, predominantly minority sample. The authors state the subtests "could be used to guide classroom-based instmction and intervention" and that the short, fluency-based format supports frequent administration and measurement of response to intervention.
requirements: Administration by trained school personnel, as the article notes administration does not require intensive training and can be done by regular school personnel
constraints: Findings are qualified to urban public school kindergarten children; the study sample did not allow exploration of validity for English language learners
target_learners: Kindergarten children in large urban public school districts, primarily low-income and minority students
target_learning_goals: Early literacy skills: alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, and alphabetic principle (decoding)
examples: The district administered DIBELS districtwide three times per year (October, February, May) by trained early childhood staff; the study validated the three end-of-kindergarten subtests against teacher report, individual assessments, and nationally standardized tests.
key_sources: Rouse, H. L., & Fantuzzo, J. W. (2006). Validity of the Dynamic Indicators for Basic Early Literacy Skills as an Indicator of Early Literacy for Urban Kindergarten Children. School Psychology Review, 35(3), 341-355. https://doi.org/10.1080/02796015.2006.12087971

article_title: Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt
citation: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w
title: Diversion explanation of the seductive details effect
description: Within the cognitive theory of multimedia learning, the diversion explanation holds that seductive details harm learning when learners "build mental models around irrelevant contents (included in seductive details) rather than around the pertinent content". Diversion is stronger when learners erroneously consider the irrelevant content relevant, activating and integrating inadequate prior knowledge. This study designed an irrelevance prompt to make diversion unlikely and found supporting evidence, concluding diversion rather than disruption mainly drives the effect.
requirements: Learners must allocate attention to the seductive information (distraction) before diversion can occur, per the article's framing of distraction as a necessary pre-condition.
constraints: The article notes diversion is hard to sharply distinguish from disruption empirically; the irrelevance prompt may in principle have affected both processes.
target_learners: students learning with multimedia instruction containing interesting but irrelevant details
target_learning_goals: recall and comprehension of pertinent instructional content
examples: Learners who thought the details were relevant reported longer processing times on them and had worse recall outcomes.
key_sources: Kienitz, A., Krebs, M.-C., & Eitel, A. (2023). Seductive details hamper learning even when they do not disrupt. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09632-w

article_title: Stealth assessment of creativity in a physics video game
citation: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940
title: Score creativity from both novel solutions and creative products, distinguishing creativity from game exploitation
description: When assessing creativity in games, in-game behaviors that violate the rules and mechanics of the game should not count as evidence for creativity, because creativity requires both novelty and relevance/appropriateness. The article illustrates this with the Need Fulcrum level, where drawing lines under the ball solved the level without using any agents of force and motion; this hack was tried by many students and thus was neither original nor rule-abiding. Stealth assessment must differentiate creative solutions from solutions that exploit game features.
requirements: Scoring rules must encode both novelty and appropriateness relative to the rules and mechanics of the game
constraints: Differentiating creative solutions from exploitative ones is level-specific; the authors note establishing indicators and scoring rules can be tricky depending on the nature of a given level
target_learners: 8th and 9th grade students playing educational games
target_learning_goals: creativity (originality, fluency, flexibility)
examples: In the Need Fulcrum level, a solution drawing lines under the ball without any agent of force and motion was scored as providing no evidence for originality because it violated the game's rules
key_sources: Shute, V. J., & Rahimi, S. (2020). Stealth Assessment of Creativity in a Physics Video Game. Computers in Human Behavior. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563220303940

article_title: Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts
citation: Annette Kujawski Taylor. (2011). Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts. Teaching of Psychology, 38(4), 278-281. https://doi.org/10.1177/0098628311421330
title: Choose text delivery medium on cost and convenience grounds, since comprehension is equivalent when students actually read
description: The article concludes that when students actually sit and read the text, the delivery method does not matter, so instructors may adopt digital texts for their practical advantages. As the author puts it, "there is no pedagogical reason to avoid using digital texts. The convenience, in addition to the cost savings, may be important factors in considering the adoption of digital texts." The real instructional challenge is getting students to read in the first place.
requirements: Students must actually read the assigned text; the equivalence finding applies to students who completed the reading under supervised conditions.
constraints: Findings come from a single laboratory study with unfamiliar microeconomics material and marginally passing quiz scores; reading time was not assessed, so effects of reading time on comprehension remain undetermined.
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of textbook material
long-term retention of course readings
examples: In the study, 74 students were randomly assigned to read a supply-and-demand chapter from either a paperbound or digital text and were quizzed immediately and 1 week later, with no medium differences emerging.
key_sources: Annette Kujawski Taylor. (2011). Students Learn Equally Well From Digital as From Paperbound Texts. Teaching of Psychology, 38(4), 278-281. https://doi.org/10.1177/0098628311421330

article_title: Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study
citation: Yılmaz, E., Yel, S., & Griffiths, M. D. (2022). Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104548
title: Use educational and serious videogames and active traditional games to support children's social problem-solving development
description: Based on their regression findings, the authors recommend that games primarily produced for educational or serious purposes, which positively predicted SPSIC scores, be used "not only for education and knowledge acquisition but also in the development of social problem -solving skills in school settings". They also advise encouraging children to play such games in out-of-school time and to engage in traditional games keeping them physically and mentally active.
requirements: Games must match children's daily-life play rather than researcher-developed single games, per the study's rationale
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and non-experimental, so a direct effect cannot be determined as the article states
target_learning_goals: social problem-solving skills
examples: The regression analyses found serious and educational videogames and action, strategy-intelligent, role-playing and sports traditional games positively predicted SPSIC scores
key_sources: Yılmaz, E., Yel, S., & Griffiths, M. D. (2022). Comparison of children's social problem-solving skills who play videogames and traditional games: A cross-cultural study. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104548

article_title: Individual differences in algebraic cognition: Relation to the approximate number and semantic memory systems
citation: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Rouder Jeffrey N. (2015). Individual Differences in Algebraic Cognition: Relation to the Approximate Number and Sematic Memory Systems. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.07.010
title: Differential cognitive systems account of algebraic competence
description: The article proposes that different brain and cognitive systems support different components of algebraic competence: the approximate number system is engaged in spatial-numerical (coordinate plane) and numerical-only (expression evaluation) quantity judgments, while the hippocampal-dependent semantic memory system supports committing arithmetic facts to long-term memory and forming schema memories for algebra equations. As the authors state, "difficulties in committing addition facts to long-term memory may presage slow formation of memories for the basic structure of algebra equations." The account is grounded in the study's differential regression results and motivates targeted interventions and brain imaging work.
requirements: Assessment of component algebraic skills separately rather than only overall algebra achievement
Control of demographic and domain-general covariates including intelligence, working memory, and symbolic number processing fluency
constraints: The correlational, largely concurrent design means causal relations cannot be inferred
The tasks do not cover all components of algebraic competence, such as factoring and systems of equations
target_learning_goals: Algebraic competence including coordinate plane knowledge, expression evaluation fluency, and equation schema memory
examples: The study developed a new coordinate plane placement task and adapted expression evaluation and equation memory tasks to measure three component algebra skills in 171 ninth graders
key_sources: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Rouder Jeffrey N. (2015). Individual Differences in Algebraic Cognition: Relation to the Approximate Number and Sematic Memory Systems. Journal of experimental child psychology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2015.07.010

article_title: Developmental Gains in Visuospatial Memory Predict Gains in Mathematics Achievement
citation: Li Y, Geary DC (2013) Developmental Gains in Visuospatial Memory Predict Gains in Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(7): e70160. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0070160
title: Differential developmental gains across working memory components change their relative contributions to mathematics learning
description: The article proposes that the three Baddeley-Hitch working memory components—central executive, phonological memory, and visuospatial memory—mature at different rates, so their relative contributions to mathematics achievement shift across development. The authors argue that "differential gains in the central executive, phonological memory, and visuospatial memory could result in across-grade changes in the relative contribution of these components of working memory to mathematics performance." This explains why visuospatial memory relates inconsistently to mathematics in children but consistently in adulthood.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of working memory components across multiple grades to detect differential gains
constraints: The study's non-experimental method does not allow for strong inferences about mechanisms, per the authors
target_learners: children in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
working memory development
examples: The study assessed 177 children's working memory in first and fifth grade and modeled achievement growth from kindergarten to fifth grade
key_sources: Li Y, Geary DC (2013) Developmental Gains in Visuospatial Memory Predict Gains in Mathematics Achievement. PLoS ONE 8(7): e70160. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0070160

article_title: The association between children's numerical magnitude processing and mental multi-digit subtraction
citation: Linsen, S., Verschaffel, L., Reynvoet, B., De Smedt, B. (2014). The Association between Children's Numerical Magnitude Processing and Mental Multi-digit Subtraction. Acta Psychologica. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2013.10.008
title: Strategy categorization of mental multi-digit subtraction by underlying operation: direct subtraction versus indirect addition
description: The article categorizes children's mental multi-digit subtraction strategies by the operation underlying the solution process: direct subtraction strategies, in which the subtrahend is directly subtracted from the minuend, and indirect addition strategies, in which one determines how much needs to be added to the subtrahend to get to the minuend. A rational task analysis indicates indirect addition is particularly efficient when minuend and subtrahend are close, as in "81 - 79 = ?". The study used this taxonomy to construct items eliciting each strategy type.
requirements: Items must be constructed so that subtrahend size relative to the difference and minuend-subtrahend distance elicit the intended strategy
constraints: The article notes a third class, the indirect subtraction strategy, is excluded from this two-type categorization
target_learners: third-grade children in the number domain 20-100
target_learning_goals: mental multi-digit subtraction calculation
examples: The study constructed 32 subtraction items, half designed to elicit indirect addition (small distance, e.g. 72-67) and half direct subtraction (large distance, e.g. 83-27)
key_sources: Linsen, S., Verschaffel, L., Reynvoet, B., De Smedt, B. (2014). The Association between Children's Numerical Magnitude Processing and Mental Multi-digit Subtraction. Acta Psychologica. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actpsy.2013.10.008

article_title: Handwriting Fluency in Children
citation: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127
title: Digitizing-tablet measures of handwriting automaticity (stroke pressure and stroke frequency)
description: This element is the measurement setup used in the study: a digitizing tablet recording stroke pressure and stroke frequency while children perform a copying task, used to index automaticity of handwriting. The abstract states that "automaticity of handwriting, stroke pressure, and stroke frequency were measured on a digitizing tablet, while visual-motor integration and orthographic skills were assessed by means of standardized tests." These process measures entered the SEM model as indicators of automaticity.
requirements: A digitizing tablet and a copying task are needed to capture stroke-level process measures
constraints: Assessed in a cross-sectional design with fourth-grade children copying text
target_learning_goals: assessment of handwriting fluency and its component processes
examples: Handwriting speed and legibility were assessed by means of a copying task.
key_sources: Wicki, Werner; Hurschler Lichtsteiner, Sibylle; Saxer Geiger, Andrea; Müller, Marianne (2014). Handwriting fluency in children. Swiss Journal of Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1024/1421-0185/a000127

article_title: The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children’s Academic and Socioemotional Functioning
citation: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/
title: Integrative conceptual model linking diversity and belongingness perspectives to population stratification
description: The article proposes an integrative conceptual model connecting two developmental perspectives on school racial/ethnic composition. The diversity perspective, drawing on Piagetian disequilibrium, holds that "exposure to diverse worldviews and life perspectives provides opportunities for valuable cognitive exercise," predicting academic gains from heterogeneous student bodies. The belongingness perspective, rooted in attachment theory, holds that meaningful social connections are a fundamental need, predicting socioemotional benefits from same-racial/ethnic peer representation. The model integrates these with a population approach treating race/ethnicity as a marker of position in the U.S. stratification system, hypothesizing suppression effects between the two composition dimensions and moderation by group position.
requirements: Testing requires modeling diversity and proportion same-racial/ethnic peers simultaneously to detect suppression effects
Requires outcome domains disaggregated into academic and socioemotional measures
Requires multiple-group analyses to test stratification-based moderation
constraints: Developed for the transition into elementary school; the authors note the role of diversity and matching might change as children grow and navigate more heterogeneous contexts
Associations are correlational; unobserved confounds cannot be fully ruled out
target_learners: Kindergarten and early elementary school children
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in reading and mathematics
Socioemotional adjustment including externalizing behavior and interpersonal skills
examples: The authors illustrate the model with two Latino students in schools of identical diversity (.66) but different same-racial/ethnic peer representation, showing the two dimensions vary independently
key_sources: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/

article_title: The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children’s Academic and Socioemotional Functioning
citation: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/
title: Design diverse school contexts that also protect a critical mass of same-racial/ethnic peers to support both academic and socioemotional needs
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that school composition policy should pursue both dimensions simultaneously rather than treating diversity and same-racial/ethnic peer representation as competing goals. The authors state: "If school diversity is a compelling state interest, we must not only embrace the benefits of diversity but also acknowledge the advantages of having more same-racial/ethnic peers so that we can better ensure that diverse school contexts support both the academic and socioemotional needs of all U.S. children." This follows from findings that diversity benefits for achievement were strongest when children also had more same-racial/ethnic peers, and that matching independently supported socioemotional adjustment.
requirements: School assignment or composition decisions must attend to both overall student-body diversity and the representation of each child's own racial/ethnic group
Adequate representation of multiple groups is needed so that matching does not come at the cost of diversity
constraints: The National Research Council suggests a minimum racial/ethnic representation threshold of 15% to protect against feelings of isolation, which the authors propose testing in future studies
Benefits for minority children's achievement were not observed in this kindergarten sample, possibly due to limited exposure duration
target_learners: Elementary school children across racial/ethnic groups
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Socioemotional well-being and school belonging
examples: The authors cite the National Research Council's 15% minimum representation threshold used in higher education affirmative action and K-12 race-conscious school assignment decisions as a candidate critical-mass benchmark
key_sources: Benner Aprile D.; Crosnoe Robert. (2011). The Racial/Ethnic Composition of Elementary Schools and Young Children's Academic and Socioemotional Functioning. American Educational Research Journal. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4554342/

article_title: How do different aspects of spatial skills relate to early arithmetic and number line estimation?
citation: Véronique Cornu, Caroline Hornung, Christine Schiltz, Romain Martin. (2017). The predictive role of spatial skills for arithmetic and number line estimation in kindergarten children. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2017.09.002
title: Assess and differentiate specific spatial-skill aspects when predicting or supporting early mathematical development
description: Because spatial skills are non-unitary, assessment and support of early mathematics should distinguish which spatial aspect is being measured or targeted. The study shows spatial orientation predicted both arithmetic and number line estimation, while visuo-motor integration predicted arithmetic, supporting differentiated rather than composite spatial measurement. The authors underline "the importance to differentiate within the construct of spatial skills when it comes to understanding numerical development".
requirements: Separate measures of distinct spatial aspects (e.g., spatial orientation, spatial visualization, visuo-motor integration) rather than one global spatial score
constraints: Evidence comes from kindergarten children and a four-month longitudinal window; predictive, not causal, relations
target_learning_goals: early arithmetic
number line estimation
examples: The study administered three distinct spatial tasks at Time 1 and used hierarchical regression to identify which aspects predicted Time 2 arithmetic and number line estimation
key_sources: Véronique Cornu, Caroline Hornung, Christine Schiltz, Romain Martin. (2017). The predictive role of spatial skills for arithmetic and number line estimation in kindergarten children. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogdev.2017.09.002

article_title: Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing
citation: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17
title: Differential aging account: processing speed mediates fluency changes asymmetrically across letter and category tasks
description: The article proposes that aging adversely affects some but not all cognitive domains, and that age-related decline in processing speed contributes to age-related changes in fluency in task-specific ways. For category fluency, slowing partially drives the age-related decline, though a significant portion of the decline remains independent of processing speed. For letter fluency, the relationship is reversed: slow processing masks an enhancement that occurs during the transition from young to middle age. In both cases the age-related change is independent of IQ as measured by the NART. The account holds that decline in one domain may contribute to the apparent decline in another domain that may otherwise remain stationary or even improve with aging.
requirements: Assessment of both fluency types alongside a processing speed measure to detect the differential mediation pattern
constraints: Derived from a cross-sectional design, so results may be confounded by a cohort effect across generations
Sample was highly educated and healthy, which may not represent the true population
target_learners: adults across the lifespan from young adulthood to old age
target_learning_goals: understanding which cognitive domains decline, remain stable, or improve with normal aging
distinguishing normal age-related cognitive change from impairment warranting further evaluation
examples: Older adults would be able to generate more words in the specified time period if they were not slower than younger adults, per the authors' interpretation of the letter fluency ANCOVA result
key_sources: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17

article_title: The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults
citation: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8.
title: Dichotic listening preexposure paradigm with CS-scoreboard instrumental conditioning task
description: An experimental apparatus and procedure for studying latent inhibition in adult humans. Subjects attended to one ear of a dichotic tape recording, counting repetitions of paired nonsense syllables, while a white-noise CS was superimposed on one track. In the testing phase, subjects watched a scoreboard and pressed a button whenever they expected a point to be raised, aiming to bring their score down to zero. The criterion for learning was the number of CSs to termination of the experiment, and eye movements were monitored via a mirror to verify which ear was attended.
requirements: Subjects must attend to the designated ear during preexposure, verified by monitoring eye movements
constraints: The experiment terminated either after five consecutive correct presses to the CS or after 31 presentations of the CS
target_learning_goals: learning the rule connecting a white-noise CS to scoreboard point changes
examples: Forty undergraduates were randomly divided into four groups, with the restriction that two males and eight females be included in each group
key_sources: A. Ginton, G. Urca, and R. E. Lubow. (1975). The effects of preexposure to a nonattended stimulus on subsequent learning: Latent inhibition in adults. Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society, 1975, Vol. 5 (1), 5-8. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03336682

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: Digital policies should attend to the learning needs of those on the margins of access through affordable Internet and appropriate, timely, consistent digital learning opportunities
description: The article argues that digital inclusion policy equating access to a connection with inclusion masks persistent inequalities in use and experience. It recommends that policy be designed for those on the margins "who will benefit most from affordable Internet and from appropriate, timely, and consistent opportunities for digital learning," grounded in ethnographic evidence that access is contingent and precarious.
requirements: Policy must be informed by the actual experiences of people at the margins of digital access, not only by model-user imaginaries.
constraints: The article focuses on the Canadian policy context and a single community-based computing site; recommendations are framed for adult educators and policy makers in that setting.
target_learners: Adults on the margins of digital access, including low-income adults, new immigrants, and seniors
target_learning_goals: Digital literacy and meaningful participation in online environments
examples: The Digital Café provided free access, computers, and just-in-time volunteer tutor support for tasks like email, job applications, and government forms.
key_sources: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: The Digital Café: a drop-in public-access computing and learning space
description: The Digital Café is a two-hour weekly drop-in program in a suburb of Vancouver, BC, offering free Internet, computers, and just-in-time volunteer tutor support for tasks such as email, job applications, online government forms, and social media. It began in 2008 as a Community Access Program site. The room was often full before the 3 p.m. start time with adults between 35 and 75, mostly new immigrants.
requirements: Volunteer tutors to provide one-to-one just-in-time support; a sociable, informal atmosphere (coffee, tea, snacks).
constraints: The article notes the program operated on a shoestring and that participants' security of access rested precariously on the availability of working computers and volunteer tutors.
target_learners: Adults aged 35-75, mostly new immigrants, referred by employment or social service agencies or the library
target_learning_goals: Everyday computer tasks, email, job applications, government forms, and social media use
examples: Malek attended almost weekly over a year, progressing from being unable to use a computer to emailing family and using Facebook, before his fluency faltered when his laptop and home connection failed.
key_sources: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334

article_title: Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children With Mathematical Learning Disability
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046
title: Distinct-deficits account: retrieval, procedural, and number-processing deficits arise from partly separable mechanisms rather than one fundamental magnitude deficit
description: The article frames competing accounts of mathematical learning disability: Butterworth's hypothesis that a fundamental deficit in representing and processing numerical magnitude underlies most deficits, versus the possibility of several distinct deficits or delays. The study tests this by asking whether retrieval, procedural, number sets, and number line deficits co-occur, predicting that "If the mechanisms contributing to the procedural, number processing, and retrieval deficits and delays are distinct, then some children should show one or two of these deficits but not all of them." The longitudinal dissociation findings support the distinct-deficits view.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of multiple mathematical cognition tasks in the same children to test whether deficits co-occur or dissociate
constraints: Conclusions drawn from children in one school district followed from kindergarten to fourth grade
target_learners: elementary school children with mathematical learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: arithmetic fact retrieval
arithmetic procedural competence
numerical magnitude processing
examples: The study separated LA children into mild and severe fact retrieval subgroups and compared their trajectories on retrieval, procedural, number sets, and number line measures
key_sources: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., & Bailey, D. H. (2012). Fact Retrieval Deficits in Low Achieving Children and Children with Mathematical Learning Disability. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 45(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219410392046

article_title: Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood
citation: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007
title: Difference-driven account of small-group collaboration: differing opinions drive individual gains while joint constructions play a tangential role
description: The article's organizing account holds that individual understanding is promoted through exchanging differing opinions, while the joint analyses groups construct play a tangential role. As the abstract states, "individual understanding can be promoted through exchanging differing opinions, the joint analyses that groups construct while collaborating play a tangential role". Acceptance of constructions depends on reflection and reconciliation triggered by difference, sometimes occurring after the group session. The reported study tested whether this account extends to adolescence and early adulthood.
requirements: Group dialogue must involve the exchange of differing opinions for the mechanism to operate
constraints: Evidence base in the available text is research with middle to late childhood plus the reported 10-to-22 sample
target_learning_goals: individual conceptual understanding gained through small-group collaboration
examples: The reported study of 46 pairs aged 10 to 22 on the falling-objects task confirmed the key role of differing opinions and the limited relevance of collaborative constructions
key_sources: Howe, Christine; Zachariou, Antonia. (2017). Small-group collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition: The processes of growth during adolescence and early adulthood. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.10.007

article_title: Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice What Adults Miss
citation: Plebanek, D. J., & Sloutsky, V. M. (2017). Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice what Adults Miss. Psychological Science, 28(6), 723-732. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617693005
title: Developmental shift from distributed to selective attention account
description: The article proposes that early attention is distributed across multiple stimulus dimensions because attention-control circuits are immature, so young children process task-irrelevant information well; with maturation, top-down selective attention develops, bringing efficiency for relevant information at the cost of attenuated processing of non-selected information. The article states that "Distributed attention early in development (stemming from the immaturity of attention-control circuits, Posner & Rothbart, 2007) results in greater processing of task-irrelevant information than more mature selective attention." Selection is described as supplementing, not replacing, diffuse attention within an attentional hierarchy.
requirements: Immature attention-control circuits in early development for the distributed-attention prediction; mature circuits for the selective-attention prediction
constraints: Young children are unlikely to exhibit top-down selectivity because supporting neural circuits are not fully developed; adults may distribute attention under high task demand such as high working memory load, and aging may also weaken top-down control
target_learning_goals: Processing of task-relevant and task-irrelevant information
development of selective attention
examples: Experiment 1 cued/uncued change detection and Experiment 2 visual search with recognition of relevant and irrelevant features, both showing the predicted reversal
key_sources: Plebanek, D. J., & Sloutsky, V. M. (2017). Costs of Selective Attention: When Children Notice what Adults Miss. Psychological Science, 28(6), 723-732. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617693005

article_title: Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection
citation: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002
title: Insert a period of distraction before idea selection to improve selection of one's most creative idea
description: When learners have generated multiple ideas and must choose which to pursue, the article recommends a brief period of distraction during which unconscious thought can operate, rather than immediate selection or deliberate conscious deliberation. Participants "who had unconsciously thought about their ideas, however, were able to select their most creative and least creative idea from several self-generated ideas", whereas immediate and conscious-thought participants performed poorly at selection. The article presents this as "a means to enhance individuals' creative performance".
requirements: A set of self-generated ideas to choose among, and a roughly 2-minute unrelated distracting task to prevent task-relevant conscious thought
constraints: The benefit appeared for idea selection, not for the number or average creativity of generated ideas; the proposed evaluative-tagging mechanism is acknowledged as speculative
target_learning_goals: selecting one's most creative idea for further elaboration and implementation
examples: In both experiments, participants first listed ideas for 2 min, then unconscious-thought-condition participants performed a rapid circle-clicking distraction task for 2 min before selecting their most creative idea.
key_sources: Ritter, S.M.; van Baaren, R.B.; Dijksterhuis, A.J. (2012). Creativity: The role of unconscious processes in idea generation and idea selection. Thinking Skills and Creativity, 7, 21-27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2011.12.002

article_title: Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence
citation: Thillay A, Roux S, Gissot V, Carteau-Martin I, Knight RT, Bonnet-Brilhault F and Bidet-Caulet A (2015) Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:519. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00519
title: Distinct brain maturation trajectories account: sustained attention matures with frontal cortical development while prediction is mature by age 12
description: The article proposes that sustained attention and prediction, though both frontal-dependent optimization processes, follow distinct developmental trajectories through adolescence. Sustained attention continues to mature after age 12, evidenced by improved detection performance and "a frontal shift in P3 and CNV topographies with increasing age", whereas "predictive processing appeared to be mature at age 12". The account attributes the difference to a larger and longer recruitment of the frontal cortex when attention is sustained than during simple predictive processing, with prediction maintenance possibly achieved at lower hierarchical levels such as visual areas.
requirements: EEG recording with tasks that separately load on sustained attention and on manipulated target predictability, as in the visual target detection paradigm used
constraints: The study's gender distribution was biased towards males in the three subsamples
The authors note the study would have been stronger with larger samples, though effects showed large effect sizes
target_learning_goals: sustained attention
predictive processing
proactive cognitive control
examples: EEG recorded in 36 participants aged 12–24 in three age groups performing a visual target detection task with random versus predicted targets
key_sources: Thillay A, Roux S, Gissot V, Carteau-Martin I, Knight RT, Bonnet-Brilhault F and Bidet-Caulet A (2015) Sustained attention and prediction: distinct brain maturation trajectories during adolescence. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 9:519. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2015.00519

article_title: Seeing What We Build Together: Distributed Multimedia Learning Environments for Transformative Communications
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Seeing What We Build Together: Distributed Multimedia Learning Environments for Transformative Communications. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 3(3), pp.285-299. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190574
title: Distributed multimedia learning environments grounded in the social and material embeddedness of communication
description: The article proposes that distributed multimedia learning environments, delivered via broadband telepresence, can establish transformative communications for learning. Its central design argument is that such environments succeed only when they 'adequally acknowledg[e] the social and material embeddedness of everyday communication' — that is, when the technical design respects that real communication is situated in social relationships and material settings rather than being context-free information transfer.
requirements: Broadband telepresence infrastructure capable of supporting distributed multimedia interaction among learners
target_learning_goals: Sustaining transformative communication for collaborative learning
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1994). Seeing What We Build Together: Distributed Multimedia Learning Environments for Transformative Communications. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 3(3), pp.285-299. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190574

article_title: Teacher–Student Dialogue During Classroom Teaching: Does It Really Impact on Student Outcomes?
citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Turn-level and lesson-level dialogue coding scheme adapted from Hennessy et al. (2016)
description: An observational scheme coding every speaker turn for codes such as ELI, EL, REI, RE, OI, UC, Q, SC, RC, RB and RW, plus five holistic lesson-level ratings (Aims, Monitoring, Reflection, Talk Rules, Student Participation). The article reports that "Video-recorded dialogue was analyzed using a scheme based on work reported by Hennessy, Rojas-Drummond and colleagues", with reliability checks on 9952 turns yielding Pearson rs from .65 to 1.00 (M=.79).
requirements: Video recordings with teacher and ambient microphones
Independent coding of lessons by two researchers for reliability checking
constraints: CI and RC were seldom detected and coordination codes were dropped from further analysis
Talk Rules ratings were discounted because 89% of lessons were rated 0
target_learning_goals: Characterizing the quality of teacher-student classroom dialogue
examples: A teacher turn praising a student and elaborating the one-speaker-at-a-time rule was coded A plus EL
key_sources: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1

article_title: Apprenticeship as a developmental mechanism in argumentation skill development
citation: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218
title: Dialogical model of argument skill development (social-to-individual passage)
description: The dissertation discusses a dialogical model of argument skill development in which higher-order intellectual skills pass "from a social to individual level": engagement in dialogic argumentation with partners, even similarly skilled ones, fosters individual argument skill. The finding that both experimental and comparison groups advanced in individual dialogic argument skills is presented as support for this model, alongside the apprenticeship account.
requirements: Learners must engage in dialogic argumentation on controversial issues, with assessments of individual skill before and after engagement.
constraints: The abstract notes the theoretical significance of the results was discussed in relation to both an apprenticeship model and a dialogical model; it does not adjudicate between them.
target_learning_goals: individual dialogic argument skill
transfer of argument skill to individual performance
examples: Both the apprenticeship group and the same-ability comparison group advanced in individual dialogic argument skills following their engagement in argumentation.

citation: MULLER MIRZA, Nathalie et al. (2007). Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo. International journal of computer-supported collaborative learning, vol. 2, n° 2-3, p. 247–272. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9021-5
