description: Digalo is a graphical tool that the article uses as its worked example of computer-supported collaborative learning. The title names it directly: "An example with Digalo", positioned within "Using graphical tools in a phased activity". The article's keywords list "Argumentation" and "TIC" (ICT), indicating that Digalo serves argumentation activity supported by technology. In the wiki, Digalo functions as an instructional component: a shared graphical medium around which learners' dialogical activity is organized across activity phases.

target_learning_goals: dialogical skills
argumentation
examples: The article presents Digalo as its example graphical tool deployed in a phased activity for dialogical skills.

article_title: A prism of CSCL research
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2010). A prism of CSCL research. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-010-9087-3
title: Distributed leadership as a group-level collaborative process extending the theory of group cognition
description: The editorial describes distributed leadership as a reciprocal or interactive definition in which leadership necessarily involves uptake or influence on followers, making it a group-level phenomenon rather than a property assigned to individuals. By combining quantitative and qualitative analyses, Gressick and Derry distinguish different specific forms of leadership with different emergent patterns of distribution. The editorial states the study "extends the theory of group cognition by specifying forms of distributed leadership as a collaborative process at the group unit of analysis."
requirements: Analysis at the group unit of analysis rather than the individual
Groups allowed to interact without assigned leadership roles
constraints: Studied with university students in a regular semester-long course taking place largely online
target_learners: University students in online or blended courses
target_learning_goals: Collaborative learning processes
Group leadership and coordination
examples: Gressick and Derry's semester-long online university course study distinguishing specific forms of leadership with different emergent patterns of distribution

article_title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
citation: Pifarré, M. & Kleine Staarman, J. (2011). Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together. International Journal of Computer Supported Collaborative Learning, 6(2), 187-205. https://www.springer.com/journal/11412
title: Dialogic space and intersubjectivity as a framework for analysing wiki-supported collaborative learning
description: The article adopts a dialogic perspective, drawing on Wegerif's notion of a "dialogic space" — the social realm within which people think and act collectively — and on intersubjectivity, the process of developing communality in joint activity through reciprocal perspective setting and taking. It applies Mercer's three-part typology of talk (Disputational, Cumulative, Exploratory) as a heuristic framework to characterise wiki interaction, arguing this dialogic approach is needed to capture the collaborative dimension of computer-supported collaborative learning and to help educators diagnose and scaffold missing aspects of students' collaboration.
requirements: Participants must develop an intersubjective orientation towards each other's perspectives for collaborative knowledge co-construction
constraints: The typology is used as a heuristic frame of reference, not a validated coding scheme in this study
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
reasoning and argumentation in science writing
examples: The study analysed two groups of six students' negotiation-space episodes using the talk typology

article_title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
citation: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y
title: Dialogism plus a cohesion-based model of discourse as the theoretical foundation for assessing CSCL collaboration
description: The article grounds its collaboration assessment in a joint theoretical frame: dialogism together with "a cohesion-based model of discourse". It treats collaboration as the intertwining of ideas or points of view among participants, "a central element of dialogue performed in CSCL environments". This frame motivates both computational models the article proposes and validates for collaboration assessment.
requirements: Collaboration must be analyzed as dialogue in which ideas and points of view intertwine among participants, as the article defines it.
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge building in CSCL environments
key_sources: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y

article_title: Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, & Gerry Stahl. (2018). Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 359–364. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9291-0
title: When digital resources replace the textbook as the main resource, designers and teachers must establish additional supports and scaffolds
description: The editorial argues that the sequential organization of textbooks historically provided well-established structures for student actions, but "when other resources become more important, designers, teachers, and students need to establish additional forms of supports and scaffolds for learning." Working with digital resources makes students' and teachers' tasks more complex and in need of more social and cognitive framing. The first two papers of the issue address how to support students working with digital resources.
requirements: Additional social and cognitive framing of tasks when learning is embedded in digital environments and infrastructures
target_learners: K-12 and upper secondary students working with digital resources
target_learning_goals: sensemaking with computational artifacts
digital literacy
conceptual understanding of science
examples: Ingulfsen et al. supported students interpreting real-time graphs; Solli et al. structured Gephi use through six scaffolding activities
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, & Gerry Stahl. (2018). Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 359–364. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9291-0

article_title: Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study
citation: Saqr, M., & López-Pernas, S. (2021). Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09356-4
title: Diffusion-based centrality framework for measuring uptake in CSCL discourse graphs
description: A framework representing threaded CSCL discussion as a directed post-reply network in which centrality measures operationalize the uptake of ideas and stimulation of further discussion. It combines diffusion-specific measures — "Maximum Neighborhood Component (MNC) is the cardinality of connected neighboring nodes excluding the target node", coreness ("similar to H-index"), cross clique connectivity, and diffusion degree — with traditional degree, closeness, betweenness and eigenvector centralities, positioning uptake capability as a function of position, connectedness and embeddedness in the network.
requirements: A graph representation of post-reply interactions with source, target, and thread structure
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction and argumentation
examples: In the article's fictional scenario, node G in the network core achieved the highest diffusion centrality while the highest-degree node A ranked only third
key_sources: Saqr, M., & López-Pernas, S. (2021). Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09356-4

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Assess the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes with theoretically refined, operationalized dimensions of interaction rather than coding alone.
description: The editorial reports that Meier, Spada and Rummel differentiated as many as nine dimensions of interaction for quantitative analysis, derived through bottom-up qualitative content analysis refined by top-down theory-informed considerations. Once operationalized for reliable application, these dimensions supported a rating scheme whose successful application suggested "such a ranking approach has advantages over coding for many research questions, while still allowing a quantitative comparison of alternative conditions."
requirements: Dimensions must be operationalized for reliable application, deriving from a combination of bottom-up qualitative analysis and top-down theory-informed refinement.
constraints: The rating approach is suggested as advantageous for many research questions; it is applied to dyads of college students engaged in videoconferencing, as the editorial reports.
target_learning_goals: Improving the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes
examples: The rating scheme was developed and successfully applied to assess the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes among dyads of college students engaged in videoconferencing.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8

article_title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
citation: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2
title: Dialogic reflection as reflection occurring through discourse with others in a community
description: The article frames dialogic reflection as reflection occurring in a collaborative context, focusing on "the reflection in a community, that is, 'discourse with others'" (Mann & Walsh, 2013), similar to collaborative reflection and reflection through critical friendship, where participants give voice to their thinking while being heard constructively and critically. As an outcome, whether alternative views and others' perspectives are concerned indicates reflection quality, positioning dialogic reflection above routine/technical or descriptive levels and featuring cycles of weighing claims, exploring alternatives and gaining new insights.
requirements: A collaborative context in which participants' voices are heard in a constructively critical way
constraints: The article focuses on interpersonal reflection in a community rather than intrapersonal reflection
target_learning_goals: reflective thinking
productive classroom discourse
examples: VSDR operationalises this account by mediating students' discourse about classroom talk with visualisations
key_sources: Pengjin Wang · Fan Chen · Deliang Wang · Gaowei Chen (2025). Enhancing students' dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09443-2

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: Two types of conceptual indicators: direct behavioral indicators versus latent constructs inferred from oral and written inputs
description: The review synthesizes the varied conceptual indicators used to model individual participation into two general types. The first, direct behavioral indicators, are "represented by log data or specific, countable behaviors reflecting individual active or passive participation," such as counts of utterances, submissions, shared-document additions, and forum posts. The second type comprises latent constructs inferred from individuals' conversational, physical, and textual inputs, classified (drawing on the reviewed theories) into individual cognitive participation, metacognitive participation, and socioemotional participation, plus coordinative participation for logistics management. The review notes the direct indicators "demonstrate deliberate and intentional engagement in group work but without necessarily interacting with other group members."
requirements: Distinguishing passive attention indicators (logged-in duration, gazing) from active contributions is stated to be critical for modeling participation
constraints: The latent-construct classification is grounded in the theories the reviewed studies themselves used (regulation of learning, Community of Inquiry)
target_learners: collaborative learning researchers and teachers assessing individual participation
target_learning_goals: gauging individual engagement and contribution from process data in collaborative learning
examples: Direct behavioral indicators included the number of utterances, the number of different types of submissions, additions or revisions in a shared document, and post and reply counts in a forum; latent constructs included negotiating ideas, monitoring task understanding, and expressing social support
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: Teaching about complex systems is no simple matter: building effective professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction
citation: Yoon, Susan A.; Anderson, Emma; Koehler-Yom, Jessica; Evans, Chad; Park, Miyoung; Sheldon, Joshua; Schoenfeld, Ilana; Wendel, Daniel J; Scheintaub, Hal; Klopfer, Eric. (2016). Teaching about complex systems is no simple matter: building effective professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9388-7
title: Professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction should provide differentiated opportunities for teachers to build expertise
description: This principle holds that professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction should vary the opportunities offered to teachers to build expertise, matching teachers' differing starting points. The article's abstract lists "providing differentiated opportunities to build expertise" among the instructional supports it demonstrates to be needed for improving implementation of such curricula. It is one of the two teacher-facing supports the 2-year study foregrounds, alongside addressing teacher beliefs.
requirements: Professional development programs must diagnose and respond to differences in teachers' current abilities with computer-supported complex systems curricula, per the study's gathered data on teacher abilities and perceptions.
constraints: The article frames this support as needed for improving implementation of computer-supported complex systems curricula specifically, as demonstrated in its 2-year study.
target_learners: science teachers learning to deliver computer-supported complex systems curricula
target_learning_goals: effective classroom implementation of complex-systems science instruction
examples: The 2-year professional development study gathered data on teachers' abilities and perceptions regarding delivery of computer-supported complex systems curricula, and presented multi-year results demonstrating the need for this support.

article_title: Dynamics of university students’ epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course
citation: Ketonen, E. E., Kruskopf, M., Lonka, K., & Mattlin, M. (2026). Dynamics of university students' epistemic emotions during game-based learning in an international relations course. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09771-2
title: Integrated Diplomacy course design alternating lectures and game sessions
description: A university international relations course built around the board game Diplomacy, with alternating "1.5-hour lectures and 2-hour game sessions" in a weekly cycle of reading, lectures with small-group discussion, game sessions, and online discussion tasks. Students played in two-player teams including a peace-mediator team, a feature added by the teacher; game performance formed one-quarter of course evaluation. Three revised win-conditions correspond to offensive realism, liberal-institutionalism and constructivism.
requirements: Same teacher (a co-author) taught or supervised all course elements
Negotiation success is central, making it a combination of strategy game and conflict negotiation simulation
constraints: Course design allows only a very limited number of participants
Findings are specific to this particular game, as the authors state
target_learning_goals: Understanding international relations concepts such as the security dilemma, trust-building, and diplomatic negotiation
examples: Games were evaluated as one-quarter of the course grade; debriefing sessions at course end collected self-reported emotions including emotional exhaustion.

article_title: The Effects of Group differentiation by students’ learning strategies
citation: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0
title: Differentiation by learning strategies grounded in self-regulated learning and metacognition
description: The article frames differentiation by learning strategies within the self-regulated learning framework of Pintrich and de Groot (1990). Learning strategies encompass metacognitive skills (planning, monitoring, evaluation) and cognitive strategies (rehearsal, elaboration, organizing). The article defines metacognition as "one's ability to regulate cognitive processes" that is "strongly related to learning outcomes", explicitly distinguishing learning strategies from the concept of learning styles, which it rejects citing Kirschner (2017).
requirements: Teachers need good knowledge of how students differ on learning strategies to offer appropriate differentiated instruction
constraints: Learning strategies are subject and situation specific; there is no ground to argue students have one strategy for all subjects
target_learning_goals: Self-regulation, metacognition, and subject-matter learning
examples: The intervention grouped students by five MSLQ learning strategy scales: organization, elaboration, metacognitive self-regulation, time and study environment, and effort regulation
key_sources: Carla Haelermans. (2022). The Effects of Group differentiation by students' learning strategies. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09575-0

article_title: Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images
citation: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0
title: Design educational science images so matched pairs of visual units are in direct spatial placement to support structural alignment
description: The article recommends that when student learning is the priority, image designers should place matched visual units so their correspondences are clear and unobstructed: "If student learning is the main priority, then designers of educational images should aim to support relevant cognition first and foremost." Direct placement minimizes competing matches and facilitates the intended alignment, and the authors argue it "could be applied broadly to increase the effectiveness of educational science images" at little cost to developers.
requirements: Matched pairs should be laid out so horizontal-axis units are stacked vertically and vertical-axis units are placed side by side, yielding direct placement
constraints: Designers may need to preserve realism, capture attention, follow domain visual conventions, or fit pre-specified page dimensions, which can force tradeoffs; supports may be less helpful for highly knowledgeable learners
target_learners: novice learners studying from textbook images
target_learning_goals: structural alignment of matched visual units
comprehension of relational scientific structure in images
examples: The study found 47 of 103 comparison images had direct placements only, while 25 of 103 contained one or more impeded placements; a horse-evolution diagram with vertical layout of vertically oriented bones exemplified impeded placement, while a comparable diagram in another textbook achieved direct placement
key_sources: Benjamin D. Jee, Bryan J. Matlen, Monica Greenlaw, Nina Simms, Dedre Gentner. (2022). Spatial supports for comparison in educational science images. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09599-0

article_title: Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds
citation: Martin, Nicole D., Tissenbaum, Catherine Dornfeld, Gnesdilow, Dana, Puntambekar, Sadhana. (2019). Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9474-0
title: Distributed scaffolding and complementarity between material and teacher scaffolds
description: Distributed scaffolding is the framework in which support for complex project-based learning is spread across multiple tools, routines, activities, and the teacher, forming a system that simultaneously supports all students in a classroom. The article stresses that "the agents, tools, and resources must complement one another, so that they all work together in a system of scaffolding". Material scaffolds address anticipated difficulties and can be faded in printed tools, while teacher scaffolding supplies the responsive, contingent support that static materials cannot. The study tests this framework by examining how two teachers' moves complemented or merely replicated fading material scaffolds in the Scientist's Journal.
requirements: Support distributed across tools, activities, and the teacher must be integrated so the components complement rather than duplicate one another
constraints: Material scaffolds in printed tools provide a fixed set of prompts identical for all students and cannot tailor support to individual learners' needs in the moment
target_learners: sixth-grade middle school science students in mixed-ability classrooms
target_learning_goals: science practices such as hypothesis writing and data interpretation
physics concepts of forces, motion, and energy
examples: Two teachers used the same Scientist's Journal with fading High, Medium, and Low material support across nine experiments; one complemented it with responsive moves, the other largely replicated the static support
key_sources: Martin, Nicole D., Tissenbaum, Catherine Dornfeld, Gnesdilow, Dana, Puntambekar, Sadhana. (2019). Fading distributed scaffolds: the importance of complementarity between teacher and material scaffolds. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9474-0

article_title: Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school
citation: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8
title: Use dialogical heuristic worked examples with deliberate errors to support solving of reality-based mathematics tasks
description: The article recommends worked examples that simulate expert modeling by presenting "a dialogue between two fictitious students who discuss their ideas, go a little wrong sometimes, discuss their detours and mistakes, and ultimately demonstrate adequate strategies." The erroneous detours are meant to support active processing and sensitize students to pitfalls, while the dialogue format encourages spontaneous self-explanations without explicit prompts. The authors report this "dialogical approach" showed excellent effectiveness in their study.
requirements: Examples segmented into the four modeling steps and built on reality-based tasks adapted to the grade curriculum
Fictitious students ultimately solve the problem adequately
constraints: For fifth graders the approach improved strategy knowledge but not modeling competency, so the authors give first hints that promotion of metacognitive strategies should not be started too early
Effects were short-term, present about 1 to 3 days after treatment
target_learners: lower secondary school students, particularly seventh graders
target_learning_goals: solving reality-based mathematics tasks with adequate strategies
metacognitive self-regulation during mathematical modeling
examples: Students studied worked examples in which fictitious students Paul and Sara negotiated solutions to tasks such as the Mohawk problem for 45 minutes
key_sources: Hänze, M., & Leiss, D. (2022). Using heuristic worked examples to promote solving of reality-based tasks in mathematics in lower secondary school. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09583-8

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: Dialogic and non-dialogic networks: an ANT-based categorization of classroom talk structures
description: Applying ANT to classroom talk, the article defines networks of human and non-human actors (texts, boards, instructions) that constitute the socio-material structure of talk. A network is dialogic when no human actor is subordinated: "We call such a network, in which all the human actors have agency, and no actor, human or non-human subordinates them, as dialogic". Conversely, "We define such a network in which some human actors are subordinated as a non-dialogic network". Roles are not predetermined but translated in interactions, and networks can be blackboxed.
requirements: Tracing actors, connections, translations, shifts, outcomes, connections to other networks, and black boxes through the article's seven-step recursive ANT analysis procedure
constraints: The authors adopt ANT as a methodology rather than a theory, since they look a priori for delineating dialogic and non-dialogic networks, which would have been unacceptable for ANT as a theory
target_learners: Grade 7 students in dialogic education programs
target_learning_goals: Dialogic argumentation and collaborative reasoning across disciplines
examples: In one small-group episode, five girls subordinated themselves to the Bristol board and instructions (non-dialogic), then shifted to collaborative argumentation voicing their own opinions (dialogic), then back to card classification
key_sources: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5

article_title: Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues
citation: Baruch B. Schwarz, Udi Tsemach, Mirit Israeli, Erez Nir. (2025). Actor-network theory as a new direction in research on educational dialogues. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09669-5
title: DIALOGOS focus days: interdisciplinary dialogic argumentation program for Grade 7
description: The DIALOGOS Center initiated a program in four schools in a mid-size Israeli town, with a teacher professional development program for Grade 7 in mathematics, humanities, and science. Each focus day "turned around a different societal issue; disciplinary sessions (in mathematics, science and philosophy) during which students learned about ideas relevant to the societal issue, preceded an interdisciplinary session" producing a joint product. About 130 students from four seventh grades participated, all from excellent classes.
requirements: Collaboration with the DIALOGOS team to prepare activities, conducted by regular school teachers; out-of-regular-schedule learning days rather than change to regular routines
constraints: Students were all from excellent classes, and the study focused only on the interdisciplinary sessions of the focus days
target_learners: Grade 7 students from four schools in a mid-size Israeli town
target_learning_goals: Interdisciplinary dialogic argumentation on societal issues such as vaccination mandates and genetic engineering
examples: Focus day topics included 'Would it be right for the government to mandate parents to vaccinate their children?' and 'Should the government allow parents to genetically engineer their future babies?'

article_title: Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes
citation: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x
title: Disfluency theory: perceptual difficulty as a metacognitive cue activating System 2 processing via monitoring and control
description: The editorial frames disfluency theory within dual-process considerations (System 1 quick and intuitive, System 2 slow and analytic) and the Nelson and Narens metamemory framework of monitoring and control. Perceptual disfluency is hypothesized to lower confidence, thereby initiating control processes — more mental effort, longer studying — that activate analytic processing and improve performance. The authors describe the mechanism: "lower perceptual fluency (i.e., disfluency) can influence monitoring because the contents are perceived as more difficult, leading to lower confidence (on meta-level), and in turn, control processes are initiated."
requirements: The mechanism requires learners to perceive the disfluency as a metacognitive cue about their mastery, and monitoring changes must translate into adequate control processes
constraints: The special issue's results suggest disfluency did not trigger more effective control processes such as longer and more effortful studying that fostered performance
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: The editorial explains the original positive findings of Diemand-Yauman et al. (2011) via this monitoring-and-control mechanism
key_sources: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x

article_title: Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy?
citation: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0
title: Diagram self-assessment scaffold (prompting students to estimate completed and correct diagram boxes)
description: A paper-based scaffold added after diagram completion: students are prompted to "enter how many boxes you have completed in total and how many boxes you think are correct" for each diagram, without being allowed to revise the diagrams. It was designed to make the most diagnostic cue—number of correct boxes—more salient before comprehension judgments. In the experiment it required only an extra booklet page and no teacher support.
requirements: Must follow diagram completion immediately, with diagrams sealed so they cannot be changed during self-assessment
constraints: Did not increase diagnostic cue utilization or metacomprehension accuracy beyond diagramming alone; students appear to self-assess implicitly anyway
target_learners: secondary education students (11–17 years) reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate monitoring of text comprehension
self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts
examples: In the experiment, the DC + SA group answered 12 self-assessment questions (2 per diagram) after completing six pre-structured diagrams
key_sources: Pijeira-Díaz, H. J., van de Pol, J., Channa, F., & de Bruin, A. (2023). Scaffolding self-regulated learning from causal-relations texts: Diagramming and self-assessment to improve metacomprehension accuracy? Metacognition and Learning, 18, 631–658. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09343-0

article_title: Scaffolding students’ use of metacognitive activities using discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts
citation: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72353-1_2
title: Disciplinary Learning Companion (DLC)
description: The DLC is an online tool that scaffolds students' use of metacognitive activities during physics problem solving by offering discipline- and topic-specific reflective prompts. It consists of reflection modules, each linked to a particular physics textbook problem, where "students receive discipline- and even topic-specific reflective prompts, delivered in the form of multiple-choice reflection questions". After responding, students receive feedback tailored to their answers that addresses correctness, compares solving strategies, and offers actionable suggestions. Students can then download a model solution and write down a point of attention to stimulate transfer.
requirements: Students must first solve a standard physics textbook problem before engaging with the reflection module
Students must respond to each reflection question sequentially to access the complete model solution
constraints: Completion of reflection modules was voluntary and not included in course grading
Feedback is tailored to responses but not adjusted to other student characteristics, characterising it as a hard scaffold
target_learning_goals: metacognitive abilities in physics problem solving
conceptual understanding of Newtonian mechanics
examples: Integrated into an introductory Newtonian mechanics course for approximately 350 first-year bioscience engineering students at KU Leuven, with nine reflection modules corresponding to nine course topics
key_sources: Sijmkens, E., De Cock, M., & De Laet, T. (2024). Scaffolding Students' Use of Metacognitive Activities Using Discipline- and Topic-Specific Reflective Prompts. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09363-w

article_title: The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications
citation: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9
title: Assess SRL–outcome associations against outcomes distinguished by both level and structure of knowledge
description: The article recommends that research on SRL during learning specify which kind of learning outcome is being predicted, because associations differ across outcome measures. Its conclusion states that "taking the level and structure of knowledge into account helps specify the association between SRL activities during learning and the related learning outcomes." The exploratory study demonstrated this by contrasting four outcomes varying on both dimensions.
requirements: Multiple outcome measures capturing different combinations of knowledge level and structure must be collected
constraints: Findings are exploratory due to the small number of participants and should be interpreted with caution
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
deep and surface knowledge construction
examples: The study measured domain test, concept maps, transfer test, and essay scores and related each to think-aloud-coded SRL activity frequencies in a pre-/post-test SEM
key_sources: Joep van der Graaf, Lyn Lim, Yizhou Fan, Jonathan Kilgour, Johanna Moore, Dragan Gašević, Maria Bannert, Inge Molenaar. (2022). The Dynamics Between Self-Regulated Learning and Learning Outcomes: an Exploratory Approach and Implications. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09308-9

article_title: Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study
citation: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z
title: Disfluency theory as metacognitive regulation activating System 2 processing
description: Disfluency theory explains why less legible learning material can improve outcomes: the disfluency effect "can be assumed as a metacognitive regulation process during which learners assign their cognitive resources depending on the perceived difficulty of a cognitive task". Building on two processing systems, perceiving processing as difficult activates System 2, the slow, effortful, analytic and deliberate system, stimulating deeper processing and better learning outcomes. The article uses this account to motivate the WMC moderation hypothesis: only learners with sufficient capacity can absorb the extra burden and engage in deeper processing.
requirements: Learners must perceive the material as difficult and feel able to enhance effort based on their available cognitive resources
constraints: The disfluency effect has been shown only for text-based instructional material, not for spoken texts or pictures
Beneficial effects depend on learner characteristics such as sufficient working memory capacity
target_learners: University students with medium prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: Retention and comprehension of text-based instructional material
examples: The study manipulated text legibility via font (Arial vs. Haettenschweiler, grayscale) and tested whether WMC moderated outcomes on retention, comprehension and transfer tests
key_sources: Janina Lehmann, Christina Goussios, Tina Seufert. (2015). Working memory capacity and disfluency effect: an aptitude-treatment-interaction study. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9149-z

article_title: The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children’s Cognition
citation: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5
title: Displacement hypothesis within the 24-hour movement behavior framework
description: Within the 24-h movement behavior framework, time spent on movement behaviors is mutually exclusive, so changing time in one behavior changes time available for others. The article describes the displacement hypothesis, "which postulates that one behavior (e.g., sedentary behavior) can displace another behavior (e.g., physical activity)". The authors use this framework to argue that reducing physical activity is, assuming fixed sleep duration, identical to increasing sedentary behavior, and that studying reduced activity can clarify the causal role of specific behaviors in the 24-h cycle for cognitive development.
requirements: Assumes a fixed sleep duration so that time reallocations between waking behaviors are interpretable
constraints: The article notes the supporting systematic reviews are based on observational studies, which do not allow robust causal conclusions
target_learning_goals: understanding how the composition of the 24-h activity cycle relates to cognitive and academic development
examples: The article cites an isotemporal substitution analysis in preschoolers showing replacing mentally passive sedentary behavior with structured physical activity or mentally active sedentary behavior was associated with improved academic performance
key_sources: Herold, F., Ludyga, S., Mavilidi, M. F., Benzing, V., Vazou, S., Tomporowski, P. D., & Pesce, C. (2025). The Other Side of the Coin – A Call to Investigate the Influence of Reduced Levels of Physical Activity on Children's Cognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10031-5

article_title: Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis
citation: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Jinkyung Hwang. (2024). Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09960-4
title: Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): dynamic relations of skills to writing by development and measurement
description: The direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW; Kim & Graham, 2022; Kim & Park, 2019) is the explanatory framework this article uses to generate its moderation hypotheses. It "recognizes subskills of writing and associated skills and knowledge that contribute to different subskills," holding that "lower order writing skills are necessary but not sufficient for higher order writing skills." DIEW posits "dynamic relations as a function of development" — transcription skills constrain writing early, while oral language and higher order cognition play increased roles later — and "dynamic relations as a function of measurement." The article uses these hypotheses to predict stronger mathematics–writing relations in earlier developmental phases and variation by assessment characteristics.
requirements: The model presupposes that writing comprises distinguishable lower order transcription skills (spelling, handwriting/keyboarding) and higher order discourse-level composition skills
constraints: The article notes it is not aware of theoretical models of mathematics that explicitly state a similar dynamic-relations hypothesis
target_learning_goals: writing composition, spelling, and handwriting skills and their contributing language and cognitive skills
examples: The meta-analysis tested DIEW-derived predictions that the mathematics–writing relation would be stronger in primary grades and would vary with assessment reliability and standardization
key_sources: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Jinkyung Hwang. (2024). Are Mathematics and Writing Skills Related? Evidence from Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09960-4

article_title: Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities
citation: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534
title: Dialogic learning framework with seven principles underpinning DLGs
description: The review frames DLGs within dialogic learning (Flecha, 2000), an intersubjective, dialogic account of learning drawing on Bakhtin, Bruner, Freire, Mead, and Vygotsky. Flecha defined "the seven principles of DL", beginning with egalitarian dialogue in which "Participants' contributions are considered according to the validity of their arguments instead of their positions of power", followed by cultural intelligence, transformation, the instrumental dimension, creation of meaning, solidarity, and equality of differences. The review uses this framework both to define eligible studies and to organize its seven impact categories.
requirements: DLGs must be based on Flecha's principles of dialogic learning, which was the review's inclusion criterion
constraints: The review only covers evidence from gatherings based on Flecha's principles of dialogic learning, excluding other types of literary gatherings and dialogic learning environments
target_learners: children, adolescents, and adults across primary, secondary, high, special, and adult schools, family and community education, foster care, and prisons
target_learning_goals: critical thinking through dialogic interaction
collective construction of meaning from universal literature
instrumental learning of knowledge and skills
examples: DLG sessions in which participants choose passages from works such as The Odyssey or Crime and Punishment and argue agreements based on validity claims
key_sources: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534

article_title: Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities
citation: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534
title: Dialogic Literary Gathering as an educational action and learning environment
description: A DLG is "an educational action and learning environment based on the collective construction of meaning and knowledge through reading and dialogue the best universal literary works". Participants choose a classic work, agree on pages to read, and in weekly one-to-two-hour sessions share selected fragments, explaining why they chose them and giving reasons for agreeing or disagreeing, while the teacher chairs so everyone can speak. Originating in 1979–80 at La Verneda-Sant Martí School for Adults in Barcelona, DLGs are now applied in more than 10,000 schools and other educative and social settings in Europe and Latin America.
requirements: selection of high-quality universal literary works or adaptations
a teacher or moderator who chairs the discussion so that everyone has a chance to speak
participants read agreed pages before the session and choose passages to share
target_learners: preschool, primary, secondary, special education, and adult learners, families, and prison inmates
target_learning_goals: reading and dialogue about universal literature
communicative and argumentative skills
examples: weekly DLGs reading Oliver Twist in a foster care centre, and online DLGs during COVID-19 confinement
key_sources: Ruiz-Eugenio, L., Soler-Gallart, M., Racionero-Plaza, S., & Padrós, M. (2023). Dialogic literary gatherings: A systematic review of evidence to overcome social and educational inequalities. Educational Research Review, 39, 100534. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100534

article_title: A systematic review of the role of dialogic leadership: Characterization and impacts
citation: Shiza Khaqan, Gisela Redondo-Sama. (2024). A systematic review of the role of dialogic leadership: Characterization and impacts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100618
title: Dialogic leadership: a leadership framework in which community members develop leadership practices through egalitarian dialogue
description: Dialogic leadership is an educational leadership approach grounded in the dialogic framework, in which teachers, students, family members, volunteers and other stakeholders engage in dialogue to achieve common goals and, through that interaction, develop leadership practices. The review characterizes it as egalitarian and social-justice oriented, contrasting it with hierarchical models such as instructional leadership: "in dialogic leadership, the leadership role can be taken on by any community member (Padr´os & Flecha, 2014)". It was conceptualized from the INCLUD-ED project, from which Successful Educational Actions such as interactive groups were identified.
requirements: Dialogue among all participants of the educational community, with equal importance given to each individual's contribution regardless of role or education level
constraints: The review reports the approach is still in early stages of research expansion, with all included studies qualitative
target_learning_goals: inclusive quality education
reducing inequalities in education
community participation in school transformation
examples: Interactive groups in which children interact through dialogue on subject-related activities under volunteer guidance, one of the Successful Educational Actions identified in INCLUD-ED
key_sources: Shiza Khaqan, Gisela Redondo-Sama. (2024). A systematic review of the role of dialogic leadership: Characterization and impacts. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100618

article_title: The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Franz, D. J., Richter, T., Lenhard, W., Marx, P., Stein, R., & Ratz, C. (2023). The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09716-6
title: Stigma account of diagnostic labels: labels activate stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination
description: The article frames diagnostic labels within a stigma process in which a diagnosis functions as a label that carries stereotypical surplus meaning. It cites the account that "mental disorder diagnoses can be the cause of stereotypes (i.e., beliefs or cognitive schemas about people suffering from mental illness), prejudice (i.e., evaluative reactions towards mentally ill persons), and discrimination (i.e., overt negative behavior towards the mentally ill)". In the school context, the article links this to expectancy effects, interpreting the Golem effect as the negative flipside of the Pygmalion effect, with diagnostic labels as one student characteristic that can shape teacher expectations and evaluations.
requirements: The label must be stated explicitly to the evaluator while other information about the child is held constant, as in the experimental vignette and video designs the meta-analysis includes.
constraints: The article notes that findings regarding negative effects of teacher expectations are somewhat mixed, and that the empirical evidence on information amount as a moderator was inconclusive in prior studies.
target_learners: children and teenagers under 21 who receive psychological or educational diagnoses
target_learning_goals: fair and accurate evaluation of diagnosed students' academic skills, behavior, and personality by teachers and other professionals
examples: The meta-analysis tested this account by synthesizing experiments in which teachers or other adults evaluated vignettes, videos, or labels of children with and without a diagnostic label.
key_sources: Franz, D. J., Richter, T., Lenhard, W., Marx, P., Stein, R., & Ratz, C. (2023). The Influence of Diagnostic Labels on the Evaluation of Students: a Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09716-6

article_title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
citation: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w
title: Discriminative-contrast hypothesis: interleaving assists learners to discriminate between similar topics
description: The review explains the interleaving effect via the discriminative-contrast hypothesis, initially proposed by Kornell and Bjork (2008) for category learning. It posits that alternating episodes of different but similar skills or topics helps learners distinguish between them, unlike blocked practice. The authors write that "Interleaving does not involve mental rest-from-deliberate-learning but rather assists learners to discriminate between similar concepts or topics of a domain." It builds on the contextual interference hypothesis, which makes identical predictions.
requirements: Learning materials from the same domain that are similar and not readily discriminable, so learners must contrast and discriminate between them
constraints: For very obviously different, immediately discriminable materials the interleaving effect is unlikely to be obtained
The effect is not moderated by varying working memory capacity according to Sana et al. (2018) as cited in the review
target_learners: students across all stages of education, primarily novices
target_learning_goals: category learning, discrimination between similar concepts, problem-type identification
examples: Kang and Pashler (2012) interleaved paintings by the same artist with easily discriminated cartoons to test discriminative practice
key_sources: Ouhao Chen & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2021). Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: a Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09613-w

article_title: Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Jasmin Breitwieser, André Bittermann, Maria Theobald, Tim Lauer, Mirijam Schaaf, Garvin Brod. (2026). Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10164-1
title: Guiding framework of digital prompts as dynamic scaffolds with a four-dimension design typology
description: The article proposes a guiding framework that conceptualizes digital prompts as feed-forward scaffolds that directly trigger beneficial learning activities students might not initiate on their own, situating prompts within scaffolding theory with contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility as core principles. Prompt design is characterized through a typology of four dimensions: content, function, presentation, and source, adapted from Panadero and Lipnevich's feedback typology. The framework treats prompting as a dynamic, iterative scaffolding process in which student responses inform subsequent prompting, such as gradually fading support as competence increases.
requirements: Relevant student characteristics (e.g., prior knowledge, SRL skills) and momentary needs should inform the design of a prompt to provide contingent support
constraints: Unlike feedback, prompts do not necessarily communicate discrepancies between students' current state and a target goal; evaluative subdimensions such as verification and valence may be less relevant for prompting
target_learners: K-12 and university students using digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: Activation of cognitive, metacognitive, and self-regulated learning strategies through digital prompts
key_sources: Jasmin Breitwieser, André Bittermann, Maria Theobald, Tim Lauer, Mirijam Schaaf, Garvin Brod. (2026). Digital Prompting in Education: A Design Framework and Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10164-1

article_title: Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model
citation: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w
title: Difference I/E Model as a Reparameterization of the Classic I/E Model
description: The difference I/E model, proposed by Wolff (2021), is a reparameterization of the classic I/E model in which "self-concept in one domain is regressed on achievement in the same domain and on the difference between achievement in the same domain and achievement in the other domain." This operationalization aims to separate within-domain achievement effects (including social comparisons) from between-domain achievement effects (including dimensional comparisons), assigning each type of comparison to only one path. Both specifications yield identical model fit and explain the same variance in self-concepts.
requirements: Achievement data from two domains and computation of the difference between standardized achievement scores
constraints: Both model specifications yield identical model fit; differences in effect sizes reflect parameterization and variance allocation, not different psychological processes
The redistribution of variance in the difference I/E model is not unique; other transformations are conceivable
target_learning_goals: academic self-concept formation in domain-specific subjects
key_sources: Fabian Wolff, Jennifer Schumacher, Jens Möller. (2026). Revisiting the Role of Social and Dimensional Comparisons in the Internal/External Frame of Reference Model: A Systematic Comparison of the Classic and the Difference I/E Model. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10212-w

article_title: Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies?
citation: Grosz, M. P. (2023). Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies? Educational Psychology Review, 35, 57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09777-7
title: Researchers should discuss practical implications in their articles regardless of design, while transparently communicating limitations and assumptions
description: The article recommends that educational researchers "talk about practical implications in their articles regardless of the design and analysis they used", because practitioners cannot usually postpone decisions and because researchers know their studies' strengths and limitations best. Alongside this, researchers should "clearly and transparently communicate the limitations and assumptions of their findings and how they affect the practical implications", enabling educators and policy makers to make evidence-aligned decisions.
requirements: Researchers must be transparent about relevant limitations and assumptions, discuss them critically, and take them into account when contemplating causal effects and implications for practice
constraints: Experimental studies will usually be more causally informative than nonexperimental studies, so the strength of causal claims should match the design
target_learning_goals: transfer of research findings into educational practice and decision making
examples: The author argues that if nonexperimental researchers stay silent, practitioners may base decisions on anecdotal evidence and personal experiences, which are less trustworthy than nonexperimental evidence
key_sources: Grosz, M. P. (2023). Should researchers make causal inferences and recommendations for practice on the basis of nonexperimental studies? Educational Psychology Review, 35, 57. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09777-7

article_title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for Stem Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
citation: Nam Ju Kim, Brian R. Belland, & Andrew E. Walker. (2018). Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9419-1
title: Differentiate scaffolding design according to which level of higher-order thinking is addressed in problem-based learning
description: The article's meta-analytic results show scaffolding effects differ sharply by the level of higher-order thinking targeted: analysis-level scaffolding reached g = 0.537 while synthesis (g = 0.156) and evaluation (g = 0.147) effects were small. The authors draw the design implication that "scaffolding design for improving students ' higher-order thinking should be differentiated according to which level (i.e., analysis, synthesis, and evaluation) of higher-order thinking is addressed in PBL." Computer-based scaffolding can effectively support analysis with current technology, while synthesis and evaluation may need integration with one-to-one teacher scaffolding.
requirements: Scaffolding design must specify which level of higher-order thinking (analysis, synthesis, or evaluation) it intends to address in PBL.
constraints: Current technology and designs often struggle to support students' more advanced and complicated learning processes in PBL such as synthesis, application, and reflection, per the authors' discussion.
target_learners: Students engaged in problem-based learning in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Higher-order thinking skills at the analysis, synthesis, and evaluation levels of Bloom's taxonomy
examples: The Bayesian meta-analysis compared scaffolding outcomes coded as analysis, synthesis, or evaluation subcategories across 21 PBL-STEM studies, finding analysis-level effects much higher than synthesis or evaluation effects.
key_sources: Nam Ju Kim, Brian R. Belland, & Andrew E. Walker. (2018). Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9419-1

article_title: Editor’s Note
citation: Daniel H. Robinson. (2013). Editor's Note. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-013-9226-2
title: Discourage authors from including prescriptive statements in empirical research journal articles
description: This principle holds that empirical research articles should not include prescriptive statements recommending practice, because such recommendations face generalization problems even when grounded in strong causal evidence. It emerged from a 2-day meeting whose participants "ended with the decision to write a position paper discouraging authors from including prescriptives in empirical research journal articles."
requirements: A position paper articulating the rationale, as decided by the meeting participants
constraints: The article itself notes the position is controversial and warrants a range of informed responses
target_learners: Authors of empirical research journal articles in educational psychology
target_learning_goals: Responsible communication of research findings for educational practice
examples: The Meadows Center meeting participants decided to write a position paper discouraging prescriptives, and the journal solicited short responses from scholars for a subsequent issue
key_sources: Daniel H. Robinson. (2013). Editor's Note. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-013-9226-2

article_title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Diagnostic competences as coordinated application of professional knowledge in epistemic-diagnostic activities
description: The article's conceptual framework defines diagnostic competences as "dispositions enabling goal-oriented gathering and integration of information in order to make medical or educational decisions." Diagnostic processes are conceptualized as a set of epistemic activities, "including (a) identifying a problem, (b) questioning, (c) generating hypotheses, (d) constructing artifacts, (e) generalizing evidence, (f) evaluating evidence" and drawing conclusions and communicating results. The framework links learners' prior professional knowledge (conceptual and practical) and the quality of diagnostic processes and outcomes, and it organizes the meta-analysis's coding of moderators.
requirements: Outcome measures must address diagnostic quality or one or more of the epistemic-diagnostic activities for a study to be coded within the framework
constraints: The article states the current research is not specific enough to infer the type of knowledge representations—declarative or procedural—suggested by ACT-R
target_learners: higher education students in medical and teacher education
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences: gathering and integrating case-specific information to make medical or educational decisions
examples: The coding scheme for professional knowledge base, instructional support, and diagnostic context in the meta-analysis was based on this conceptual framework (Heitzmann et al. 2018b).
key_sources: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2

article_title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
citation: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2
title: Two-dimensional classification of diagnostic situations: information base and collaboration requirement
description: Adopting Heitzmann et al. (2018b), the article distinguishes diagnostic situations along two dimensions. The first is that "The first dimension is information base (e.g., where the information for diagnosis comes from), spanning the spectrum from document-based to interaction-based": document-based diagnosis uses recorded information with little time pressure, while interaction-based diagnosis processes information in real time with more time pressure and fewer opportunities for reflection. The second dimension runs from individual diagnoses to diagnoses requiring collaboration and communication with other professionals, which the article notes can be problematic even for experts.
requirements: Describing a diagnostic situation requires coding both its information base and whether collaboration with other professionals is needed
constraints: The article notes empirical studies provide evidence that collaboration and social aspects of working on the case can be problematic even for experts
target_learners: medical and teacher education students learning to diagnose
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences across varied diagnostic situations
examples: The meta-analysis coded each primary study's diagnostic situation as document-based or interaction-based and as individual or collaborative (Table 1).
key_sources: Olga Chernikova, Nicole Heitzmann, Maximilian Christian Fink, Venance Timothy, Tina Seidel, Frank Fischer, DFG Research group COSIMA. (2020). Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09492-2

article_title: The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies
citation: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0
title: Framework of direct and indirect teacher approaches to activate self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a framework in which "teachers can promote strategies directly, and they can indirectly activate SRL by providing a learning environment that incites students to self-regulate their learning." Direct promotion splits into explicit and implicit strategy instruction, while indirect promotion operates through powerful learning environments grounded in constructivist theory. The framework organizes the review's analysis of classroom observation studies, which coded teachers' practice as direct strategy instruction, indirect activation of SRL, or a combination of both.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of metacognition and strategies so they can instruct strategies explicitly and design learning environments conducive to SRL
constraints: The review notes that as a conceptual paper it does not present a complete state-of-the-art and there is a lack of quantitative synthesis of teachers' promotion of SRL
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive strategy knowledge and use
examples: The 17 reviewed observation studies were classified according to the framework as focusing on direct strategy instruction, indirect activation of SRL, or a combination of both
key_sources: Charlotte Dignath & Marcel V. J. Veenman. (2021). The Role of Direct Strategy Instruction and Indirect Activation of Self-Regulated Learning—Evidence from Classroom Observation Studies. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09534-0

article_title: Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement
citation: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2
title: Differential mechanisms of impact of different types of physical activity on different aspects of cognition
description: This account holds that different categories of physical activity affect different cognitive and academic outcomes through distinct mechanisms, rather than PA acting as a uniform cognitive enhancer. The meta-analysis found that "aerobic PA with moderate to vigorous intensity benefitted executive function outcomes", while PA integrated with academic instruction benefited mathematics and enriched PA programmes benefited language. The article situates this within cognitive explanations for change, including the skills acquisition theory, which "postulates that the motor and cognitive complexity of PA influence cognitive processes", and embodied cognition. It frames dose–response characteristics (intensity, duration, frequency, type) as the levers that select which outcome is affected.
requirements: Interventions must be characterised by type, intensity, duration and frequency so that dose–response moderators can be distinguished
constraints: Moderator analyses were exploratory and heterogeneity was high; on-task behaviour had an insufficient sample size for moderator analysis
target_learning_goals: Executive functions (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, attention, planning)
Fluid intelligence, creativity, on-task behaviour, mathematics and language achievement
examples: The meta-analysis contrasted PA with academic instruction, aerobic, sports, cognitively enriched, dance, PE and holistic movement interventions as distinct activity types
key_sources: Vasilopoulos, F., Jeffrey, H., Wu, Y., & Dumontheil, I. (2023). Multi-Level Meta-Analysis of Physical Activity Interventions During Childhood: Effects of Physical Activity on Cognition and Academic Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09760-2

article_title: On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary
citation: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417
title: Differentiated conception of lasting learning as heterogeneous phenomenon types
description: The commentary proposes that a theory of lasting learning must begin with an elaborated description of the phenomenon's variants, because "lasting learning is not a homogeneous, uniform phenomenon". It sketches two contrasting cases: topics treated once in school, such as a classical literature piece belonging to general cultural knowledge, and core concepts or principles of a discipline that recur across years, such as energy in physics. The two cases differ in learning goals, instructional demands (e.g., coherence over long periods, spiral curriculum, connectable initial teaching), and appropriate assessment, so a theory may either cover multiple variants or restrict its scope to a clearly described selected type.
requirements: An elaborated description of the types of phenomena under focus, consistent with all major variants to be explained
Alignment of learning goals, instructional methods, and assessment, following the constructive alignment triangle
constraints: The commentary does not propose a specific type of assessment; it pleads for a deliberate decision aligned to goals and methods
A first-step theory may be restricted to selected types of lasting learning
target_learners: school students across subjects and grade levels
target_learning_goals: retention and flexible use of knowledge over long periods
mastery of core concepts and principles of a discipline
examples: The commentary contrasts remembering basic aspects of a literature piece such as Faust I or Romeo and Juliet with re-occurring core concepts like energy in physics or natural selection in biology
key_sources: Katharina Scheiter, Alexander Renkl. (2026). On the challenges of investigating lasting learning: A commentary. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102417. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102417

article_title: Growth trajectories of self-concept and interest in mathematics and language – Individual differences and cross-domain relations
citation: Anna Widlund, Markku Niemivirta, Heta Tuominen, Johan Korhonen. (2023). Growth Trajectories of Self-Concept and Interest in Mathematics and Language – Individual Differences and Cross-Domain Relations. Preprint version 1. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5563-5044
title: Internal/external frame of reference and dimensional comparison theory as an account of domain-specific motivational development
description: The article applies the I/E model and dimensional comparison theory to explain why students' competence perceptions and interests become increasingly differentiated across math and L1 during adolescence. Students make external (social) comparisons of their performance against other students, and internal (dimensional) comparisons of performance in one domain against another, which "sometimes leading to negative predictions between performance and competence perceptions across domains". The study's negative cross-domain correlations, especially among girls, are read as support for this framework.
requirements: Students must experience and evaluate performance in at least two comparable academic domains for dimensional comparisons to operate.
constraints: The article states it is challenging to conclude whether dimensional comparison processes cause the gender differences or are a result of already-differentiated motivational beliefs.
target_learners: adolescent students in lower secondary education (Grades 7–9)
target_learning_goals: domain-specific academic self-concept and interest in mathematics and language
examples: The study tested the theory by estimating cross-domain correlations between intercept and slope factors of math and L1 self-concept and interest, separately for boys and girls.
key_sources: Anna Widlund, Markku Niemivirta, Heta Tuominen, Johan Korhonen. (2023). Growth Trajectories of Self-Concept and Interest in Mathematics and Language – Individual Differences and Cross-Domain Relations. Preprint version 1. https://orcid.org/0000-0001-5563-5044

article_title: Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking
citation: Frijters, S., ten Dam, G., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2008). Effects of dialogic learning on value-loaded critical thinking. Learning and Instruction, 18(1), 66-82. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.11.001
title: Paired Dialogic and Non-Dialogic lesson series for value-loaded critical thinking in Biology
description: The article describes two lesson series developed for teaching value-loaded critical thinking: "a Dialogic lesson series and a Non-Dialogic one". They were implemented in the school subject of Biology in pre-vocational secondary education with a sample of 297 students, allowing a controlled comparison of dialogic versus non-dialogic approaches to the same competences.
requirements: Lesson series must be embedded in a domain-specific school subject (here Biology) so critical thinking is taught alongside subject-matter knowledge.
constraints: Developed and evaluated for pre-vocational secondary education.
target_learning_goals: Value-loaded critical thinking
Biology subject-matter knowledge
examples: The study developed two lesson series and compared their effects on critical-thinking competences and Biology knowledge with 297 students.
