article_title: Class composition effects in achievement and interest and the role of the learning environment revisited: A conceptual replication and extension of Lavrijsen et al. (2022).
citation: Kopatz, M., Wagner, W., Neuendorf, C., Trautwein, U., Nagengast, B., and Bardach, L. (2025). Class Composition Effects in Achievement and Interest and the Role of the Learning Environment Revisited: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Lavrijsen et al. (2022). Preprint. https://osf.io/n5xur/?view_only=48daea427ab44c9abd13b21b1e2b42f6
title: Adapt instruction to individual needs in heterogeneous classes to support achievement and interest
description: The article's implications statement supports differentiating instruction in heterogeneous classrooms: "in such heterogeneous classes where teachers adapt their instruction to individual needs, students show higher achievement and motivation in German." Differentiated instruction involves altering content, materials, and teaching approaches to meet students' needs, with tiered assignments as the studied technique. The principle rests on the finding that heterogeneity alone did not affect outcomes, but heterogeneity combined with differentiated instruction did, at least in German classes.
requirements: Teachers must actually use differentiated practices (e.g., providing different tasks for different students), measured via student reports.
constraints: The advantage of differentiated instruction in heterogeneous classes emerged in German but no comparable effects emerged in mathematics, so the principle is subject-specific in this evidence.
target_learners: secondary school students in heterogeneous classes
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
academic interest
examples: The study measured differentiated instruction with four student-reported items adapted from Baumert et al. (2008) in Grade 6 classes.

article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: Expanded DIEW dynamic relations hypothesis: component skills relate to written composition as a function of measurement and dimensions of written composition
description: The expanded Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing adds a dynamic relations hypothesis stating that "the relations of component skills to the written composition vary as a function of measurement and dimensions of written composition." Measurement refers to how writing is assessed (format, genre, evaluation), while dimensions refer to aspects evaluated in the composition, such as writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing. The article argues that because the outcome is multidimensional, a theoretical model must recognize both predictors and outcome dimensions, and it tests this hypothesis with Grade 2 data, finding differential relations for higher order cognitions and reading comprehension.
requirements: A theoretical model of writing must specify both the component skills (predictors) and the dimension of written composition (outcome) being predicted, since demands of component skills differ by focal dimension.
constraints: The article elaborates only the evaluation facet (dimensions of written composition); assessment format and genre facets are noted as beyond the scope of the paper.
The hypothesis was tested with English-speaking second graders in a semirural southeastern US context; the authors call for testing across developmental phases, writing systems, and L1/L2 learners.
target_learners: Elementary school students, specifically Grade 2 beginning writers
target_learning_goals: Written composition skills including writing quality, writing productivity, and correctness in writing
examples: Structural equation models with 350 Grade 2 children showed higher order cognitive skills related to writing quality but not productivity, and reading comprehension related only to writing quality.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading–writing relations, and dynamic relations as a function of measurement/dimensions of written composition.
citation: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564
title: DIEW component skills model of writing: hierarchical, interactive, and dynamic structural relations among component skills
description: The Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing is a component skills model hypothesizing that background knowledge, socio-emotions, transcription skills, knowledge of phonology/orthography/semantics, discourse oral language, higher order cognitive and regulation skills, vocabulary and grammatical knowledge, and executive function contribute to writing. The article states that "DIEW hypothesizes and specifies hierarchical relations among the component skills," with lower order skills related to written composition via higher order skills, and posits interactive, bidirectional relations among skills. It maps component skills onto writing processes: idea generation draws on topic knowledge and reading, translation on oral language, transcription on spelling and handwriting, and evaluation on language, reading, higher order cognitions, and discourse knowledge.
requirements: Assessment and instruction can be operationalized only when the model's component skills are explicitly specified, which the authors describe as the model's singular advantage.
constraints: The model is not a model of a particular genre or task; the extent of component skill contributions varies with development and assessment factors.
Component skills are involved in the writing process only as needed, not all during the entire writing process.
target_learners: K-12 students learning to write, particularly elementary-grade developing writers
target_learning_goals: Written composition, writing processes (planning, translation, transcription, revision), and component skills such as oral language, transcription, and higher order cognition
examples: The article maps DIEW component skills onto writing processes (Figure 2) and tests the model's hypotheses with Grade 2 structural equation models.
key_sources: Grace Kim Young-Suk & Graham Steve. (2022). Expanding the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Writing (DIEW): Reading-Writing Relations, and Dynamic Relations As a Function of Measurement/Dimensions of Written Composition. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000564

article_title: Conceptual knowledge of decimal arithmetic.
citation: Lortie-Forgues, Hugues and Siegler, Robert S (2017) Conceptual knowledge of decimal arithmetic. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 374-391. ISSN: 0022-0620. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000148
title: Three theoretical interpretations of incorrect direction of effect judgments: strong conviction, operation knowledge, and cognitive conflict
description: The article distinguishes three interpretations of incorrect direction of effect judgments, to be separated by confidence ratings: "The strong conviction hypothesis, which posits that students are highly confident that multiplication produces answers greater than either operand"; the operation knowledge hypothesis, in which students are less confident about multiplication and division than addition and subtraction regardless of operand size; and the cognitive conflict hypothesis, in which confidence is lower specifically for multiplication and division of numbers between zero and one. Confidence data supported the operation knowledge account for most students, with a grade-related emergence of cognitive conflict in 8th graders.
requirements: Confidence ratings collected immediately after each direction of effect judgment on a 5-point scale
constraints: The confidence pattern differed between the subgroup whose judgments always followed whole number arithmetic and the remaining students
target_learning_goals: understanding the direction of effect of rational number arithmetic operations
examples: Study 1 collected 5-point confidence ratings after each of 16 direction of effect judgments and compared them across operation and operand size
key_sources: Lortie-Forgues, Hugues and Siegler, Robert S (2017) Conceptual knowledge of decimal arithmetic. Journal of Educational Psychology. pp. 374-391. ISSN: 0022-0620. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000148

article_title: Pedagogical psychology of report.
citation: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Distribution-of-attention account of children's report errors, with Stern's developmental stages of report content
description: The article explains children's poorer reports not by weaker concentration but by a qualitatively different distribution of attention: children notice details adults miss and overlook details adults call essential, so questioning about adult-essential details yields errors. If the child formulated the questions, the adult would report the child's essential details equally poorly. The account draws on Stern's stages, in which "the child at first notices mainly objects; later he turns his attention to their properties and to actions, and only during the last stage does he notice the relations between objects."
requirements: Applies when the report concerns details of an experience rather than material deliberately memorized for reproduction
constraints: The author states the argument is not strictly proved but made very probable, and that no one has yet determined how the child's distribution of attention differs from the adult's
target_learning_goals: accurate reporting of observed experiences
examples: The author argues that if attention distribution were identical across observers, the order of objects ranked by report accuracy would be the same for all classes of observers, which is not the case.
key_sources: Lipmann, O. (1911). Pedagogical Psychology of Report. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0070700

article_title: Sex differences in developmental pathways to mathematical competence.
citation: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Ünal Zehra E. (2023). Sex Differences in Developmental Pathways to Mathematical Competence. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000763
title: Differential contributions hypothesis of sex differences in mathematical development
description: The hypothesis holds that sex differences in math-relevant traits shape distinct developmental pathways to mathematics: boys' advantage in spatial abilities contributes relatively more to their mathematical development, while girls' advantage in in-class attention contributes relatively more to theirs. The article states that "the sex differences in spatial abilities and in-class attention differentially contribute to the mathematical development of boys and girls and counteract one another," explaining why overall mean sex differences in mathematics are small or non-existent despite trait differences. The longitudinal SEM study confirmed the hypothesis with significant sex-to-trait and trait-to-mathematics paths.
requirements: Longitudinal assessment of both spatial abilities and in-class attention alongside mathematics outcomes
Statistical control of general cognitive ability to isolate the specific pathway contributions
constraints: The article notes the data are correlational and do not allow definitive causal inferences
The spatial boost is likely unimportant in some mathematics areas and more important in others than the modest effect for general mathematics abilities found here
Lower achieving students were less likely to enroll in the longitudinal component, which could influence generalizability
target_learners: adolescents in middle school and early high school (grades 6 to 9)
target_learning_goals: mathematical competence from arithmetic fluency to algebra
examples: Model 4 fitted paths from sex to Spatial and In-Class Attention and resulted in a significant improvement in model fit, with all paths significant (ps < .028)
key_sources: Geary David C., Hoard Mary K., Nugent Lara, Ünal Zehra E. (2023). Sex Differences in Developmental Pathways to Mathematical Competence. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000763

article_title: Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW).
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Schatschneider Christopher. (2017). Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000129
title: The direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW)
description: The DIEW model extends the simple view and not-so-simple view of writing by explicitly specifying direct and indirect relations among component skills and their relations to writing. It hypothesizes that working memory is a foundational cognitive ability supporting vocabulary, grammatical knowledge, higher-order cognitive skills (inference, theory of mind), and transcription skills; these feed discourse-level oral language and transcription skills, which in turn directly support writing. The article states the model 'extends them by explicitly hypothesizing direct and indirect relations among components skills and their relations to writing based on theory and empirical evidence.'
requirements: Discourse-level oral language and transcription skills (spelling, handwriting fluency) as upper-level skills directly related to writing
constraints: Tested with beginning writers (Grade 1) for writing quality operationalized as idea development; the authors note relations might vary for older children and different writing outcomes
target_learning_goals: Writing quality (idea development and organization)
examples: Structural equation modeling with 193 Grade 1 children compared four DIEW variations (complete mediation, two partial mediation models, and a working-memory direct-path model)
key_sources: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Schatschneider Christopher. (2017). Expanding the developmental models of writing: A direct and indirect effects model of developmental writing (DIEW). Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000129

article_title: A tentative standardization of a completion test.
citation: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22
title: Score completion-test blanks with difficulty-based weights rather than assuming every blank is of equal value
description: The article argues against the practice in which "each blank space is of equal value with every other blank." Because comparisons based on equal-difficulty grading are "open to serious question" when omissions differ in difficulty, the authors recommend using a table of individual elision values, holding that the more accurate results justify "the little additional labor that will be required to use or apply them."
requirements: A standardization study must first establish the per-unit time values and per-elision difficulty weights before unequal scoring can be applied.
constraints: If the test is expected to yield only a very rough measure, rating papers by the fractional part performed would, in the authors' words, do well enough.
target_learning_goals: accurate numerical grading of completion-test performance
examples: Terman and Childs had earlier recognized unequal difficulty by mutilating four quarters of their test at 33 1-3%, 45%, 54%, and 66 2-3% and crediting elisions 6, 8, 10, or 13 by part.
key_sources: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22

article_title: Crosslinguistic transfer of higher order cognitive skills and their roles in writing for English-Spanish dual language learners.
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Wolters Alissa, Mercado Janet, & Quinn Jamie. (2022). Crosslinguistic Transfer of Higher Order Cognitive Skills and Their Roles in Writing for English-Spanish Dual Language Learners. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000516
title: Direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW) positioning higher order cognitive skills as contributors to compositional coherence
description: The article describes the direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW), in which writing processes draw on oral language skills, executive function, background knowledge, social-emotional factors, and transcription skills. DIEW "posits that higher order cognitive skills and regulation such as reasoning, inferencing, perspective taking, and monitoring are important to compositional quality, particularly for establishing coherence". Inferencing supports understanding relations among ideas, perspective taking helps writers anticipate readers' interpretations, and monitoring supports detecting and repairing breakdowns in coherence. The study's findings are framed as corroborating DIEW for dual language learners.
requirements: Coherence and quality composition are achieved when the author's intended meaning, the explicit text, and the reader's constructed meaning are congruous
constraints: The article's own evidence for the model's higher order cognition–writing link is correlational, from one sample of primary-grade dual language learners
target_learners: primary-grade students, including dual language learners
target_learning_goals: written composition quality and coherence
examples: The article frames its finding of a fairly strong relation between higher order cognition and writing quality as corroborating DIEW's hypothesis and extending it to dual language learners
key_sources: Kim Young-Suk Grace, Wolters Alissa, Mercado Janet, & Quinn Jamie. (2022). Crosslinguistic Transfer of Higher Order Cognitive Skills and Their Roles in Writing for English-Spanish Dual Language Learners. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000516

article_title: Morphology in reading comprehension among school-aged readers of English: A synthesis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling study.
citation: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797
title: Direct and Indirect Routes Framework of Morphological Awareness to Reading Comprehension
description: The article proposes a theory-driven path model (Figure 1) in which MA influences reading comprehension through one direct route and two indirect routes. Path 1 is "MA → Word Reading → Reading Comprehension", grounded in the lexical quality hypothesis and the binder-of-representations account. Path 2 is "MA → Vocabulary Knowledge → Reading Comprehension", grounded in morphological problem-solving and meaning inference. Paths 3a/3b represent a contingent direct route where MA supports in-situ lexical problem-solving and syntactic parsing during reading.
requirements: Studies must measure MA, word reading, vocabulary knowledge, and reading comprehension to test the full path model
constraints: The model was tested only in English, a deep orthography where morphology offers "islands of regularity"
The syntactic aspect (Path 3b) is noted as "the least studied yet can play a role that should not be ignored"
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Word reading
Vocabulary knowledge
examples: The MASEM study fitted this model to a pooled correlation matrix from 107 effect sizes (N = 21,818) and found very good model fits (CFI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.039)
key_sources: Zhang, D., Ke, S. (E.), & Mo, Y. (2023). Morphology in Reading Comprehension Among School-Aged Readers of English: A Synthesis and Meta-Analytic Structural Equation Modeling Study. Journal of Educational Psychology, 115(5), 683–699. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000797

article_title: Dimensional comparison effects on (gendered) educational choices.
citation: Jansen, M., Becker, M., & Neumann, M. (2020). Dimensional Comparison Effects on (Gendered) Educational Choices. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(2), 330-350. https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:0111-pedocs-220459
title: Dimensional comparison theory and the internal/external frame of reference model
description: Dimensional comparison theory (DCT) holds that "these beliefs are themselves affected by students comparing their ability across different domains", so students with similar achievement in one domain can hold different self-concepts depending on achievement in other domains. The classic operationalization is the internal/external frame of reference (I/E) model: "After controlling for the positive effect of achievement on self-concept in the same domain... dimensional comparison effects can be observed as a negative effect of achievement on self-concept across domains". This study tests DCT within an expectancy-value framework, modeling cross-domain paths from achievement, self-concept, and value to course choices and STEM intentions.
requirements: Path modeling with achievement and outcome measures in at least two domains (here mathematics and German), with within-domain effects controlled when estimating cross-domain effects
constraints: Effects here estimated from observational longitudinal data on academic-track Berlin students choosing between advanced mathematics and German courses; no causal manipulation of comparisons
target_learners: Upper-secondary academic-track students approaching course and university-major choices
target_learning_goals: Educational choice behavior, domain-specific academic self-concept, domain-specific value, STEM study intentions
examples: The article estimated a full SEM with within- and cross-domain paths from gender to achievement (grades and test-scores) to self-concept and value to advanced course choice to STEM study intentions, and found the model with cross-domain paths fit better (AIC/BIC) than a model without them
key_sources: Jansen, M., Becker, M., & Neumann, M. (2020). Dimensional Comparison Effects on (Gendered) Educational Choices. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 113(2), 330-350. https://nbn-resolving.org/urn:nbn:de:0111-pedocs-220459

article_title: An outline for institutional education and treatment of young offenders.
citation: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Diagnosis of each individual's needs is essential for successful institutional treatment of young offenders
description: The authors make diagnosis of individual needs the cornerstone of institutional treatment, insisting it be "absolutely essential for carrying out successful treatment" and correlated with educational and other therapy throughout institutional life. Diagnosis covers physical, psychological, and moral-background domains, and continues beyond admission to explain treatment failures and conduct outbreaks.
requirements: A trained diagnostician must know earlier causative factors of the delinquency, such as defective heredity and conditions of environment, in detail
constraints: The authors state that deliberately ignoring the delinquent's prior record is justifiable only when no thorough diagnosis of causation is available
target_learners: young offenders in training or industrial schools
target_learning_goals: moral recovery and social adjustment
examples: The outline specifies physical diagnosis of diseases and sensory defects, psychological diagnosis of disabilities, talents, mental content, and habits, and diagnosis of the moral background to find what normal experiences were left out or perverted
key_sources: William Healy and Augusta F. Bronner. (1916). An Outline for Institutional Education and Treatment of Young Offenders. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071384

article_title: In-FUSE-ing STEAM learning with spatial reasoning: Distributed spatial sensemaking in school-based making activities.
citation: Ramey, K. E., Stevens, R., & Uttal, D. H. (2019). In-FUSE-ing STEAM Learning with Spatial Reasoning: Distributed Spatial Sensemaking in School-based Making Activities. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000422
title: Distributed spatial sensemaking: spatial reasoning as distributed practices drawing on social and material resources
description: The article frames spatial reasoning not only as internal cognitive skills but as "a set of distributed practices, which draw on context- and activity-specific social and material resources (i.e. distributed spatial sensemaking)". Drawing on distributed theories of thinking and learning, the study examines interactions between people, tools, and representations through which spatial reasoning is enacted, and traces spatial representations across representational media. It translates the Uttal et al./Newcombe and Shipley two-by-two spatial-skills taxonomy into qualitative codes applicable to observable talk or action.
requirements: Requires studying reasoning within the sociomaterial context in which it is authentically learned and applied, using qualitative categorical coding and interaction analysis of multimodal idea units.
constraints: The framework addresses types of spatial reasoning beyond the intrinsic-dynamic skills typically measured by psychometric tests; it supplements rather than replaces laboratory, quasi-experimental, and correlational approaches.
target_learners: fifth- and sixth-grade students in school-based making activities
target_learning_goals: spatial reasoning and STEAM problem-solving
examples: The authors applied the framework via a modified version of Ramey and Uttal's (2017) coding scheme to approximately 88 hours of video from five FUSE classrooms.
key_sources: Ramey, K. E., Stevens, R., & Uttal, D. H. (2019). In-FUSE-ing STEAM Learning with Spatial Reasoning: Distributed Spatial Sensemaking in School-based Making Activities. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000422

article_title: An approach to the synthetic study of interest in education: Part I.
citation: Waples, D. (1920). An Approach to the Synthetic Study of Interest in Education: Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology, XI(6).
title: Begin motivation by diagnosing the learner's currently most intense varieties of interest, then instruct so that expression is evoked in useful content through voluntary effort of attention
description: Waples states a design principle for motivation grounded in his analysis of interest: "The first step in motivation consists in determining the varieties of interest in which expression is temporarily most intense and thereafter in such instruction as will evoke expression in useful content as the result of voluntary effort of attention." The principle presupposes individual study of the learner, since principles derived from groups require such individual study for their application. It connects interest diagnosis to the standardization of the learning process he outlines in the study's final chapter.
requirements: Individual diagnosis of the varieties of interest in which expression is temporarily most intense
Instruction designed so expression occurs in useful content via voluntary effort of attention
constraints: Principles derived from groups presuppose individual study for their application; the principles are valueless except as applied to the specific situation
target_learners: school pupils, particularly at secondary level
target_learning_goals: effective motivation of voluntary effort of attention toward useful content
examples: Waples cites Chapman and Feeler's incentive experiment as showing that diagnosis of individual interest responsive to direct appeal and standardization of the stimulus is a study of the first importance

article_title: The relation between text reading and reading comprehension varies as a function of developmental phase, orthographic depth, and measurement characteristics: Evidence from a meta-analysis.
citation: Leachman, M., Wolters, A., & Kim, Y.-S. G. (2025). The Relation Between Text Reading and Reading Comprehension Varies as a Function of Developmental Phase, Orthographic Depth, and Measurement Characteristics: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000932
title: Dynamic relations hypothesis of the Direct and Indirect Effects Model of Reading (DIER)
description: DIER proposes that relations among reading component skills are not fixed but vary systematically. The article states the "dynamic relations hypothesis, which posits that the relations between component skills and reading are not uniform, but dynamic", varying as a function of reading development, text characteristics such as orthographic depth, and measurement characteristics such as task types. Within DIER, text reading fluency acts as a mediator or bridge connecting word reading and listening comprehension to reading comprehension, and it increasingly mediates these relations with development, completely mediating word reading's relation at some developmental point but never completely mediating listening comprehension's relation. The meta-analysis tested and found support for these hypotheses.
requirements: Reading comprehension and component skills must be assessed with specified tasks, since the theory holds that measurement characteristics shape observed relations
constraints: The theory concerns correlational relations among skills; the present meta-analysis did not examine directionality of the relation
target_learners: learners from kindergarten through adulthood learning to read in alphabetic and morphosyllabic languages
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
text reading fluency
word reading
examples: The meta-analysis of 401 studies tested the hypothesis that the text reading–comprehension relation varies by developmental phase, orthographic depth, and task type, and the patterns matched the predictions
key_sources: Leachman, M., Wolters, A., & Kim, Y.-S. G. (2025). The Relation Between Text Reading and Reading Comprehension Varies as a Function of Developmental Phase, Orthographic Depth, and Measurement Characteristics: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000932

article_title: Writing fluency: Its relations with language, cognitive, and transcription skills, and writing quality using longitudinal data from kindergarten to grade 2.
citation: Kim Young-Suk Grace. (2024). Writing Fluency: Its Relations With Language, Cognitive, and Transcription Skills, and Writing Quality Using Longitudinal Data From Kindergarten to Grade 2. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(4). https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000841
title: Developmental dynamic relations hypothesis: what writing fluency taps changes across writing development
description: The article invokes the DIEW dynamic relations hypothesis (Kim & Graham, 2022), which holds that component skills' contributions to writing vary as a function of development. In the beginning phase, transcription skills are not automated and "transcription skills act as a primary determinant of writing process and outcomes", so writing fluency largely taps the transcription process; as transcription automates, other processes and associated skills become increasingly tapped. The study's null relations of oral language skills to fluency support this account for beginning writers.
requirements: Applies within a theoretical framework distinguishing writing phases and component skills (transcription, translation, revision) that draw on language, cognitive, and transcription resources
constraints: The article presents this as one of two speculative possibilities, noting sentence skills such as sentence construction might alternatively be the direct correlate of fluency, and calls for future work
target_learners: Beginning writers in primary grades (kindergarten to Grade 2)
target_learning_goals: Written composition quality
examples: The longitudinal SEM found complete mediation of transcription skills by writing fluency and no independent relation of oral language skills to fluency, consistent with the developmental hypothesis for beginning writers

article_title: Statistical learning dynamically shapes auditory perception
citation: Luthra, S., Luor, A., Tierney, A. T., Dick, F., & Holt, L. L. (2025). Statistical learning dynamically shapes auditory perception. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00328-z
title: Distributional learning sculpts a gain function via suppression of less-likely stimuli and modest enhancement of more-likely stimuli
description: The article proposes that expectation built from distributional learning across a task-irrelevant sensory dimension sculpts a gain function characterized by "modest enhancement of more-likely stimuli, and robust suppression of less-likely stimuli." Rather than prioritizing expected input alone (Bayesian-style enhancement) or solely accentuating surprising input, the account holds that "effects of expectation are largely driven by suppression of less-probable, unexpected stimuli." Expectation establishes a selection filter—variously a dimension-selective attentional filter or an experience-driven predictive filter—that is graded by distribution shape, range, and stimulus position, and is distinct from task-utility manipulations previously attributed to attention.
requirements: Extended experience with probability distributions across a continuous sensory dimension
A task-irrelevant perceptual dimension along which distributions are defined
constraints: Effects were demonstrated on tone detection in noise and tone duration decisions across acoustic frequency; whether they generalize to other modalities or task-relevant dimensions is not established by these experiments.
target_learners: adult listeners performing online psychoacoustic tasks
target_learning_goals: implicit statistical (distributional) learning across a sensory dimension
perceptual sensitivity and decision speed modulation
examples: Exp 7 showed a five-fold probability increase conferred only an average 3.7% detection improvement at the mode, while off-center frequencies decreasing in probability lost 4.7% detection accuracy.
key_sources: Luthra, S., Luor, A., Tierney, A. T., Dick, F., & Holt, L. L. (2025). Statistical learning dynamically shapes auditory perception. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00328-z

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: DIY productive failure cycle for large university classes: Exploration then Consolidation with pre-reading
description: A lesson-level pattern reversing conventional instruction: students attempt challenging, open-ended problems in small groups before explicit instruction, then receive consolidation built on their own solutions. Class time "contained two main phases, an Exploration phase and a Consolidation phase", preceded by the course's standard pre-reading and quiz. Student responses collected during Exploration become the raw material for Clicker-based formative feedback and an instructor-led Walkthrough that models expert problem-solving while eliciting student contributions.
requirements: Pre-reading assignments so students arrive with activated prior knowledge and basic vocabulary
Problems designed at higher Bloom's levels that are challenging but not frustrating
Moderate metacognitive prompts during Exploration to prevent frustration-driven disengagement
constraints: First iterations without moderate support led many students to give up out of frustration
target_learners: first-year university students in large-enrollment science courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of complex processes such as DNA replication and transcription and translation
examples: In the Transcription and Translation activity, students designed the process to mimic a cell starting from a given DNA sequence, reasoning about parts, roles, and order
key_sources: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6

article_title: DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course
citation: Sunita G. Chowrira, Karen M. Smith, Patrick J. Dubois and Ido Roll. (2019). DIY productive failure: boosting performance in a large undergraduate biology course. npj Science of Learning 4:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0040-6
title: Course instructors can design and implement PF themselves (DIY PF) and still obtain gains over established active learning
description: PF's effectiveness had been shown mainly in lessons designed and taught by learning scientists; this study tested a "Do-it-Yourself" approach in which disciplinary-expert instructors designed and implemented PF with advice from a learning scientist but no activity-specific feedback. The authors argue "Implementation by instructors (disciplinary experts) is an impor tant hurdle that novel pedagogies should clear before they can be considered relevant to a wider audience," and the results support scalability and ecological validity of PF in post-secondary biology.
requirements: Iterative refinement to achieve fidelity of PF implementation
General design guidelines (e.g., from Kapur and Bielaczyc) plus advice from a learning scientist on motivation, literature, and design principles
constraints: Only one instructor taught PF; transfer to instructors with even less support remains untested
Quasi-experimental design with self-selected sections, compensated statistically
target_learners: first-year university students in large-enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding in discipline-specific topics
examples: The PF instructor designed activities from Kapur and Bielaczyc's guidelines with a learning scientist providing only general emphases, not activity-specific feedback

article_title: Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program
citation: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program. npj Science of Learning 5:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00076-2
title: Discovery: a term-long inquiry-based biomedical engineering program delivered by graduate students with high school teachers
description: Discovery is "a term-long inquiry-focused learning model delivered by STEM graduate students in collaboration with high school teachers, in the context of biomedical engineering". Each 12-week term, entire class cohorts of Grade 11–12 students work in teams of 3–4 on projects modelled on an engineering capstone, iterating between classroom work and four visits to university teaching facilities, culminating in a research poster symposium. Deliverables include a background essay, client meeting, proposal, progress report, poster, and final presentation, assessed by high school teachers as 10–15% of the course grade.
requirements: Collaboration between university trainees (3–6 lead instructors per term at ~1:8 mentor-to-student ratio) and high school teachers, with instructor training via a teaching workshop
Students must be able to independently commute to campus for hands-on sessions (~40 min transit in this study)
constraints: Teachers may find the framework difficult to implement depending on resources and institutional support, particularly if post-secondary collaboration is inaccessible
Subjects where experiments are logistically or financially simpler may be more feasible adoption routes
target_learners: Senior high school students (Grades 11–12) in university-preparatory science courses at non-specialized public schools, from diverse cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking and problem solving through inquiry
Application of subject-specific biology, chemistry, and physics curriculum concepts to real-world biomedical engineering problems
Familiarity with the scientific method and engineering design principles
examples: Over five terms, 268 instances of participation (170 students, participating 1–4 times) completed the program at a partner school that scores in the top decile of the board's Learning Opportunities Index
key_sources: Davenport Huyer, L., Callaghan, N. I., Dicks, S., Scherer, E., Shukalyuk, A. I., Jou, M. & Kilkenny, D. (2020). Enhancing senior high school student engagement and academic performance using an inclusive and scalable inquiry-based program. npj Science of Learning 5:17. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00076-2

article_title: Does students’ awareness of school-track-related stereotypes exacerbate inequalities in education?
citation: Lisa Bardach, Claudia Neuendorf, Kou Murayama, Thorsten Fahrbach, Michel Knigge, Benjamin Nagengast, and Ulrich Trautwein. (2023). Does students' awareness of school-track-related stereotypes exacerbate inequalities in education? npj Science of Learning 8:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00203-9
title: Differentiation-polarization theory extended to students' awareness of school-track-related stereotypes
description: Differentiation-polarization theory holds that sorting students into tracks polarizes their school attitudes: higher-track belonging reflects higher status, whereas lower-track students lose status and react against the values of ability and hard work, so that an "anti-school culture" emerges in the lower tracks. The authors extend the polarization component to students' awareness of how the public perceives their track, predicting the most negative perceptions in the lowest track. The study's finding that lowest-track students reported the highest stereotype awareness in all waves is presented as supporting this extension.
requirements: The theory presupposes an institutionalized tracking system that assigns students to differentially valued tracks with visible status labels
constraints: The authors note the extension concerns awareness of stereotypes pertaining to a student's own track, not stereotypes about other tracks
target_learners: secondary school students in stratified (tracked) school systems
target_learning_goals: students' awareness of negative school-track-related stereotypes and its role in academic engagement, self-concept, and achievement
examples: The study applied the theory to predict mean differences in stereotype awareness between Hauptschule, Realschule, and Mittelschule students across four waves
key_sources: Lisa Bardach, Claudia Neuendorf, Kou Murayama, Thorsten Fahrbach, Michel Knigge, Benjamin Nagengast, and Ulrich Trautwein. (2023). Does students' awareness of school-track-related stereotypes exacerbate inequalities in education? npj Science of Learning 8:59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00203-9

article_title: Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces
citation: Zhang, Y., & Dyson, B. J. (2026). Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00414-w
title: Dice Dual zero-sum number-selection game with Pre/During/Post phase structure
description: Dice Dual is a zero-sum competitive game in which "both the participant and a computerized opponent select one number of a virtual 6-sided die on each trial", with even or odd sums determining wins, counterbalanced across participants. Each block contains Pre, During, and Post phases: exploitable opponent behaviour types (repetition, alternation) in Pre and Post, and an artificially fixed win rate in During. The authors used it across three experiments to index pattern acquisition, suppression, and reactivation via win rate and optimal behaviour rate (OBR).
requirements: A computerized opponent with exploitable behaviour types (repetition or alternation) in Pre and Post phases
A fixed win rate programmed in the During phase to simulate punishment or reinforcement
constraints: Punishment and reinforcement labels are descriptive of outcome valence, not formal operant conditioning or computational reinforcement learning mechanisms
Phase transitions were covert, with no on-screen cues marking a new phase
target_learning_goals: Strategic adaptation to opponent patterns under outcome feedback
Balancing reuse of old response patterns with acquisition of new ones
examples: Participants completed 504 trials of Dice Dual in 4 counterbalanced blocks of 126 trials, responding with 6 keys while win/lose feedback was shown as "WIN +1" or "LOSE -1"
key_sources: Zhang, Y., & Dyson, B. J. (2026). Recover or discover: How outcome feedback shapes response patterns within game spaces. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00414-w

article_title: Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently
citation: Teodóra Vékony, Claire Pleche, Orsolya Pesthy, Karolina Janacsek and Dezso Nemeth. (2022). Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently. npj Science of Learning 7:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00144-9
title: When designing learning studies, take into account the possible differences between measured competence and performance
description: The article argues that single-session measurements capture momentary performance rather than long-term acquired knowledge. It states that "the measured momentary performance is not always equivalent to the acquired knowledge (competence)" and recommends that "using only a single session to evaluate learning might be problematic" when describing long-term knowledge, since contextual factors such as fatigue, practice or overlearning can influence measured performance.
requirements: Testing in more than one instructional/measurement context, e.g. re-testing acquired knowledge under equal speed-accuracy emphasis after initial learning, as the study did with a Same Instruction Phase.
constraints: The demonstrated competence-performance dissociation concerned probability-based learning; serial-order-based learning showed no instruction effect in either phase.
target_learning_goals: procedural learning of probability-based and serial-order-based regularities
examples: Participants learned under speed or accuracy instructions and were later re-tested with equal emphasis, revealing that the speed-group advantage in probability-based learning disappeared when acquired knowledge was measured.
key_sources: Teodóra Vékony, Claire Pleche, Orsolya Pesthy, Karolina Janacsek and Dezso Nemeth. (2022). Speed and accuracy instructions affect two aspects of skill learning differently. npj Science of Learning 7:27. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00144-9

article_title: Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions
citation: Luigi A. E. Degni, Sara Garofalo, Gianluca Finotti, Francesca Starita, Trevor W. Robbins & Giuseppe di Pellegrino. (2024). Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00246-6
title: Two-bias framework of motivational cue effects on instrumental actions: direction bias and intensity bias
description: The article organizes motivational cue effects on value-based decisions into two distinct biases. The direction bias (outcome-specific transfer) occurs when an outcome-predictive cue favors actions congruent with the outcome it predicts, and is related to a cognitive top-down strategy exploiting the cue's informative value. The intensity bias (general transfer) describes how outcome-predictive cues "generally enhance or energize instrumental responses, even if directed toward different (but motivationally similar) outcomes", attributed to a general cue-induced increase of motivation. The two biases are measured with different dependent variables (percentage of congruent responses versus vigor) and, per the article, show a double dissociation across measures.
requirements: Separately trained Pavlovian stimulus-outcome and instrumental response-outcome associations, and distinct trial types and dependent measures to disentangle the two biases
constraints: The article notes the direction bias has been reported to require high-level cognitive abilities such as working memory and conscious perception of the cues, and that the intensity bias is detectable through vigor measures rather than number of responses
target_learners: adult human participants in decision-making and motivational research
target_learning_goals: understanding how motivational cues bias the direction and intensity of instrumental actions
examples: Experiment 1 used an appetitive slot-machine PIT task with tailored food rewards; Experiment 2 used an aversive space-war PIT task with 100 dB aversive noises and grip-force measurement
key_sources: Luigi A. E. Degni, Sara Garofalo, Gianluca Finotti, Francesca Starita, Trevor W. Robbins & Giuseppe di Pellegrino. (2024). Sex differences in motivational biases over instrumental actions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00246-6

article_title: The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence
citation: Levitan, D., Gal-Ben-Ari, S., Heise, C., Rosenberg, T., Elkobi, A., Inberg, S., Sala, C. & Rosenblum, K. (2016). The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.1
title: Differential-role theory: increased cortical protein synthesis promotes LTM formation whereas decreased protein synthesis promotes LTM persistence
description: An explanatory account of long-term memory phases in which protein synthesis plays different, stage-specific roles in the gustatory cortex. The article proposes that "an increase in protein synthesis promotes LTM formation, whereas reduced protein synthesis promotes LTM persistence", so that LTM remains sensitive to protein synthesis inhibition in cortex at least 3 days after acquisition. Building on this and related hippocampal findings, it further suggests "LTM persistence has at least two different time phases, each with a different underlying molecular mechanism".
requirements: Stereotactic drug infusion targeting the cortical region storing the memory trace, with delayed memory testing to unmask persistence effects
constraints: Evidence is from the CTA paradigm and the gustatory cortex in rats; the authors state additional experiments are needed to reveal the extent of generalization to other learning paradigms and brain regions
target_learners: male Wistar Hola rats undergoing conditioned taste aversion learning
target_learning_goals: formation and persistence of long-term associative taste memory
examples: Anisomycin before acquisition impaired CTA LTM formation, while the same drug 3 days after acquisition enhanced persistence tested at 14 days, and APV failed to recapitulate the enhancement
key_sources: Levitan, D., Gal-Ben-Ari, S., Heise, C., Rosenberg, T., Elkobi, A., Inberg, S., Sala, C. & Rosenblum, K. (2016). The differential role of cortical protein synthesis in taste memory formation and persistence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.1

article_title: Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus
citation: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6
title: Discriminative-contrast account of the interleaving effect: interleaved practice trains identifying which concept or approach is relevant to solve a given problem
description: This account explains why mixing problems supports learning: on exams students are tested on determining "which concept or approach is relevant to solve a given problem", a skill blocked homework never practices. Interleaving "draws learners’attention away from similar surface features and toward key structural features that deﬁne and distinguish concepts". The article also notes interleaved sets distribute topics over time, adding spacing benefits that protect learning from forgetting. The authors use this account to predict, and to explain, larger benefits for students with weaker prior knowledge.
requirements: Requires topics that can be distinguished so students can practice identifying which concept or approach applies to each problem
constraints: Interleaving benefits are reduced when discriminative contrast is disrupted by introducing spacing (fillers) between examples, per cited experiments
target_learners: Learners with lower prior knowledge or weaker mathematics preparation
target_learning_goals: Selecting the appropriate concept or problem-solving approach for a given problem
Long-lasting retention of learned concepts
examples: The study's interleaved homework sets mixed problems on different topics across assignments so students practiced both individual skills and approach identification
key_sources: Steve Bennoun, Veronica X. Yan, & Alice Xu. (2026). Mixing problems increases performance of all students but especially of low-achieving ones in college calculus. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00450-6

article_title: The Civic Mission of MOOCs: Engagement across Political Differences in Online Forums
citation: Yeomans, M., Stewart, B. M., Mavon, K., Kindel, A., Tingley, D., & Reich, J. (2018). The Civic Mission of MOOCs: Engagement across Political Differences in Online Forums. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 28, 553–589. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0161-0
title: Discourse: a software tool for human coding of MOOC forum posts in context
description: Discourse is a software tool the authors built to handle forum data formats and to let coders "read and rate within the context of the other posts in the thread that preceded it". A team of coders (at least two per post) classified 24,556 posts from both courses by writers' intent; over 90% agreement with trace metadata supported using raw trace data in the reported analyses.
requirements: Requires a team of at least two human coders per post to classify writers' intent in conversational context
constraints: Validated against trace data in these two courses; coder consensus agreed with the metadata structure over 90% of the time
target_learners: MOOC forum participants in politically-themed courses
target_learning_goals: Measuring peer interaction and deliberative engagement across political differences
examples: Coders labelled each reply and comment as substantive, a short yes, or off-topic; off-topic posts (0.5% of all posts) were removed and 64% of on-topic comments counted as substantive

article_title: Can Online Discussion Participation Predict Group Project Performance? Investigating the Roles of Linguistic Features and Participation Patterns
citation: Jaebong Yoo & Jihie Kim. (2014). Can Online Discussion Participation Predict Group Project Performance? Investigating the Roles of Linguistic Features and Participation Patterns. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0010-8
title: A framework for predicting project performance from online discussion participation features
description: The article presents a procedural framework in which online student activity data is collected from discussion platforms, pre-processed (noise removal, normalization), transformed into predictive variables, and analyzed against project grades. "Predictive V ariable Generation in Fig. 7 mainly consists of four modules: Role (Sink/Source) classifiers, Linguistic Tools (LIWC and Coh-Metrix), Work Patterns, and Degree of Participation." Its purpose is instructional assessment: alerting instructors about students who may need assistance.

Human-annotated training data is needed to build the automatic role classifiers
constraints: The presented work focused on a computer science course; the authors plan to apply the approach to other engineering courses
Discussion was optional and not graded in the studied course
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in project-based computer science courses

identifying students needing assistance
examples: Eight semesters of phpBB and Moodle data from an Operating Systems course were transformed into a consistent XML format and analyzed with the framework

article_title: Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor
citation: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2
title: Dialog-box interface that lets the software perform rule steps
description: LOGAX uses a dialog box in which the student chooses which rule to apply and fills in step numbers or formula parameters, while the software performs the step. The article explains: "The reason to use a dialog box in LOGAX to add new proof lines is that a student can concentrate on proof construction." Grounded in scaffolding theory on reducing degrees of freedom, this design lets students focus on steps closely related to the learning goal and reduces syntax errors, since only small formulae still need to be entered by hand.
requirements: Students should already have extensive training in writing syntactically correct formulae before using the interface
constraints: Students can still make syntax errors in the smaller formulae entered when adding, for example, an axiom instantiation
target_learners: students in logic courses who already write correct formulae
target_learning_goals: concentrating on proof construction strategies rather than formula syntax
examples: To add a Modus Ponens the student fills in at least two of the three line numbers and LOGAX performs the step automatically, adding a forward or backward step to the proof.
key_sources: Josje Lodder, Bastiaan Heeren, Johan Jeuring, Wendy Neijenhuis. (2021). Generation and Use of Hints and Feedback in a Hilbert-Style Axiomatic Proof Tutor. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:99-133. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00222-2

article_title: The Evolution of Research on Digital Education
citation: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z
title: Six fundamental trends structure the evolution of AIED and learning technologies
description: The article organizes 25 years of AIED research around six trends: more physical, less semantic, more social, less design, more open, and more teachers. The author states: "I deconstruct the evolution of learning technologies into six fundamental trends." Each trend traces a shift in what learning environments are and who participates in them, and together they "form a beam of evolution vectors" rather than isolated changes.
requirements: Analysis takes a broad perspective covering communities around AIED, including Intelligent Tutoring Systems, CSCL, Learning Sciences, Learning Analytics, Education Data Mining and MOOC communities
constraints: The six trends are artificially segmented from each other; in reality they form a beam of evolution vectors
The 25-year span is an arbitrary time span defined by the journal anniversary
target_learners: researchers and designers of learning technologies
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical evolution of AI in education research
examples: The trends are used to structure the whole article, one section per trend, from physicality to teacher orchestration
key_sources: Pierre Dillenbourg. (2016). The Evolution of Research on Digital Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0106-z

article_title: Going Beyond the Problem Given: How Human Tutors Use Post-Solution Discussions to Support Transfer
citation: Sandra Katz, David Allbritton, John Connelly. (2003). Going Beyond the Problem Given: How Human Tutors Use Post-Solution Discussions to Support Transfer. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.79-116. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197313
title: A framework for describing distributed plans for reflection spanning problem solving and post-solution discussion
description: The article proposes a framework describing how reflective activity is distributed across problem-solving discussion and post-solution dialogue in tutoring. It was induced from Study 1 analyses that identified "several tutorial strategies that are distributed between problem solving and post-solution reflection." The framework organizes these strategies as plans for reflection rather than as isolated post-hoc activities, grounded in the observed roles of post-solution dialogues such as explaining conceptual knowledge and integrating it with strategic knowledge.
requirements: Applicable to tutoring contexts where problem-solving dialogue and post-solution reflection both occur, as observed in Andes tutoring sessions
constraints: Proposed based on analyses of a small set of tutors (seven tutors, 15 students) in one physics tutoring domain
target_learners: physics students working with human tutors in the Andes tutoring system
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and transfer in physics problem solving
examples: Study 1 tutors guided 15 students through Andes problems, and transcript analysis identified tutorial strategies distributed between problem solving and reflection
