article_title: The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations
citation: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3
title: Paradigm shift from cognitivist belief-models to dialogue as collective thinking
description: The article argues that the theory underlying the negotiation model was radically changed over 20 years: "from a cognitivist model of thoughts underlying dialogue, to a view of dialogue itself as one manifestation of collective thinking". Methodologically this means "the group rather than individuals is taken as the unit of cognitive analysis", focusing on co-elaboration of the discursive object using the communicative acts and transformation operators of the original model. The shift followed the 1990s situated cognition debate and the move to computer-mediated group communication, and it reframes collaborative learning as the relation between acceptance in dialogue and what students believe.
requirements: Analysis of interaction corpora at the group level rather than attribution of underlying individual beliefs
constraints: The author concluded the original NTD model was not, in all its elements, a basis for analysing significant bodies of interaction corpus data
target_learning_goals: co-elaboration of knowledge in and by dialogue
examples: An attempted beliefs-desires-intentions analysis of a 40-minute physics dialogue transcript was abandoned as empirically unfeasible
key_sources: Michael J. Baker. (2015). The Negotiation of Meaning in Epistemic Situations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0050-3

article_title: A Collaborative Case Study System for Distance Learning
citation: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307
title: Collaborative case study work at a distance as a learning design
description: The pattern is distance learning from case studies: two or more learners at a distance collaborate on a case study activity using a shared web-based environment. The article frames it as "enabling collaboration between two or more learners at a distance on a case study activity," with learners "required to collaborate in order to solve a case study." LeCS instantiates this pattern with collaboration tools and learning-process support.
requirements: A collaborative learning environment must be provided so that distant learners can work together on the case study solution
target_learning_goals: case study problem solving through collaboration
examples: The empirical study simulated a scenario in which a pair of subjects at a distance collaborated on a case study, and LeCS was built to support such scenarios.
key_sources: Marta C. Rosatelli, John Self. (2004). A Collaborative Case Study System For Distance Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 14, pp.97-125. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197307

article_title: Uncovering Blind Spots in Education Ethics: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
citation: Ana Mouta, Ana María Pinto-Llorente, Eva María Torrecilla-Sánchez. (2023). Uncovering Blind Spots in Education Ethics: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00384-9
title: Dialogic ethics framework for AIED recognising AI as a non-neutral tool
description: The review frames AIED ethics through dialogic ethics that reflect participation from diverse educational communities, and argues for recognising AI as a non-neutral tool. It proposes that "Ethical reasoning seems to be able to offer such considerations and possible transitions a sustainable conceptual support", asking how ethical frameworks can incorporate dialogic ethics reflecting diverse communities' participation. The framework spans data ownership, equity, emotions, and training, aiming to strengthen debates on the ethics of education itself.
requirements: Ethical frameworks must incorporate dialogic ethics reflecting the principles of participation from diverse educational communities
constraints: The review limits its evidence base to peer-reviewed publications from 2011–2022 in English, French, Portuguese, and Spanish
target_learners: K-12 and higher education stakeholders including teachers, governance bodies, technology industry, and policy-makers
target_learning_goals: Ethical use and design of AI in education
Ethical development of educational stakeholders
examples: The review synthesises 107 papers mapping applications, cultural inclusion, emotions, capacity building, and regulations to identify blind spots in AIED ethics
key_sources: Ana Mouta, Ana María Pinto-Llorente, Eva María Torrecilla-Sánchez. (2023). Uncovering Blind Spots in Education Ethics: Insights from a Systematic Literature Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00384-9

article_title: Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT
citation: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3
title: DiCE-based counterfactual modelling configured with mutable, range-constrained features to generate feasible prescriptive pathways
description: DiCE (Diverse Counterfactual Explanations) is used in Step 6 to simulate what-if scenarios and generate candidate prescriptive feedback suggestions by treating counterfactual generation as an optimisation problem. The article notes that "counterfactual modelling needs to be performed using features upon which actionable steps can be taken," so a new model was trained on predominantly mutable features, with immutable demographics removed and features constrained to feasible and realistic ranges. Several candidate pathways are generated, unrealistic ones filtered and discarded, and the most realistic selected for feedback generation.
requirements: A separate predictive model trained on an alternative, predominantly mutable feature set, with some compromise in accuracy expected
Features constrained within feasible and realistic value ranges to generate feasible pathways
constraints: Use of only actionable features tended to produce weaker models, so stabilising features like Age Description were retained
target_learners: at-risk learners for whom tailored remedial advice is generated
target_learning_goals: identifying minimal changes in learning behaviour (engagement, assignment marks, on-time submissions) that would flip the prediction to successful completion
examples: Target features included engagement levels with the VLE, average assignment marks, and total number of on-time assignment submissions; immutable features like learner age were removed from counterfactual variation
key_sources: Teo Susnjak. (2024). Beyond Predictive Learning Analytics Modelling and onto Explainable Artificial Intelligence with Prescriptive Analytics and ChatGPT. Int J Artif Intell Educ 34:452–482. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00336-3

article_title: Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners’ Willingness to Communicate
citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: DiMaCA: a dialogue management model combining communication strategies and affective backchannels to foster WTC-friendly agent conversations
description: DiMaCA is a dialogue management model specifying rules for when an embodied conversational agent deploys communication strategies (CS) and affective backchannels (AB) during L2 conversations. Its rationale is 'increasing L2 learners' confidence via CSs and reducing their level of anxiety towards communication via ABs', in line with MacIntyre's WTC model. The model is implemented as a strategies management module that detects six conversation states (e.g., learner silent, learner NUNA, agent NUNA) and triggers adapted CS and AB accordingly, with CS chosen in a heuristically predefined order and AB chosen stochastically.
requirements: A dialogue script defining the conversation domain, intent detection via external speech recognition services, and databases of CS and AB options per conversation state
constraints: The Guessing strategy is only an approximation: the agent does not perform dynamic reasoning about learner intention from a wide range of possibilities but relies on a narrow range of expected answers specified in advance in the dialogue script
target_learners: Japanese undergraduate and graduate EFL learners
target_learning_goals: Willingness to communicate in English as a second language
examples: In a restaurant scenario, when the learner is NUNA the system first uses Repetition, then Simplification, then Code-switching across successive turns to make it progressively easier for the learner to overcome the difficulty
key_sources: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6

article_title: Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners’ Willingness to Communicate
citation: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6
title: Nine communication strategies and four categories of affective backchannels implemented in DiMaCA
description: The authors selected nine communication strategies from Dörnyei and Scott's taxonomy (including Simplification/Approximation, Code-switching, Asking clarification, Suggesting AP, Asking confirmation, Asking repetition, Expressing NU, Guessing, Repetition) chosen for probable WTC-friendliness and technical feasibility. They also introduce four categories of affective backchannels — Congratulatory, Encouraging, Sympathetic, and Reassuring AB — 'to enable ECAs to explicitly convey thoughtful support to learners by congratulating them, cheering them up, or showing sympathy in accordance with the interaction state'.
requirements: CS selection follows a heuristically predefined order per state; AB selection is stochastic within the triggered category
constraints: Response reject was excluded because it cannot be considered a WTC-friendly strategy, illustrating the selection criteria applied
target_learners: L2 learners with low willingness to communicate
target_learning_goals: Overcoming communication pitfalls and reducing anxiety during L2 conversation
examples: When the learner remains silent, the system first applies a Reassuring or Encouraging AB and then conducts a comprehension check to determine whether the learner is NUNA or UNA
key_sources: Emmanuel Ayedoun, Yuki Hayashi, Kazuhisa Seta. (2018). Adding Communicative and Affective Strategies to an Embodied Conversational Agent to Enhance Second Language Learners' Willingness to Communicate. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-018-0171-6

article_title: Instructional design for tutoring on interactive platforms: creating educational interventions overcoming the digital gap
citation: Rodríguez Rincón, Y., Munárriz, A., Campión Arrastia, M. J., & Goicoechea López-Vailo, M. I. (2025). Instructional design for tutoring on interactive platforms: creating educational interventions overcoming the digital gap. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10516-8
title: Diagnostic-then-reinforcement flow with hint and No Answer options as metacognitive axis
description: The article's core pedagogical pattern is a flow chart in which a first diagnostic multiple-choice question (correct answer, at least three incorrect answers, a NA option, and a hint option) routes students: correct answers advance to the next concept; incorrect or NA answers trigger a tutoring process with theory and exercises of progressive difficulty; the hint option displays a theoretical orientation followed by a second diagnostic question of similar difficulty. The article states that "Both hint and NA answer options constitute the metacognitive axis of the model since they allow learners to reflect on whether they have adequate control over the concepts to be reinforced."
requirements: Diagnostic questions must integrate all theories related to the concept so competence can be demonstrated with a single question
Students must complete all exercises correctly before advancing to the next concept
constraints: The hint should be a mere orientation and should not include the theory itself
target_learning_goals: quantitative concept mastery
metacognitive self-assessment
examples: Fig. 3 shows the flow chart of the instructional design for educational reinforcement
key_sources: Rodríguez Rincón, Y., Munárriz, A., Campión Arrastia, M. J., & Goicoechea López-Vailo, M. I. (2025). Instructional design for tutoring on interactive platforms: creating educational interventions overcoming the digital gap. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10516-8

article_title: Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach
citation: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y
title: Nine design principles for teaching digital innovation skills through authentic learning
description: A pattern for designing learning environments that develop digital business innovation skills, refined over three DBR iterations at a South African university. The final principles are: "Ensure collaboration takes place", "Provide opportunities for students to find their own solutions", "Implement a working digital innovation in a business", "Incorporate a design-thinking ethos", "Ensure that students utilise interdisciplinary skills", "Implement a formal process of reflection", "Allow for experimentation", "Ensure that tasks culminate in a capstone project", and "Partner with entrepreneurs". Each principle is mapped to authentic learning elements (A1–A9) and skill sets (S1–S8) from the Kereluik et al. framework.
requirements: Industry partners willing to host student digital innovation projects
A blended learning environment supporting online and face-to-face collaboration
Assessment rubrics covering the entire process, not just the end product
constraints: Conducted at a single university, limiting generalisability of the findings
The study's design and approach may not apply to other contexts or disciplines
target_learners: Information Systems students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Digital innovation skills
Collaboration
Design thinking
Interdisciplinary problem-solving
examples: Students worked in groups of five with industry partners to design and implement digital innovations such as eCommerce websites using design thinking and agile methods
key_sources: van den Berg, C., & Bozalek, V. (2024). Design principles to develop digital innovation skills: a design-based research approach. Education Tech Research Dev, 72, 947–972. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10308-y

article_title: Supporting school teachers’ rapid engagement with online education
citation: Abaci, S., Robertson, J., Linklater, H., & McNeill, F. (2021). Supporting school teachers' rapid engagement with online education. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 29-34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09839-5
title: Future versions of the TPD-for-OBL framework should differentiate between school and higher education settings
description: Because schools and higher education institutions operate within different parameters, the authors suggest "future versions of the framework should differentiate between these settings". The differing parameters they name include institutional autonomy, in-house resources and staff for professional development, and student engagement and parental involvement in online learning. This recommendation follows directly from their application of the framework to primary and secondary teacher support during emergency remote teaching.
requirements: Framework developers should account for operational differences between educational levels when synthesizing TPD components
constraints: Derived from one team's reflection on a single emergency support effort in Scotland; the authors state evaluation of the webinar series is still to be undertaken
target_learning_goals: design of teacher professional development for online and blended learning
examples: The authors recommend policy makers, initial teacher education institutions, and professional bodies develop a clear vision of teaching that includes capacity to practice outside physical classrooms
key_sources: Abaci, S., Robertson, J., Linklater, H., & McNeill, F. (2021). Supporting school teachers' rapid engagement with online education. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 29-34. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09839-5

article_title: Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire
citation: Peart, M., Gutiérrez-Esteban, P., and Cubo-Delgado, S. (2020). Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, pp. 3327-3351. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11423-020-09824-Y
title: DIGISOC questionnaire: a self-assessment instrument for digital and socio-civic skills of young people aged 16–35
description: The DIGISOC questionnaire is a self-report instrument developed to invite young people aged 16–35 to assess their own digital and socio-civic skills. The article states the aim is to "develop a valid and reliable instrument that invites young people, aged 16–35, to assess their digital and socio-civic skills." It was produced in English and Spanish and validated for content and construct validity and reliability.
requirements: Content and construct validity and reliability were assessed as part of the instrument's development
constraints: Designed for young people aged 16–35
target_learning_goals: digital skills
socio-civic skills
digital citizenship
examples: The development process involved a literature review, designing and constructing dimensions and items, and assessing validity and reliability
key_sources: Peart, M., Gutiérrez-Esteban, P., and Cubo-Delgado, S. (2020). Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, pp. 3327-3351. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11423-020-09824-Y

article_title: Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire
citation: Peart, M., Gutiérrez-Esteban, P., and Cubo-Delgado, S. (2020). Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, pp. 3327-3351. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11423-020-09824-Y
title: Digital citizenship as capacity to foster growth opportunities and minimize risks and divides from digital technology use
description: The article frames digital citizenship as a dual capacity: it includes the ability to create opportunities through digital technology while also reducing its harms and inequalities. The article states that "digital citizenship includes the capacity to foster growth opportunities and also, can help to minimize risks and divides from the use of digital technology." Educating youth through digital and socio-civic skills is presented as the route to improving digital citizenship.
requirements: Education of youth in digital and socio-civic skills to improve digital citizenship
constraints: Framed for today's society and education contexts
target_learning_goals: digital citizenship
digital and socio-civic skills
examples: The study intends to identify core aspects that help or hinder youth participation and contribute to educating youth in digital citizenship
key_sources: Peart, M., Gutiérrez-Esteban, P., and Cubo-Delgado, S. (2020). Development of the digital and socio-civic skills (DIGISOC) questionnaire. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, pp. 3327-3351. https://doi.org/10.1007/S11423-020-09824-Y

article_title: Instructional interface’s blueprint for guiding instructional-technological interactions’ research: the Big Bang shift in K-12
citation: Assaf, N. (2021). Instructional interface's blueprint for guiding instructional-technological interactions' research: the Big Bang shift in K-12. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 207–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09885-z
title: Treat the shift to digital as a creators' mindset shift, not merely a technology shift
description: The article argues that when education shifts to digital formats, the change required is not only technological but a transformation in how creators of learning experiences think. It states that "shifting to digital is not just a tech shift but a worldwide creators' mindset shifts." Designers of online instruction should therefore approach digital transitions as opportunities to rethink instructional design rather than simply port content to new platforms.
requirements: Designers of instructional-technological interactions must reconceive their role during digital transitions
constraints: Articulated in the context of the COVID-19 emergency shift to digital K-12 education
target_learners: K-12 learners in online and remote learning
target_learning_goals: Effective instructional design for digital learning environments
key_sources: Assaf, N. (2021). Instructional interface's blueprint for guiding instructional-technological interactions' research: the Big Bang shift in K-12. Education Tech Research Dev 69, 207–211. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09885-z

article_title: Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs
citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0
title: An interdisciplinary framework differentiates diagnostic competences into professional knowledge base, epistemic-diagnostic activities, and diagnostic quality
description: The article adopts the framework by Heitzmann et al. (2019), shown in its Fig. 2, for facilitating diagnostic competences with simulations. Knowledge and competences are differentiated "according to types of knowledge (i.e., the structure of knowledge) as well as content-related facets of knowledge". The framework links individual learning prerequisites, instructional support (scaffolding such as prompting, role-taking, and reflection phases), epistemic-diagnostic activities like generating hypotheses and evaluating evidence, and diagnostic quality comprising accuracy and efficiency, within a learning-process and test-performance loop.
requirements: Requires conceptualization of professional knowledge base, epistemic-diagnostic activities, and diagnostic quality in the simulated diagnostic situation
constraints: Serves simulations assessing and training knowledge and competences in medical education and teacher education
target_learners: medical and teacher education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: diagnostic competences, including diagnostic accuracy and efficiency
examples: COSIMA's research committee drafted a preliminary conceptual model based on this framework in its grant proposal
key_sources: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0

article_title: How the design and complexity of concept maps influence cognitive learning processes
citation: Felix Krieglstein, Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey. (2022). How the design and complexity of concept maps influence cognitive learning processes. Education Tech Research Dev 70, 99–118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10083-2
title: Disorientation as a meaningful supplement to current extraneous cognitive load measurement
description: The authors propose that navigational disorientation should be treated as a distinct, measurable source of extraneous cognitive load. They argue current ECL questionnaires capture "extraneous processing while learning relatively unspecific", and that even the instrument distinguishing navigation subsumes it in a single item whose adequacy is "questionable from a psychometric view". Because disorientation and ECL "correlate very highly with each other", structure-driven disorientation may be a specific precursor that current instruments miss.
requirements: Future measures should capture navigational disorientation specifically, e.g. with factor-analytically validated items about structure overview and getting lost
constraints: The proposed items "require factor-analytical examinations" before use
target_learners: higher education students learning with concept maps or hypertext-like materials
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous cognitive load during learning with structured visual materials
examples: The authors list five candidate items such as "It was difficult to get an overview of the structure of the learning material."
key_sources: Felix Krieglstein, Sascha Schneider, Maik Beege, Günter Daniel Rey. (2022). How the design and complexity of concept maps influence cognitive learning processes. Education Tech Research Dev 70, 99–118. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10083-2

article_title: A set of discriminable surface colors and symbols for coding in animated training panels
citation: Twyford, L. (1959). Research Abstracts. https://eric.ed.gov
title: A set of discriminable surface colors and symbols for coding in animated training panels
description: A Naval Training Devices Center technical report developed a color-code and symbol system for animated training panels indicating organizational and functional relationships among components and changes in physical state, such as fuel as it is burned. Ten colors were selected with federal specification numbers, and the symbols included diamonds, pyramids, dashes, squares, wavy line, straight line, large dots, and small dots. Codes were chosen from a literature study and laboratory-tested against selected backgrounds.
requirements: Codes were laboratory-tested against selected backgrounds before selection, using discrimination of Landolt broken rings in four positions against ten pre-selected background panels.
constraints: The system was developed for use on animated training panels in naval training devices, indicating relationships among components and changes in the physical state of matter.
target_learners: naval trainees using animated training panels
target_learning_goals: reading organizational and functional relationships among components and changes in physical state on training panels
examples: Color discrimination was tested with Landolt broken rings of various colors in four positions against ten pre-selected background panels; symbol coding involved ranking pairs of symbols presented in two spatial orders.
key_sources: Twyford, L. (1959). Research Abstracts. https://eric.ed.gov

article_title: Designing for interaction, thinking and academic achievement in a Tanzanian undergraduate chemistry course
citation: Sydney Enock Msonde, Jan Van Aalst. (2017). Designing for interaction, thinking and academic achievement in a Tanzanian undergraduate chemistry course. Education Tech Research Dev (2017) 65:1389–1413. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9531-4
title: Use asynchronous discussion forums as a low-bandwidth interactive e-learning design, optionally coupled with podcasts where bandwidth allows
description: The article recommends that instructors in higher education in low-bandwidth contexts design e-courses around asynchronous discussion forums, because "effective use of discussion forums can produce important learning effects and is a low-bandwidth strategy". Coupling podcasts with forums may further enhance learning effects, but podcasts are "not a low-bandwidth addition" and require more bandwidth and additional instructor effort. The article suggests distributing podcast materials offline where live streaming is infeasible.
requirements: Instructor pedagogical strategies that facilitate and deepen online discourse, including questions on ideas and questions for ideas
Students and instructors develop expertise in using forums and podcasts effectively
constraints: With the present technological infrastructure in Tanzania, live streaming of podcasts is unlikely to be feasible, especially in rural areas with limited bandwidth
The HIL design requires more bandwidth and additional instructor effort
target_learners: Undergraduate students in large-enrollment science courses in Tanzania and similar low-bandwidth higher-education contexts
target_learning_goals: Student interaction and engagement
Higher-order thinking (cognitive and metacognitive)
Academic achievement in chemistry
examples: In the study, 102 undergraduates were randomly assigned to tutorial sections using NIL, MIL (discussion forums added) or HIL (podcasts plus forums) designs across three chemistry topics, with achievement measured by pre- and post-tests per unit
key_sources: Sydney Enock Msonde, Jan Van Aalst. (2017). Designing for interaction, thinking and academic achievement in a Tanzanian undergraduate chemistry course. Education Tech Research Dev (2017) 65:1389–1413. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9531-4

article_title: Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
citation: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2
title: Digital tutors as intermediaries between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
description: The article proposes the concept of a chatbot-based digital tutor that acts as an intermediary among the three actors of large-scale lecture settings. It addresses three identified communication flaws through three mediated communications: students interact with the tutor in "simulated one-to-one tutoring settings based on the computers are social actors paradigm", teaching assistants get feedback about student progress, and lecturers get access to feedback about students' learning progress and state of knowledge. The concept targets long-term support across a whole lecture period rather than short-term chatbot use.
requirements: The tutor must provide a natural language and social interaction interface (R1) and be available all the time on common student devices (DP2)
constraints: Designed for large-scale formal educational settings where one-to-one instruction cannot be achieved due to resource constraints such as the lack of lecturers and teaching assistants
target_learners: students in large-scale university lecture courses
target_learning_goals: individualized learning support and feedback during a full lecture period, including practicing content and formative assessment
examples: The concept was implemented as a progressive web app and evaluated in an introductory statistics lecture at a large German university over a four-month field study
key_sources: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2

article_title: Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers
citation: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2
title: Chatbot-based digital tutor app (progressive web app) for large-scale lectures
description: The developed artifact is a fully-functional progressive web app with a chat-based student interface, content overlays, and a sidebar, built with the Bootstrap framework and AJAX calls to RESTful web services, with a separate AdminLTE-based interface for teaching assistants and lecturers. Message processing uses the NLP.js library, with the natural language processing classifier "trained with approximately 3000 dialog entries". It integrates a learning object data storage, a micro content database, formative quiz question storage, an audience response system, and a learning action log.
requirements: Learning objects, micro contents, and quiz questions must be authored and stored in the backend components; the NLP classifier requires training dialog entries
constraints: The tutor can deliver materials such as lecture slides or recordings only as files (e.g., PDFs or videos) rather than conversing about their content
target_learners: students in an introductory statistics lecture
target_learning_goals: question answering, formative practice with instant feedback, learning content provision, and feedback collection across a lecture period
examples: In the field study the app collected over 9100 audience response responses in in-class sessions and approximately 1100 during self-study times
key_sources: Sebastian Hobert, Florian Berens. (2023). Developing a digital tutor as an intermediary between students, teaching assistants, and lecturers. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10293-2

article_title: Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club
citation: Yuzhu Xia, Adria Patthoff, Liana Balloffet, Marco A. Bravo, Kip Téllez. (2025). Beyond boundaries: leveraging technology for differentiated professional development with lesson study video club. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10524-8
title: Teacher PD should center teachers' specialized contexts and experience spectrum rather than one-size-fits-all delivery
description: The article argues that school- or district-wide, one-size-fits-all PD delivery should be minimized in teachers' regular PD experiences because teaching is specialized by grade level, content area, experience, and programmatic structures. It states that "Teacher PD structures, as such, should center the spectrum of teachers' years of experience as well as other specialized and contextualized nature of teaching," requiring developers to cater to individual needs while enabling collaborative learning. This aligns with the study's finding that growth patterns differed by career stage.
requirements: Recognition of individual teachers' distinct challenges and differentiated support structures
constraints: Traditional PD with outside experts delivering skills and leaving is described as not substantively effective
target_learners: teachers across grade levels, content areas, and career stages in specialized programs
target_learning_goals: teaching efficacy and sustained professional growth
examples: The LSVC model centered progressive, teacher-led semi-structured conversations on specialized content throughout an academic year.

article_title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
citation: Marcus Pietsch · Dana-Kristin Mah. (2025). Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10439-w
title: Digital mindset of school leaders as a four-dimensional belief system: empathy, innovativeness, openness, agility
description: A digital mindset is a multidimensional combination of beliefs activated in the context of digitalization, divided into self-oriented and situation-oriented components. Drawing on Pabst von Ohain's expert-based study of prototypical digital transformation leaders, the article characterizes it in four dimensions: "empathic, innovative, open, and agile." The article measures one facet per dimension (perspective taking, technology orientation, openness to change, proactivity) and models these facets as antecedents of leadership practices and, indirectly, AI integration.
requirements: Measurement requires domain- and context-specific scales; the article adapted existing seven-point scales for each facet
constraints: Empirical research on what constitutes a digital mindset and how to measure it is scarce, as the article notes
target_learning_goals: leading digital transformation
implementing AI in schools
examples: The survey measured perspective taking with three items from Davis' interpersonal reactivity index, e.g. "When I'm upset at someone, I usually try to 'put myself in his shoes' for a while."

article_title: Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills
citation: Ioannou, A., Miliou, O., Georgiou, Y., Timotheou, S., Barkhuus, L., & Rode, J. (2025). Learning design for short-duration e-textile workshops: outcomes on knowledge and skills. Education Tech Research Dev, 73, 443–463. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10411-8
title: In short-duration e-textile workshops with young novices, include some direct instruction and in-situ scaffolding and facilitation, which is not incompatible with the making ethos
description: The article argues that under limited time, novice learners, and novice educators, "some direct instruction and in-situ scaffolding and facilitation may be required for the objectives to be achieved." Although this may be in tension with openness in the making ethos, teachable moments and just-in-time instruction let learners pursue their own projects while receiving support on identified knowledge gaps. The detailed four-hour workshop design—preparation and hands-on practice followed by project development—is offered as a model other educators can use.
requirements: Facilitators need to be well-informed about the properties and limitations of available e-textile materials and ready to assist
Novice educators need workshop models and examples explaining how to handle the variety of e-textile tools and materials
constraints: Recommended under specific circumstances: limited time, novice learners with respect to e-textiles and microprocessors, novice educators regarding STEAM or making practices, and lack of workshop models
target_learners: young children with no prior e-textile or microprocessor experience
target_learning_goals: circuitry knowledge and computational making skills in short STEAM-oriented workshops
examples: The workshop demonstrated micro:bit basics, practiced button-trigger actions and LED control, covered Ohm's Law with practical activities, and used the 2D circuit diagram discussion before crafting as an example of direct facilitation that worked very well

article_title: Shifting to open education in our digital learning
citation: Kimmons, R. (2021). Shifting to open education in our digital learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09949-8
title: Diffusion of innovations explains slow OER adoption by lack of established relative advantage
description: The editorial applies Rogers' diffusion of innovations model to OER adoption, treating relative advantage as the primary driver of uptake. It argues that "lack of relative advantage is the primary reason for slow or limited adoption," so OER's relative advantage must be established in the literature and made clear to faculty and administrators for adoption to increase. The special issue's responses then complicate this account.
requirements: For OER adoption to increase, their relative advantage must be firmly established in the literature and made clear to faculty and administrators
constraints: The editorial argues relative advantage alone will not lead to rapid adoption if it is merely conceptualized as cost savings
target_learning_goals: adoption of open educational resources in course design
examples: The editorial frames Hilton's efficacy and perceptions reviews as instrumental in establishing OER's relative advantage in the literature.
key_sources: Kimmons, R. (2021). Shifting to open education in our digital learning. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09949-8

article_title: Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict-observe-explain-diagnose-based approach to scientific inquiry
citation: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5
title: Embed misconception diagnosis with targeted feedback in inquiry-based learning rather than answer-only evaluation
description: The article argues that inquiry-based evaluation should go beyond judging answers to diagnosing the misconceptions behind wrong judgments. It states that without analysis and feedback on learners' misconceptions, "the learning effects of inquiry-based learning activities may be worse than expected", and that diagnosing possible misconceptions from wrong judgments makes it possible "to provide learning guidance" that helps students construct accurate knowledge.
requirements: Diagnostic questions that probe both factual knowledge and conceptual understanding, plus supplementary learning materials students can consult when diagnosed with misconceptions
constraints: The article's evidence comes from a small sample of 55 eighth graders in one science topic over six weeks, so it cautions the results may not generalize to other groups or subjects
target_learning_goals: accurate conceptual understanding in science
metacognitive self-assessment of understanding
examples: The study replaced the POEE evaluation phase with a two-tier diagnostic test in VR, and behavioral analysis showed experimental students read supplementary materials after errors and then answered correctly
key_sources: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5

article_title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
citation: Davy Tsz Kit Ng, Jac Ka Lok Leung, Jiahong Su, Ross Chi Wui Ng, Samuel Kai Wah Chu. (2023). Teachers' AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10203-6
title: DigCompEdu framework adapted for teachers' AI competency across six areas
description: The article adapts the European Framework for the Digital Competence of Educators (DigCompEdu) as an educator-specific competency framework defining teachers' key competencies and proficiency levels. It organizes components "within six major areas": professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, empowering learners, and facilitating learners' digital competency, and discusses how each applies to AI-driven tools such as recommendation engines, chatbots, and learning analytics dashboards.
requirements: Teachers need to connect digital tools to content knowledge and pedagogy, and customize settings before teaching
constraints: The article notes the learning and teaching dimension of DigCompEdu is narrower than the revised TPACK model because it does not emphasize subject-specific content knowledge
target_learning_goals: educator digital competence
AI-enhanced teaching, learning and assessment

article_title: Each discipline is different: teacher capabilities for future-focussed digitally infused undergraduate programmes
citation: Louise Starkey, Anne Yates, Mairead de Roiste, Karsten Lundqvist, Adreanne Ormond, John Randal, Allan Sylvester. (2023). Each discipline is different: teacher capabilities for future-focussed digitally infused undergraduate programmes. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10196-2
title: Disciplinary-culture-centred account of digital-era pedagogical change in Higher Education
description: The article frames educational systems as dynamic and emergent, using complexity thinking and appreciative inquiry to explain how digital technologies alter disciplines and teaching. It argues that "Disciplinary culture is the basis of Higher Education teacher identity and underpins pedagogical practice and use of digital technology", which in turn determines the digital capabilities teachers need. Disciplines are described as evolving rather than static, with digital technology superimposed on older disciplines and central to newer ones.
requirements: Teachers' capability development must be understood within each discipline's culture, traditions, skills and knowledge
constraints: Findings derive from five disciplines in one New Zealand university and the first three phases of an appreciative inquiry
target_learning_goals: Discipline-appropriate pedagogical practice and digital capability development
examples: Case studies of Information Systems, Geography, Statistics for Business, Critical Indigenous Studies and Computer Science written by disciplinary experts
key_sources: Louise Starkey, Anne Yates, Mairead de Roiste, Karsten Lundqvist, Adreanne Ormond, John Randal, Allan Sylvester. (2023). Each discipline is different: teacher capabilities for future-focussed digitally infused undergraduate programmes. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10196-2

article_title: Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies
citation: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6
title: Instruments for measuring digital distraction, including self-developed Digital Distraction Scales and the Internet Addiction Test
description: This element covers the measurement instruments used across the 26 reviewed studies. Fourteen studies utilized instruments to measure digital distraction, nine of which reported self-developed instruments. Three studies designed a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with contextual purpose, and the Internet Addiction (IA) Test was another commonly included measurement. The review tabulates these instruments study by study (Table 3), noting that "Three of the studies specifically designed a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with contextual purpose."
requirements: Empirical studies of digital distraction require a defined instrument, and the review's inclusion criteria required a clearly defined methods section
constraints: Most instruments were self-developed rather than validated external scales, and 12 of 26 studies reported no instrument for measuring digital distraction
target_learning_goals: measuring digital distraction and off-task device use
examples: Göl et al. (2023) used a Digital Distraction Scale (DDS) with DD components questionnaires; Chen et al. (2020) used DD intensity items with the Internet Addiction Test and Barratt Impulsiveness Scale
key_sources: Florence Martin, Siyu Long, Katy Haywood, Kui Xie. (2025). Digital distractions in education: a systematic review of research on causes, consequences and prevention strategies. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10550-6

article_title: Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review
citation: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454
title: A 14-theme taxonomy of children's digital engagement conceptualisations
description: Through inductive thematic analysis of definitions and measures of engagement across the 88 included studies, the review developed a taxonomy of engagement themes: effort, interpersonal skills or behavior, attention, enjoyment, participation, skills, interest, usability, motivation, valuing, and miscellaneous themes (belonging, responsibility, tension). The review states "This resulted in the identification of 14 themes (see Table 4; Clarke & Braun, 2017)", each with related terms and example definitions and measures. The taxonomy shows engagement's multidimensional nature in children's digital learning contexts.
requirements: Applicable to studies of children's engagement with digital technology in formal or semi-formal educational settings
constraints: The abstract refers to ten key themes while the results section reports 14 themes identified through thematic analysis
Definitions referring broadly to behavioural, emotional and cognitive components were not included in the theme table
target_learning_goals: characterising and measuring children's engagement with digital technology in play and learning
examples: Table 4 lists example definitions such as Attard's (2018) 'individual thoughts that are projected outwards in terms of a person's investment and effort towards learning' under effort, and example measures such as time-on-task observation under participation
key_sources: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454

article_title: Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review
citation: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454
title: Theoretical foundations of children's digital engagement draw primarily from motivational theories spanning educational and digital disciplines
description: The review synthesised nine theories or models of engagement referenced across the eight theorising studies, classifying them as education-only (BSCS 5E Instructional Model, ARCS model, Guthrie and Wigfield's reading engagement), digital-only (Immersion Theory, Positive Technological Development framework), both (Malone and Lepper's intrinsic motivation theory, CAMIL), or context-general (Flow Theory, Self Determination Theory). The review states these theoretical foundations were "primarily rooted in motivational theories", noting Flow Theory and Self Determination Theory are "widely used to understand motivational processes in a variety of settings, including education".
requirements: An explicit link between engagement and a well-established theory, framework, or model was required for a study to count as theorising engagement
constraints: References to Fredricks and colleagues' (2004) categorisation were excluded because it is a meta-construct drawing on a multitude of theories rather than a single theory
target_learning_goals: conceptualising children's engagement with digital technology in educational settings
examples: Table 3 maps each theory to studies: Flow theory (Csikszentmihalyi, 1988) referenced by Jingili et al. (2024) and Barreto et al. (2017); CAMIL (Makransky & Petersen, 2021) referenced by Molloy and Farrell (2024)
key_sources: J. Harverson, C. Zomer, C. Chu, S. Horwood, M. Horwood, M. Nicholas, L. Paatsch. (2026). Children's engagement with digital technology in educational spaces: A scoping review. Computers & Education 240 (2026) 105454. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105454

article_title: The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance
citation: Mehrvarz, Mahboobe; Heidari, Elham; Farrokhnia, Mohammadreza; Noroozi, Omid. (2021). The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance. Computers & Education 167 (2021) 104184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104184
title: Digital informal learning as a three-aspect construct (cognitive, metacognitive, social-motivational)
description: The article treats digital informal learning (DIL) as unstructured, technology-mediated learning outside formal settings. It defines it as "the unstructured technology-mediated learning opportunities in informal learning settings", in which learners control what, when and how they learn. Following He and Li (2019), the article structures DIL into three measured aspects: "cognitive learning (CL), metacognitive learning (MCL), and social and motivational learning (SML)", each operationalised with a four-item questionnaire subscale in the study. The Discussion adds that the article attributes a self-determination-theory basis to DIL via He and Li (2019).
requirements: Learners need access to digital technologies in informal, out-of-class contexts for DIL to occur
DIL demands proper digital competence to form optimal learning and behavior in such a digital-based learning environment
constraints: Measured here by self-report questionnaires only; no empirical intervention was used
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning with digital technologies
academic performance
examples: The study measured DIL with He and Li's (2019) questionnaire covering cognitive, metacognitive, and social-motivational subscales, with Cronbach's alpha of 0.89 for overall DIL

title: Digital competence frameworks: DigComp 2.1's five dimensions and Calvani et al.'s three-dimensional framework
description: The article reviews two theoretical frameworks for digital competence. DigComp 2.1, as described via Carretero et al. (2017), "includes 21 sub-competencies structured to improve citizens' digital competence, consisting of five dimensions: information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, digital safety, and problem-solving", with eight proficiency levels. Calvani et al.'s (2012) framework "includes three technical, cognitive, and ethical dimensions". The study adopted Calvani's framework because it is multi-dimensional and interconnected with other basic competencies such as reading, problem-solving, and metacognitive skills.
requirements: Digital competence instruments must be grounded in a multi-dimensional framework covering technical, cognitive and ethical aspects
constraints: The study operationalises digital competence via self-report only (He and Zhu's 2017 questionnaire)

safe and ethical technology use
examples: The article notes the scope of digital competence is beyond digital literacy and includes attitude and mindset besides the skills

citation: Mehrvarz, Mahboobe; Heidari, Elham; Farrokhnia, Mohammadreza; Noroozi, Omid. (2021). The mediating role of digital informal learning in the relationship between students' digital competence and their academic performance. Computers & Education 167 (2021) 104184. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104184
title: Three self-report questionnaires measuring digital competence, digital informal learning, and perceived academic performance
description: The study's measurement battery comprises three validated self-report instruments. Digital competence was measured with He and Zhu's (2017) questionnaire based on Calvani's framework, with three dimensions: technical skills (11 items), cognitive skills (12 items), and ethical knowledge (6 items) on 5-point Likert scales; six low-loading items were removed and overall Cronbach's alpha was 0.90. DIL was measured with He and Li's (2019) questionnaire with CL, SML, and MCL subscales of four items each (alpha 0.89). Academic performance was measured by students' self-perception with Yu et al.'s (2010) four-item questionnaire (alpha 0.86).
requirements: Prior CFA-based validation in the study sample, with factor loads at 0.30 and above
constraints: Academic performance is perceived, not actual; the authors note students may give socially acceptable or over-/under-estimated self-reports
target_learning_goals: measuring digital competence, digital informal learning, and perceived academic performance
examples: Example items include "I can use some software programs to deal with data visualization." and "I have learned how to perform my coursework efficiently successfully."

article_title: The strength and direction of the difficulty adaptation affect situational interest in game-based learning
citation: Koskinen, A., McMullen, J., Hannula-Sormunen, M., Ninaus, M., & Kiili, K. (2023). The strength and direction of the difficulty adaptation affect situational interest in game-based learning. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104694
title: Strength and direction of difficulty adaptation as two dimensions affecting motivational outcomes in adaptive digital learning environments
description: The article proposes that motivational outcomes of adaptive learning environments depend on two under-examined dimensions of difficulty adaptation: strength (how much difficulty is adjusted) and direction (upwards or downwards). It operationalizes this as five adaptation levels applied via estimation-accuracy thresholds, and argues that examining only overall adaptation effects can mask these dimensions, since "the non-significant main effect between difficulty conditions on situational interest indicates that without examining the effects of strength and direction of adaptation, our results would have indicated that adaptation of difficulty does not affect motivational outcomes."
requirements: Adaptive systems must log or assign adaptation strength and direction so their separate effects can be analyzed
Manipulation checks must confirm the adaptation mechanism worked as designed before motivational effects are interpreted
constraints: Findings come from one game-based fraction-learning context with fifth-graders
target_learning_goals: Conceptual fraction knowledge (number line estimation)
examples: In the Number Trace game, basic-game level performance assigned participants to six levels of adaptation, and motivational outcomes were compared across content-matched level pairs.

article_title: Digital competence in higher education research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhao Yu, Pinto Llorente Ana María, Sánchez Gómez María Cruz. (2021). Digital competence in higher education research: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 168, 104212. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104212
title: DigComp five-component framework of digital competence
description: The European Commission's Digital Competence Framework (DigComp), established to identify and support EU citizens' digital competence, presents five components: information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, digital content creation, safety, and problem solving. It was updated into Digcomp 2.1 in 2017 with the same key dimensions, and sub competences can be evaluated across different levels of proficiency. In this review it is the most-used basis for assessment instruments in higher education.
requirements: Assessment instruments built on it operationalize its five dimensions across proficiency levels
constraints: The review reports only 27% of reviewed publications applied assessment based on Digcomp
target_learning_goals: digital competence
examples: Nine reviewed publications followed and established instruments on the basis of the Digcomp dimensions

article_title: Digital competence in higher education research: A systematic literature review
citation: Zhao Yu, Pinto Llorente Ana María, Sánchez Gómez María Cruz. (2021). Digital competence in higher education research: A systematic literature review. Computers & Education, 168, 104212. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104212
title: DigCompEdu six-area framework of educators' digital competence
description: Within the DigCompEdu project of the European Commission, digital competence is considered the ability of users to make safe, critical and creative use of ICT to satisfy different objectives. Redecker (2017) categorized an educator's digital competence into six areas: professional engagement, digital resources, teaching and learning, assessment, empowering learners, and facilitating learners' digital competence. The review reports this framework has been consolidated and spread internationally, and the Spanish Common Digital Competence Framework for Teachers (INTEF) adapts DigComp and DigCompEdu into five competence areas including 21 competencies.
requirements: Built on the basis of DigComp; used for training, evaluation, certification and accreditation purposes
constraints: Addresses educators' digital competence specifically, not students'

professional development
examples: Cabero-Almenara et al. (2020) measured the reliability and validity of the DigCompEdu Check-In questionnaire covering these six areas

citation: Jara, I., Claro, M., Hinostroza, J. E., San Martin Gutiérrez, E., Rodríguez, P., Cabello, T., Ibieta, A., & Labbé, C. (2015). article_title: How does students' general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance?
citation: James Wakefield & Jessica K. Frawley. (2020). How does students’ general academic achievement moderate the implications of social networking on specific levels of learning performance? Computers & Education. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131519302477?via%3Dihub
title: Distraction-conflict theory as an account of social networking's disruptive effect on learning performance
description: The article draws on distraction-conflict theory to explain how social networking use may harm learning performance. Within the stimuli-intensive environment of students' studies and SNS use, the authors note "there is the strong possibility of conflicts in students’ attention and additional cognitive load, that is not relevant to students’ studies". This framework frames Facebook use as imposing attentional conflict and extraneous cognitive load that disrupts performance, particularly for lower-achieving students.
requirements: The account assumes social networking use occurs concurrently with, or in proximity to, study activities where attention is divided.
constraints: The article states it assumes social networking use has linear performance implications and did not explore possible non-linear implications.
target_learning_goals: academic performance in equation and problem solving centric subjects

This responds to findings that children lack critical approaches to screens despite handling devices easily.

Family education schemes guiding parents and children toward healthier coexistence

responsible technology use

citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: Digital toy technology from the CACHET project
description: The CACHET project uses freestanding electronic soft toys that can move, speak and respond to a child's touch, and can be linked wirelessly to a PC running compatible software. The toys respond through body sensors, gesture with programmed motion, and speak with a digitised vocabulary of more than 4,000 words, extended by the software to 10,000 words. The child interacts with the toy, the software, and the toy-software link, which mediates the child's actions.

constraints: The toys can receive radio signals more than 3 metres away from the transmitter at the PC

article_title: Writing Instruction Improves Students' Writing Differentially Depending on Focal Instruction and Children: A Meta-Analysis for Primary Grade Students
citation: Young-Suk Grace Kim, Dandan Yang, Marcela Reyes, Carol Connor. (2021). Writing instruction improves students' writing skills differentially depending on focal instruction and children: A meta-analysis for primary grade students. Educational Research Review 34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100408
title: Direct and indirect effects model of writing (DIEW)
description: The DIEW is the theoretical framework guiding this meta-analysis's moderation questions. It posits that writing quality draws on "a comprehensive set of skills and knowledge such as domain-general cognitions (e.g., working memory), language skills (e.g., vocabulary), transcription skills (spelling and handwriting/keyboarding), higher order cognitions and regulations (e.g., inferencing, perspective taking, monitoring, goal setting), topic and discourse knowledge, and socio-emotions." Crucially, it holds that relative contributions of these skills differ dynamically by composition dimension and developmental phase: productivity relies more heavily on transcription, while quality requires a broader skill set, and transcription's constraining role is largest early in development.
requirements: Instruction targeting writing quality must address a more comprehensive set of skills and knowledge than single-skill instruction
constraints: The dynamic relations hypothesis concerns the initial versus later phases of writing development
target_learning_goals: written composition skills including quality, productivity, and fluency
examples: The meta-analysis tested DIEW-derived predictions that multi-component instruction (SRSD) would outperform single-skill transcription instruction on writing quality

Writing instruction improves students' writing skills differentially depending on focal instruction and children: A meta-analysis for primary grade students. Educational Research Review 34. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2021.100408

article_title: The Effect of Digital Story Applications on Students' Academic Achievement: A Meta-Analysis Study
citation: Nurullah Sahin and İsmail Coban. (2020). The effect of digital story applications on students' academic achievement: A meta-analysis study. African Educational Research Journal, Special Issue 8(3), S62-S75.
title: Digital storytelling and its seven components
description: Digital storytelling is defined in the article as "short, individual and multimedia stories that share information using multimedia tools or resources", resulting from integrating traditional storytelling with technology. The Center for Digital Storytelling stated that digital storytelling has 7 components: Perspective, A Dramatic Question, Emotional Content, Economy, Voice, Music, and Pacing/Rhythm. Robin and Pierson added Story Purpose, Image Quality, and Good Grammar and Language Use for educational purposes.
requirements: In educational use, digital story is used to present specific course content as teaching material and for students learning content, telling stories, motivation, and presentation
target_learners: students of all ages and all levels

digital literacy and related 21st-century skills

article_title: Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics Education Research: A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses
citation: Young, J.R. (2016). Unpacking TPACK in Mathematics education research: A systematic review of meta-analyses. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 2(1), 19-29. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.2.1.19
title: Three didactical functionalities of digital technology in mathematics classrooms
description: Drawing on Drijvers, Boon, and Van Reeuwijk (2010), the review organizes mathematics technology by three didactical functionalities: "(1) doing mathematics, (2) practicing skills, and (3) conceptual understanding." Doing mathematics uses technology to complete tasks that could be done by hand, enhancing computational efficiency; practicing skills supports repetitive tasks with immediate feedback for procedural or instrumental understanding; conceptual understanding involves building deeper understandings and making connections, similar to relational understanding. The review maps calculators to computational efficiency, CAI/CBI to instrumental understanding, and mathematics-specific software to relational understanding, then shows effect sizes vary across these functions.
requirements: Categories are applied "based on the primary functionality as established in the literature," so tools with complex, multiple functions must be classified by their primary use
constraints: The article states the didactical functionalities "are not exhaustive nor mutually exclusive, as many of the tools have complex functions and multiple adaptations"
target_learners: postsecondary statistics students in some included meta-analyses
target_learning_goals: computational efficiency
procedural or instrumental understanding
conceptual or relational understanding of mathematics
examples: Calculators were categorized as computational enhancement devices; CAI/CBI as instructional delivery tools supporting practice; mathematics-specific software and virtual manipulatives as tools for relational understanding

article_title: The role of digital teaching methods in supporting practical skills training in the academic training of health professions - a scoping review.
citation: Stamer Tjorven, Machinek Nora, Steinhäuser Jost, Goujard Mathilde, Flägel Kristina. (2026). The role of digital teaching methods in supporting practical skills training in the academic training of health professions – a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08785-9
title: Digital teaching in health professions education: time-and-place independence, scalability and tracking, with weaker support for social skills
description: The review's background framework characterizes digital teaching by a set of affordances and limits. It states that "Digital teaching allows learning to be independent of time and place, which is beneficial for the individual needs of students", that online courses make it easier to scale courses to larger numbers, and that learning management systems and tracking tools can record and evaluate learners' progress. It also holds that digital formats promote independent and collaborative learning and can promote understanding and long-term retention of knowledge, while being demonstrably less effective for teaching social skills.
requirements: Continuous didactic and technical development of digital teaching, which the review calls essential to ensure long-term quality of education
constraints: Digital teaching is demonstrably less effective for teaching social skills, per the review's background synthesis
target_learners: students in academic health professions programs
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge, digital skills, and practical skills supported by digital formats
examples: The review cites blended learning and e-learning formats' continued use beyond the COVID-19 pandemic as instances of these affordances

description: The review compiles a catalogue of digital learning tools with digital microscopy integrated, described as "Interactive digital tools with digitized slides integrated, annotations, quizzes, and additional materials." article_title: Hands-on Distance Simulation of Technical Skills: A Systematic Review.
citation: Wei W, Nielsen MS, Nielsen AB, Han Y, Russell L, Konge L, Cold KM. (2026). Hands-on Distance Simulation of Technical Skills: A Systematic Review. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000881
title: Three-format taxonomy of distance simulation delivery: home-based, facility-based, and mobile
description: The review classifies distance simulation delivery into three descriptive formats. "Home-based distance simulation" involves trainees using portable simulators at home or other remote locations; "facility-based distance simulation" has trainees physically at a training center receiving instruction remotely via telecommunication; and "mobile simulation" transports a simulator to the learners' location. The review used these categories to group studies and interpret implementation strategies, finding home-based formats in 64 studies, facility-based in 39, and mobile in 1.
requirements: Learners must have access to portable simulators or training facilities and to telecommunication channels connecting them with remote facilitators
constraints: The review notes home-based formats are only suitable for basic technical training because they typically lack advanced simulators and facilities

examples: Home-based microsurgical training used smartphone camera zoom as a microscope substitute, while 5 facility-based ophthalmic trainings required advanced microscopes at training centers

citation: Wei W, Nielsen MS, Nielsen AB, Han Y, Russell L, Konge L, Cold KM. (2026). Hands-on Distance Simulation of Technical Skills: A Systematic Review. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000881
title: Simulator types used in distance technical skills training, from bench-top box trainers to household items
description: The review catalogs the physical simulators used across 104 studies: bench-top models in 61 studies (commercial and homemade box trainers, suturing pads, phantom vessels), part-task trainers in 20 studies, human models in 13 ultrasound studies, organic models in 9 studies, commercial virtual reality stations in 7 studies, and in 5 studies everyday household items such as "shoelaces for knot tying and sponges, fabrics, and bananas for suturing exercises." Researchers also crafted custom trainers, such as a 3D-printed dry-laboratory model and a portable acrylic-resin vascular model.
requirements: Real-time interaction typically requires cameras, microphones, and online meeting platforms for 2-way observation and communication between trainees and remote instructors
constraints: The review notes benefits of technologies like 3D printing and XR depend on local infrastructure and resource availability, and XR implementation is limited by high cost and reliance on stable high-speed Internet

examples: In a neuroendovascular training study, researchers developed a portable vascular model from acrylic resin with a backlight panel displaying vessel grooves and cameras capturing real-time images for bidirectional observation

description: The review's meta-aggregation of 41 findings from 16 qualitative studies yielded three synthesised findings describing the competence patients expect of healthcare professionals in digital counselling. As the review states, 'competence in digital counselling includes the competence to provide digital counselling that is efficient and enables counselling to be implemented in health care, supports patients to self-manage and establishes a reciprocal counselling relationship in a digital environment.' This framework organises patient expectations into actionable competence domains for professional development.
requirements: Digital counselling competence requires a range of mutually supportive knowledge, skills, attitudes and values, as competence is defined in the review's background.
constraints: The synthesis is based on qualitative studies of adult patients in healthcare settings where communication was reciprocal (text-based or video-mediated), excluding one-sided interactions such as chatbots or viewing digital material.

Understand patient expectations of digital counselling competence

The authors state that "future simulations should consider implementing virtual SUD patients with characteristics that may be more representative of diverse, real-world clinical populations to help overcome any pre-existing stereotypes." Educators should also adjust scenario complexity to learners' experience levels.
requirements: Future simulations should consider implementing virtual SUD patients with characteristics that may be more representative of diverse, real-world clinical populations to help overcome any pre-existing stereotypes.

article_title: Digital Competence among Healthcare Leaders: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review.
citation: Laakkonen Noora, Jarva Erika, Hammarén Mira, Kanste Outi, Kääriäinen Maria, Oikarinen Anne, Mikkonen Kristina. (2024). Digital Competence among Healthcare Leaders: A Mixed-Methods Systematic Review. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/2024/8435248
title: Digital competence in healthcare as a multidimensional construct spanning technical, methodological, personal, and social skills
description: The review adopts a conception of digital competence as "the confident and critical use of Information Society Technology (IST) for work, leisure and communication" and reports, citing Mainz et al., that digital competence in healthcare can be divided into technical, methodological, personal, and social skills. Technical competencies encompass basic computer use, digital health skills, technology administration, and ethical and legal aspects; methodological include data processing and project management; personal include self-reflection and critical thinking; social include teamwork and communication. The review uses this framing to argue leaders' digital competence is broad and multifaceted.
requirements: Assessment of leaders' digital competence should address all four skill domains rather than only knowledge and skills
constraints: The review notes earlier leader-focused work focused on knowledge and skills, dismissing personal and social skills
target_learners: Healthcare leaders and managers in social and healthcare contexts
target_learning_goals: Digital competence development for leadership in digitalising healthcare
examples: The review's synthesis of leaders' experiences covers knowledge needs, implementation expertise, perceptions, and advocacy across these domains
