article_title: "Diagnose, Treat, and SUPPORT". Clinical competencies in the management of older adults with aspiration pneumonia: a scoping review.
citation: Yoshimatsu Yuki, Ohtake Yoichi, Ukai Mamiko, Miyagami Taiju, Morikawa Toru, Shimamura Yoshinosuke, Kataoka Yuki, Hashimoto Tadayuki. (2023). “Diagnose, Treat, and SUPPORT”. Clinical competencies in the management of older adults with aspiration pneumonia: a scoping review. European Geriatric Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41999-023-00898-4
title: The 'Diagnose, Treat and SUPPORT' competency framework for managing older adults with aspiration pneumonia
description: A mnemonic framework organising 12 clinical competencies for aspiration pneumonia management in older adults. 'Diagnose' stands for diagnosis, 'Treat' for treatment, and SUPPORT is an acronym for the remaining ten: Swallow and nutrition intervention, Underlying condition management, Prognosis evaluation and decision making, Prevention and palliation, Oral management, Rehabilitation, and Team approach. The article states the phrase "is intended to be shared with team members to identify areas that need to be addressed and to ensure the necessary multidimensional care", sequencing accurate diagnosis and antibiotic treatment as the first key steps followed by multidisciplinary supportive care.

constraints: Developed for bedside and community healthcare professionals rather than education/management-focused competency domains

target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies in diagnosing, treating, and providing supportive multidisciplinary care for older adults with aspiration pneumonia

article_title: Distributional Moderation Analysis: Unpacking Moderation Effects in Intervention Research
citation: Wiedermann, W., Reinke, W. M., & Herman, K. C. (2025). Distributional moderation analysis: Unpacking moderation effects in intervention research. Journal of School Psychology, 108. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2024.101399
title: Distributional treatment effects framework: intervention effects can manifest in mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and scale-endpoint parameters
description: The framework defines an intervention effect in its most general form as a difference in post-intervention outcome distributions between treatment and control conditions: "aninterventioneffectisestablishedthroughfocusingonthedifferenceinthepost-interventiondistributions(P)oftheoutcomeacrossinterventionandcontrolconditions." Beyond the mean (ATE), it formalizes effects on variance (ATE2), skewness (ATE3), kurtosis (ATE4), and the probabilities of reaching the scale minimum and maximum (ATEf, ATEc). Variance effects indicate whether the intervention works predictably for most students or induces heterogeneity; skewness and kurtosis effects indicate differential or extreme differential responses; endpoint effects capture floor/ceiling change. The article also presents four prototypical moderation patterns combining mean shifts with variance, skewness, kurtosis, and endpoint changes.
requirements: Randomization such that baseline distribution parameters (e.g., mean, variance) are equal across conditions, so post-intervention distributional changes can be attributed to the intervention
Transparent documentation of any evaluation of outcome parameters other than the mean, ideally at the pre-registration phase of a trial
constraints: The exact nature of skewness- and kurtosis-based effects requires case-by-case evaluation depending on the type of change and the distributional shape of pre and post scores
target_learners: Students in school-based intervention research (kindergarten through third grade in the empirical example)
target_learning_goals: Characterizing for whom and in what distributional parameters a classroom behavior intervention is effective
examples: The article illustrates variance-based interpretation with a disruptive behavior intervention: a variance reduction alongside a mean reduction implies the intervention works for most students in a predictable and regular way, whereas a variance increase suggests the treatment is more beneficial for some students than others
key_sources: Wiedermann, W., Reinke, W. M., & Herman, K. C. (2025). Distributional moderation analysis: Unpacking moderation effects in intervention research. Journal of School Psychology, 108. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsp.2024.101399

article_title: Teaching English Tense and Aspect with the Help of Cognitive Grammar: An Empirical Study
citation: Jakub Bielak, Mirosųaw Pawlak. (2010). Teaching English tense and aspect with the help of cognitive grammar: An empirical study. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 1(3), 365-400. http://www.ssllt.amu.edu.pl
title: Written discrete-item grammar test of mostly explicit knowledge with three components and split-block test versions

Three parallel versions (A, B, C) were shuffled across testing sessions via a split-block procedure to equalize difficulty.

article_title: The Effect of Written Corrective Feedback on Omani Students' Accuracy in the Use of English Prepositions
citation: Ahmed Ali Saleh Al Ajmi. (2015). The Effect of Written Corrective Feedback on Omani Students’ Accuracy in the Use of English Prepositions. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.1p.61
title: Provide direct, focused written corrective feedback supported by metalinguistic explanation when targeting specific linguistic error categories
description: The article recommends that WCF for specific error categories such as prepositions be direct (providing corrections), focused on particular mistakes at a time, and accompanied by metalinguistic explanation. Students reported that direct WCF "is rich in information about their errors, is clear, is effective", and that focused WCF helps them avoid confusion and frustration. The experimental treatment combining WCF with an oral metalinguistic tutorial produced large accuracy gains.
requirements: Feedback should target specific linguistic features the learners commonly confuse
Metalinguistic explanation of the relevant rules should accompany the corrections
constraints: The article states WCF's effectiveness was tested over only a short period, seven weeks, for logistical reasons
The study was conducted in one Omani college with pre-intermediate Arabic-speaking students in intact classes, so random assignment was not possible
target_learners: Arabic-speaking pre-intermediate EFL foundation-year students in higher education
target_learning_goals: Accurate use of English prepositions in writing
examples: The experimental group received WCF on their writing, a 15-minute oral metalinguistic tutorial, and a treatment task on their pre-test, then WCF only on subsequent writings, while the control group received only general comments such as praise for organization

article_title: New Teaching Techniques to Improve Critical Thinking. The Diaprove Methodology
citation: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas. (2016). New Teaching Techniques to Improve Critical Thinking. The Diaprove Methodology. Educational Research Quarterly, Vol. 40.1. https://www.pensamiento-critico.com
title: DIAPROVE: a best-explanation methodology for critical thinking instruction
description: DIAPROVE (DIAgnosis, PROgnosis and VErification) is the authors' instructional methodology that shifts the center of critical thinking from argumentation toward "the best explanation", treating efficacy as the defining feature of critical thinking. It reorganizes instruction around "three fundamental aspects: learning to look, learning to combine conditional and causal structures and, finally, learning to rule out explanations or hypotheses". It was added to the ARDESOS program without removing existing components and tested against the unmodified program.
requirements: Instruction must give maximum priority to achieving maximum efficacy in problem-solving, not merely a solution
Observation of facts in context, combination of facts with deduction, and disconfirmation procedures require specific teaching techniques
constraints: In the reported study the methodology could only be fully applied to the deductive and inductive dimensions; other factors were only partially developed
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
problem-solving
explanation and hypothesis evaluation
examples: Group 2 received the ARDESOS program with DIAPROVE added, over the same 16-week, four-block structure as group 1, delivered by two expert instructors
key_sources: Carlos Saiz, Silvia F. Rivas. (2016). New Teaching Techniques to Improve Critical Thinking. The Diaprove Methodology. Educational Research Quarterly, Vol. 40.1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1166695

article_title: Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension?
citation: Hamid Marashi, Mojgan Khaksar. (2013). Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension? li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 1, January-March.
title: Dictogloss four-stage dictation-reconstruction task pattern
description: Dictogloss, developed by Wajnryb (1990) from dictation, is a meaning-based collaborative dictation task embodying "the four steps of preparation, dictation, reconstruction, and analysis besides correction". Learners listen to a short text read multiple times, take notes, reconstruct the text in small groups, then analyze and correct their versions against the original. The article used this pattern across 10 sessions with teenage EFL learners.
requirements: A short text read aloud multiple times without pauses
Small groups for reconstruction
Teacher withholds language input during reconstruction
constraints: The board with pre-taught vocabulary is erased before listening so the task remains challenging
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension
Note-taking
Producing grammatically accurate, cohesive texts
Cooperative language use
examples: In the study, learners listened to an audio recording three times, took notes on the second and third listenings, and reconstructed the text in groups of three in about 10 minutes.
key_sources: Hamid Marashi, Mojgan Khaksar. (2013). Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension? li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 1, January-March. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068862

article_title: Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension?
citation: Hamid Marashi, Mojgan Khaksar. (2013). Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension? li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 1, January-March.
title: Dicto-phrase (dictation-paraphrase) gist-completion task
description: Dicto-phrase (Zahedi, 2004) is a dictation variant described as "an interface between teaching and testing" for tapping listening abilities. After listening, learners complete a passage with blanks using the gist of missing propositions rather than exact words, with wh-questions in brackets to aid recall. Unlike dictogloss, learners work individually, take no notes, and rely on long-term memory; texts are normally authentic.
requirements: A passage with blanks accompanied by wh-questions in brackets
Authentic texts to encourage attentive listening
Learners listen without note-taking
constraints: The task does not permit note-taking and is not concerned with collaboration
target_learners: EFL learners in classroom listening instruction
target_learning_goals: Listening comprehension
Recall of idea units
Paraphrasing propositions in learners' own words
examples: In the study's dicto-phrase group, learners worked individually and spent nearly five minutes reconstructing their stories after three listenings without notes.
key_sources: Hamid Marashi, Mojgan Khaksar. (2013). Dictogloss or Dicto-Phrase: Which Works Better for Listening Comprehension? li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 1, January-March. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068862

article_title: Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence from a Literacy Intervention
citation: David M. Quinn, James S. Kim. (2017). Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence From a Literacy Intervention. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217717692
title: Differentiate implementation management by teachers' intervention experience: fidelity focus for novices, structured adaptation for experienced implementers
description: The article's findings support matching implementation management to teachers' prior experience with the intervention: teachers new to a program benefit from fidelity-focused structures, while teachers who have already mastered the program as designed benefit from structured adaptive opportunities. The article reasons that "Teachers with less curricular knowledge may perform better under a stricter fidelity approach, while more experienced or effective teachers may be capable of improving the program under the freedom offered by an adaptive approach." The trial's condition-by-experience interactions empirically support this differentiation.
requirements: Baseline information about which teachers have prior experience with the intervention
Both fidelity-focused learning structures and structured adaptive working groups must be available
constraints: The adaptive approach assumes teachers have the knowledge and skill to make adaptations consistent with program theory; without deep program knowledge, adaptations are unlikely to improve the program and may even be harmful
target_learners: elementary school teachers implementing literacy programs
target_learning_goals: teacher learning about the intervention
incorporation of intervention practices into regular classroom instruction
student reading comprehension
examples: In the trial, all teachers regardless of prior experience participated in their condition's learning structures, and effects were compared for teachers with and without prior Core READS experience
key_sources: David M. Quinn, James S. Kim. (2017). Scaffolding Fidelity and Adaptation in Educational Program Implementation: Experimental Evidence From a Literacy Intervention. American Educational Research Journal. https://doi.org/10.3102/0002831217717692

article_title: Discover Summer School: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Torgerson, D., Torgerson, C., Jefferson, L., Buckley, H., Ainsworth, H., Heaps, C., & Mitchell, N. (2014). Discover Summer School Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Discover Summer School four-week literacy transition programme
description: A four-week summer programme for children transitioning from Year 6 to Year 7, targeted at pupils predicted to achieve below Level 4b in English at Key Stage 2. It included "morning workshops focused on writing and poetry delivered by trained teachers, professional authors and poets, and enrichment activities" such as drama, sports and trips around London. Delivery followed a usual school week (9am-3pm, Monday to Friday) by trained 'Story Builders', teachers and volunteers, with free transport provided to encourage attendance. Teaching was framed around the book The Unforgotten Coat.
requirements: Requires trained teachers, professional authors and poets, and Story Builders to deliver workshops
Requires free transport arrangements from multiple collection and drop-off points to support attendance
constraints: Delivered as a supplementary intervention in the summer holiday rather than an alternative core intervention during the normal school day
Attendance was low: 36.8% of allocated pupils never attended any sessions
target_learners: Year 6 pupils predicted to achieve Level 3c to Level 4c in English at Key Stage 2, transitioning to Year 7
target_learning_goals: improve reading and writing skills, specifically for less able writers
examples: Pupils meeting eligibility criteria were recruited through 29 primary schools near the Discover Children's Story Centre in Stratford, London; 76 were randomly selected to attend and 48 formed a comparison group
key_sources: Torgerson, D., Torgerson, C., Jefferson, L., Buckley, H., Ainsworth, H., Heaps, C., & Mitchell, N. (2014). Discover Summer School Evaluation Report and Executive Summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581103

article_title: Average Differences in Effect Sizes by Outcome Measure Type. What Works Clearinghouse Working Paper
citation: Wolf, R. (2021). Average differences in effect sizes by outcome measure type (WWC 2021). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, What Works Clearinghouse. https://github.com/betsyjwolf/Average-Effect-Sizes-by-Outcome-Measure-Type
title: Differentiate findings based on researcher and developer measures from those based on independent measures when reporting intervention evidence
description: The paper recommends that evidence systems account for systematic effect size differences by outcome measure type, because researcher and developer measures yield larger average effect sizes than independent measures even within the same studies. It states the WWC "should consider whether findings based on researcher and developer measures should be differentiated from those based on independent measures to meet the evidence needs of all WWC stakeholders". Suggested approaches include meta-regression or Bayesian adjustment, additional study qualifications, and different evidence characterizations for different stakeholder groups.
requirements: Effect sizes must be tagged by outcome measure type (broad, narrow, developer, researcher) before findings are compared or reported
constraints: The article notes classification of outcome measure types is inherently subjective, and the analysis is limited to literacy, STEM, and behavior domains
target_learners: practitioners and policymakers selecting educational interventions
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of intervention effectiveness evidence
examples: The paper found that restricting ESSA Tier 1 and 2 badges to non-researcher, non-developer measures would lower the badged share of studies from 23% to 15%
key_sources: Wolf, R. (2021). Average differences in effect sizes by outcome measure type (WWC 2021). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, What Works Clearinghouse. https://github.com/betsyjwolf/Average-Effect-Sizes-by-Outcome-Measure-Type

article_title: Interactive Digital Kitchen: The Impact on Language Learning
citation: Nor Fadzlinda Ishak and Paul Seedhouse. (2012). Interactive Digital Kitchen: The impact on Language learning. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://digitalinstitute.ncl.ac.uk/ilablearn/kitchen
title: The Digital Kitchen: a sensor-equipped instrumented kitchen giving step-by-step spoken cooking instructions for task-based language learning
description: The Digital Kitchen is a version of the Ambient Kitchen, originally developed to help people with dementia, adapted for language teaching. It is "equipped with sensors and different wireless communication technologies" and uses accelerometers on utensils and ingredient containers to monitor users' activities. It gives "step by step cooking instructions" with verbal feedback via a touch-screen interface on which users can request repetition with written text, skip, or go back to instructions. In the study the experimental group followed instructions from this system while cooking.
requirements: Users must be able to control the process through the touch-screen interface, requesting repetition, skipping, or returning to instructions
constraints: The kitchen was still undergoing technical enhancements at the time of the study
target_learners: intermediate level English learners in a university pre-sessional programme
target_learning_goals: everyday English vocabulary
instruction patterns for cooking tasks
examples: In the study, pairs of learners cooked 'Apple Crumble' following system instructions, with a pre-test, post-task vocabulary exercises, an immediate post-test, and a delayed post-test ten days later
key_sources: Nor Fadzlinda Ishak and Paul Seedhouse. (2012). Interactive Digital Kitchen: The impact on Language learning. EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://digitalinstitute.ncl.ac.uk/ilablearn/kitchen

article_title: Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications
citation: M. N. Modebelu & C. C. Ogbonna. (2014). Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 2(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.48
title: Diversify mathematics instructional strategies to accommodate students' different learning styles
description: Because students learn in different ways and at different rates, mathematics instruction should employ varied strategies so that learners of every style can benefit. The article's reform-based treatment operationalized this by employing varied instructional strategies, discussion so every student talks mathematics, manipulatives, and short reviewed written exercises. The authors state "there is need to diversify instructional strategies and learning tasks", and recommend that mathematics teachers approach teaching with methods that are learner centered, challenging, promote skill development, provide continuous assessment, immediate feedback, and opportunity to demonstrate mathematics skills.
requirements: Teachers must know students' learning styles, e.g. via a learning style questionnaire
Instruction must include multiple strategy types within the same lessons
constraints: Evidence base is a single quasi-experimental study in Nigerian Colleges of Education on coordinate geometry content
target_learners: Secondary and tertiary mathematics students, including NCE year-one students
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and retention of mathematics knowledge
examples: The reform-based group's lessons combined whole-class discussion, manipulatives for demonstration and interaction, and supervised short written review exercises at the end of each lesson
key_sources: M. N. Modebelu & C. C. Ogbonna. (2014). Reform-Based-Instructional Method and Learning Styles on Students' Achievement and Retention in Mathematics: Administrative Implications. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies 2(2). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.48

article_title: The Effect of Differentiated Mathematics Programs on the Mathematics Attitude of Gifted Children
citation: Deringöl, Y., & Davaslıgil, Ü. (2020). The effect of differentiated mathematics programs on the mathematics attitude of gifted children. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 8(1). http://mojes.um.edu.my/
title: Researcher-developed differentiated fifth-grade fractions program built on the Grid Curriculum Model, the Parallel Curriculum Model, and Project M3 materials
description: A differentiated mathematics program for the fifth-grade 'Fractions' unit, developed by the researcher using Kaplan's Grid Curriculum Model, Tomlinson et al.'s Parallel Curriculum Model, and the M3 (Mentoring Mathematical Minds) teaching materials. The article states the Grid model is "a model developed to construct the necessary elements and format for the differentiated curriculum". Content, process and product were differentiated around a 'Balance' theme, with fractions taught across Social Sciences, Music, Science and Turkish, projects, discussions and games, guest academicians working in a master-apprentice fashion, and M3 'Deep Thinking' worksheets, activity cards and activity tools. The researcher added subheadings on multiplication and division, fraction problems, ratio and percentage.
requirements: Gifted students previously diagnosed as gifted; a theme-based curriculum with content and process goals moving in the same direction
constraints: Applied only to the Fractions unit of the fifth-grade curriculum in one Turkish pilot school for gifted education
target_learners: fifth-grade students diagnosed as gifted and talented
target_learning_goals: mathematics attitudes toward the fractions topic
deep mathematical thinking and inference
examples: Activities such as 'What would happen if there were no fractions?' and 'Find the business areas where fractions are used' extended the content to real life

article_title: Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Tim Jay, Ben Willis, Peter Thomas, Roberta Taylor, Nick Moore, Cathy Burnett, Guy Merchant, Anna Stevens. (2017). Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/
title: Dialogic Teaching intervention programme (11 cycles, mentoring, video, handbooks)
description: A Year 5 classroom-talk intervention developed by the Cambridge Primary Review Trust and the University of York, entailing "a structured programme of 11 cycles arranged in two school terms, preceded by induction and training days". Phase 1 expanded talk repertoires; phase 2 applied them in English, maths, science, and a non-core subject. Each cycle had a compulsory directed focus and an adaptable responsive focus. Schools received handbooks, recording equipment, and mentor support; cost was estimated at £52 per pupil per year.
requirements: Year 5 teachers deliver the approach within regular lessons, supported by a school mentor running planning and review sessions for each of the eleven cycles
constraints: Delivery showed variability in which resources were engaged with, duration of mentor meetings, and extent of routine application across the full curriculum
target_learners: Year 5 pupils in primary schools with over 20% FSM eligibility
target_learning_goals: attainment in English, maths, and science
higher-order talk: reasoning, discussing, arguing, explaining
examples: Schools received a handbook, monitoring booklet, Alexander (2015) Towards Dialogic Teaching, the Talk Science Primer, a repertoires card, and video/audio recording equipment
key_sources: Tim Jay, Ben Willis, Peter Thomas, Roberta Taylor, Nick Moore, Cathy Burnett, Guy Merchant, Anna Stevens. (2017). Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581114

article_title: Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Tim Jay, Ben Willis, Peter Thomas, Roberta Taylor, Nick Moore, Cathy Burnett, Guy Merchant, Anna Stevens. (2017). Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/
title: Dialogic teaching as talk that is cumulative, supportive, reciprocal, collective, and purposeful
description: The dialogic teaching approach, developed by Alexander and influenced by Vygotsky, Bruner, and Bakhtin, is positioned in opposition to monologic classroom talk dominated by teacher-led Initiation-Response-Feedback exchanges. The report states that "Dialogic teaching, on the other hand, involves talk that is cumulative, supportive, reciprocal, collective, and purposeful (Alexander, 2008)": questions provoke thoughtful answers, answers prompt further questions, and exchanges are chained into coherent lines of enquiry. The intervention applies this framework across the curriculum to develop pupils' reasoning, discussion, argument, and explanation.
requirements: teacher and pupil talk repertoires (questioning, exposition, feedback, probing, building on pupil contributions) introduced and refined for application across varied contexts
constraints: Lefstein and Snell (2014) show related dialogue-based approaches vary in strategy and in underlying notions of dialogue's nature and purposes
target_learners: primary school pupils, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking and articulacy through classroom dialogue
examples: The intervention's six-week phase 2 programme applied the repertoires in English, mathematics, science, and one non-core subject
key_sources: Tim Jay, Ben Willis, Peter Thomas, Roberta Taylor, Nick Moore, Cathy Burnett, Guy Merchant, Anna Stevens. (2017). Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581114

article_title: Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Tim Jay, Ben Willis, Peter Thomas, Roberta Taylor, Nick Moore, Cathy Burnett, Guy Merchant, Anna Stevens. (2017). Dialogic Teaching: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/
title: Development team video analysis of classroom talk (134 lessons, Observer XT coding)
description: Separately from the independent evaluation, the project development team video-recorded lessons in intervention and control schools at baseline and towards the end of the trial to compare changes in teacher and pupil talk. Fifteen intervention and 11 control teachers were recorded; because not all designated teachers taught science, "the total number of lessons record ed was 134 (67 in each phase)". A coding system of verbal indicators was applied using Observer XT 12.5 software and analysed in SPSS, with cross-validation by internal and external analysis. Interim findings appear in the process evaluation; full findings were to be published separately.
requirements: coders trained and checked to maximise coding consistency
constraints: this work has not been scrutinised or validated by the independent SHU evaluation team
target_learners: Year 5 pupils in intervention and control schools
target_learning_goals: measuring changes in teacher and pupil classroom talk over time
examples: Recordings were made in the week beginning 21 September 2015 and the fortnight beginning 22 February 2016

article_title: The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching
citation: Evangelin Arulselvi. (2016). The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching. Excellence in Education Journal, 5(2). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Effectiveness+of+Content-Based+Instruction+in+English+Language+Teaching%22
title: Dictogloss technique for CBI lessons
description: Dictogloss is "a classroom activity where learners are required to reconstruct a short text by listening and noting down key words". Students listen twice to a short content passage — first for the main idea, then for details — take notes, and reformulate their notes into a reconstructed text. The article lists it as one of the techniques used to teach the selected content in the CBI experimental condition, giving learners note-taking practice.
requirements: A short passage on appropriate content read aloud twice
target_learning_goals: listening for main ideas and details
note taking
text reconstruction
examples: Used in the experimental group's CBI lessons on Optional I English content

article_title: On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context
citation: Mahnaz Saeidi, Elaheh Zaferanieh & Hafez Shatery. (2012). On the Effects of Focus on Form, Focus on Meaning, and Focus on Forms on Learners' Vocabulary Learning in ESP Context. English Language Teaching, 5(10). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n10p72
title: Dictogloss task sequence for form-focused vocabulary learning
description: Dictogloss is a form of dictation in which students hear and reconstruct a whole text rather than doing so line by line (Wajnryb, 1990). In the study's FoF condition, the teacher first activated background knowledge with questions, students read a text, then "teachers read a short text containing new words twice and at a normal speed," students noted what they could, and in "small groups of three" reconstructed the text and compared and analyzed the different versions produced. The pattern integrates listening, note-taking, collaborative reconstruction, and form analysis.
requirements: A short text containing the target new words; small groups for reconstruction; a comparison and analysis phase of the produced versions
constraints: In this study the technique was used with beginning-proficiency Iranian ESP learners and technical vocabulary from their field of study
target_learners: University ESP students at beginning proficiency level
target_learning_goals: Productive knowledge of new technical vocabulary
examples: The FoF group's full treatment: topic questions, text reading, dictogloss listening twice at normal speed, note-taking, group reconstruction in threes, and version comparison

article_title: Evaluation of Features of Development of Sports Way of Swimming of Students of Various Sports Specialization
citation: Yermahanova, A., Nurmakhambetova, D., Bozhig, Z., & Imanbetov, A. (2016). Evaluation of Features of Development of Sports Way of Swimming of Students of Various Sports Specialization. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(18), 10895-10904. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
title: Differentiated swimming-training program pattern: specialization-specific exercise sets with assistive equipment, per-group plans and varied exercise dosage
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern in which swimming instruction is differentiated by students' long-term sport specialization and initial ability. Distinctive features include "The use of fins, 'a net', auxiliary belts, partner employment assistance" for developing swimming equipment skills, increased practice volume through fins, specialization-specific foot and hand exercises, high-density lessons with optimal rest pauses, and a separate plan of educational material for each group with differing exercise volume, intensity, rest intervals and repetitions.
requirements: Determination and systematization of basic common errors committed by athletes of different sports
Preparation of sets of exercises tailored to individual and group characteristics caused by long-term specialization
constraints: Student training is limited to the number of allocated hours for swimming training
target_learners: bachelor students of physical culture and sport of various specializations
target_learning_goals: mastering swimming techniques (front crawl, back crawl, breaststroke) and navigation methods
examples: Cyclic-sport sessions included flexibility and upper-body mobility exercises and longer uniform swimming segments; breaststroke instruction for cyclic-sport students emphasized leg exercises and hand-leg-breathing coordination

citation: Oleg V. Sidorov, Lyubov’ V. Kozub, Alexander V. Goferberg, Natalya V. Osintseva. (2018). Organization and Carrying out the Educational Experiment and Statistical Analysis of its Results in IHL. European Journal of Contemporary Education. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.1.177
title: Didactic set of high-tech educational laboratory equipment with digital program control for material-processing methods
description: A created complex of teachware comprising the course program and lecture course «Bases of Electrophysical and Electrochemical Methods of Processing of Materials», a set of educational and laboratory installations on electrospark, high-frequency electrospark processing, and metal hardening by currents of high frequency that, as the article prints, "was designed and made", plus methodical recommendations for laboratory workshops and educational tests for determining the level of mastering basic concepts. Methodical recommendations to the laboratory course including tasks explaining production processes from the point of view of Physics and Chemistry

examples: Students made educational and research experiments varying the type of work environment, electrical parameters, and the time of tool influence on details

citation: Tuncer, M., & Bahadır, F. (2014). Effect of screen reading and reading from printed out material on student success and permanency in Introduction to Computer Lesson. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 13(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ

description: Based on findings that printed material outperformed screen reading on access and permanency measures, the authors recommend that younger learners be steered toward print. retention of lesson content

article_title: Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools
citation: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581
title: Diagnostic toolkit for assessing levels of cognitive independence components
description: The authors developed tests, questionnaires, and assessment methods to measure each component at high, medium, and low levels. These included 500 test questions with 40 randomly sampled per student, the questionnaire "Multimedia tools in Education" scored 0-2 per answer, project-product assessment on technological, informative, and ergonomic levels (20, 50, 15 points), criteria-based evaluation of student-compiled test tasks on a 10-point scale, and published questionnaires for motivational, emotional-volitional, and reflexive components.
requirements: Expert assessors from relevant departments and a defined grading scale for level boundaries
constraints: Level boundaries were selected in accordance with recommendations of Ye. Sidorenko and the university's credit-system assessment policy
target_learning_goals: Measuring development of informative, operational, motivational, emotional-volitional, and reflexive components of cognitive independence
examples: The article states the proposed tools are adapted as a whole to train future Informatics teachers to use multimedia in their activities
key_sources: Yakymchuk, N. V., Kazachenok, V. V. (2018). Developing Cognitive Independence of Future Informatics Teachers by Multimedia Tools. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 7(3), 581-597. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2018.3.581

article_title: On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement
citation: Magableh, I. S. I., & Abdullah, A. (2020). On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 533-548. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13237a
title: Differentiated instruction framework: four differentiation areas (content, process, product, learning environment) guided by readiness, interests and learning profile
description: The article presents differentiated instruction as an approach and philosophy for responding to learner variance in mixed-ability classrooms, grounded in Gardner's multiple intelligences, Vygotsky's ZPD and Bloom's taxonomy. It can be applied in "different areas like the content, process, product ... and learning environment" based on "students' readiness, interests and learning profile". The study operationalised the first three areas through homogeneous grouping, tiered assignments and tiered instruction.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of students' readiness, interests and learning profiles to select differentiation areas
constraints: The study applied differentiation to content, process and product only, not the learning environment
target_learning_goals: overall English achievement
examples: The experimental group's teacher modified Action Pack 8 content, formed three homogeneous groups, and gave product choices
key_sources: Magableh, I. S. I., & Abdullah, A. (2020). On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 533-548. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13237a

article_title: On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement
citation: Magableh, I. S. I., & Abdullah, A. (2020). On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 533-548. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13237a
title: Schools and ministries should provide formal professional development and materials to support differentiated instruction in mixed-ability classrooms
description: Based on the study's findings and barriers reviewed, the article recommends institutional commitment: "The Ministry of Education in Jordan should organize formal professional development sessions about differentiated instruction strategies" and schools should train teachers and provide necessary materials. Teachers should also "provide more scaffolding for learners who lack some basic skills and provide more challenge to above grade level students according to the Zone of Proximal Development".
requirements: Commitment from school administrations to train teachers and provide materials
Teachers' commitment to alter teaching strategies
constraints: Barriers include planning time, heavy standard curriculum, preparation demands and group noise as reviewed in the article
target_learning_goals: achievement across proficiency levels
examples: The experimental group teacher received nine training sessions in total before and during the treatment
key_sources: Magableh, I. S. I., & Abdullah, A. (2020). On the Effectiveness of Differentiated Instruction in the Enhancement of Jordanian Students' Overall Achievement. International Journal of Instruction, 13(2), 533-548. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2020.13237a

article_title: An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. Revised
citation: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Kaleena Burgess. (2013). An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Distribute problems of a kind across future assignments instead of blocking all practice of a kind into one assignment
description: The article contrasts the common arrangement in which "problems of the same kind are arranged in blocks" with an alternative in which only a small block of the day's problems appears together and the remainder are spread across subsequent assignments. This redistribution is the mechanism by which interleaved assignments were produced, and it underlies the large final-test advantage reported for the interleaved condition.
requirements: Assignments spanning multiple lessons must be schedulable, so problems from a given lesson can be deferred to future assignments
constraints: Evidence comes from one middle school experiment over an 8-week period with 10 assignments
target_learning_goals: mathematics problem-solving accuracy on a delayed, unannounced test
examples: In the blocked condition all 12 problems of a kind were in a single assignment; in the interleaved condition 4 appeared together and 8 were distributed across subsequent assignments.
key_sources: Doug Rohrer, Robert F. Dedrick, Kaleena Burgess. (2013). An Efficacy Study of Interleaved Mathematics Practice. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563060

article_title: Improving Junior High School Students' Mathematical Analogical Ability Using Discovery Learning Method
citation: Maarif, S. (2016). Improving junior high school students' mathematical analogical ability using discovery learning method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 114-124. https://www.ijres.net
title: Discovery learning cycle with worksheet-guided group investigation and physical props for geometry
description: The article implements discovery learning as group work on student worksheets, following the discovery process described as "orientation, generating hypotheses, testing hypotheses, making inferences and evaluation (control)". Students manipulate physical props such as origami and HVS paper to fold shapes, measure sides and angles, and induce relationships (e.g. triangle area as half a rectangle), while the teacher circulates to monitor and scaffold. Questions on the worksheets are designed to provoke analysis, analogy-finding, and generalization.
requirements: Worksheet questions must "stimulate students' thinking process optimally" and be answerable within students' reach so they do not fail or lose confidence
Teacher performs didactic-pedagogical anticipation in the lesson plan, predicting student responses before teaching
constraints: At the first meeting group formation caused friction; some students initially refused to work with particular peers
Low-ability students had difficulty understanding worksheet problems and could not resolve all worksheet items
target_learners: junior high school (grade VII) mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematical analogical ability
geometry concepts (triangle, square, rectangle area and perimeter)
generalization and pattern-finding
examples: Students folded origami paper to relate rectangle and triangle area formulas
Students used HVS paper divided into two-centimetre lengths to derive K = 2(p + l) and L = p × l for rectangles
key_sources: Maarif, S. (2016). Improving junior high school students' mathematical analogical ability using discovery learning method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 114-124. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105169

article_title: A Comparison of Two Curricular Models of Professional Development to Increase Teacher Repertoires for Instructing Students with Autism
citation: Dille, L. (2013). A Comparison of Two Curricular Models of Professional Development to Increase Teacher Repertoires for Instructing Students with Autism. Journal of the American Academy of Special Education Professionals (JAASEP), Fall 2013. https://jaasep.org
title: Four researcher-developed assessment instruments for teacher knowledge, self-efficacy, self-report of use, and application to hypothetical cases
description: The researcher developed four instruments based on literature about each treatment approach: a 30-item Teacher Knowledge questionnaire (split-half reliability .77, coefficient alpha .846), a 30-item self-efficacy checklist scored 0-3 (split-half .94, alpha .97), a 30-item self-report frequency checklist scored 0-4 (split-half .94, alpha .97), and a Performance Assessment of Application using "four case studies in which two depict hypothetical students with mild to moderate autism and two case studies depict students in the moderate to severe range", scored 0-3 per response with a 72-point maximum. Face validity was checked by thirteen reviewers of teachers, clinicians, and experts in both approaches, and inter-rater reliability on application scoring was Kappa=.90 pre-test and Kappa=.91 post-test.
requirements: Face validity review by teachers, clinicians, and experts experienced in both behavioral and socio-emotional approaches
Two raters scoring the application measure with Kappa-checked consistency
constraints: The article states the assessments were developed by consultation with experts and that this may have been a limitation; a factor analysis for each assessment is warranted and more extensive item analysis should be performed
target_learners: Teachers of students with autism in school-based, inclusion, preschool, early intervention, and home-based programs
target_learning_goals: Teacher knowledge of autism diagnosis, symptoms, and educational approaches
Teacher self-efficacy and frequency of use of instructional methods, strategies, and learning supports
Application of instructional methods to students with mild/moderate and severe autism
examples: The application instrument presented a consistent set of six questions across all four case studies, with each severity category scored out of a 36-point maximum
key_sources: Dille, L. (2013). A Comparison of Two Curricular Models of Professional Development to Increase Teacher Repertoires for Instructing Students with Autism. Journal of the American Academy of Special Education Professionals (JAASEP), Fall 2013. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135486

article_title: Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills
citation: Nurhan Aktaş & Hayati Akyol. (2020). Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills. https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2020.248.20
title: Digital writing workshop implementation pairing each writing-process stage with a different digital platform
description: The experimental implementation carried out "each stage of the writing process (preparation, planning, creating a draft, review, redaction and publication)" using a digital platform chosen for that stage: Spider Scribe for mind maps at preparation, Edmodo for sharing drafts, Story Jumper for revision after feedback, Wikispaces for final revisions, and Emaze for publishing presentations. The programme ran 4 lesson hours per week over 14 weeks, with one hour of story-writing instruction, two hours of platform practice, and one group hour for exchanging ideas and feedback.
requirements: a continually available internet connection and a laboratory or classroom having an adequate number of computers
students possessing technological tools for use outside school
constraints: the digital platforms used during the research process were operated on one single type of text (the story)
target_learning_goals: story writing skills
writing motivation
new literacy skills
examples: Students created mind maps in Spider Scribe, shared drafts in Edmodo, revised in Story Jumper and Wikispaces, and published presentations in Emaze
key_sources: Nurhan Aktaş & Hayati Akyol. (2020). Effect of Digital Writing Workshop Activities on Writing Motivation and Development of Story Writing Skills. https://doi.org/10.29329/ijpe.2020.248.20

article_title: The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties
citation: Ahmad Abdulhameed Aufan Al-Makahleh. (2011). The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties. International Education Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v4n4p199
title: Direct Instruction strategy as a behavioral, teacher-directed mastery model
description: The article describes Direct Instruction as a behavioral instructional strategy in which "instructions are given explicitly and sequentially when a skill is to be learned" and high-level skills are analyzed into component parts with sequential training until mastery. Its main goal is to bring students to "the mastery level before learning a new skill." The article uses this model as the experimental treatment for students with mathematics learning difficulties.
requirements: Well-planned, neat, and organized lessons
Training revolving around small modules with teacher-directed instructional process
constraints: The article frames the strategy as appropriate for students with learning difficulties in resource-room settings
target_learners: 4th- and 5th-grade students with mathematics learning difficulties
target_learning_goals: Mastery of basic mathematical skills and concepts
examples: The experimental treatment trained students on basic Math skills using the Direct Instruction Strategy in resource rooms
key_sources: Ahmad Abdulhameed Aufan Al-Makahleh. (2011). The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties. International Education Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v4n4p199

article_title: The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties
citation: Ahmad Abdulhameed Aufan Al-Makahleh. (2011). The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties. International Education Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v4n4p199
title: Eight-step direct instruction lesson sequence for skill mastery
description: The article enumerates the steps of the Direct Instruction strategy: measuring student performance directly pre-teaching, setting operationally formulated goals, analyzing and sequencing the instructional task, allocating sufficient time, providing performance feedback, having students practice mastered tasks, displaying performance graphically, and providing problem-solving forms and matched practice. The article applies this sequence as the experimental treatment in mathematics.
requirements: Goals set accurately and operationally formulated
Sufficient time allocated for task learning
Feedback provided regarding student performance
target_learning_goals: Basic mathematical skills and computational operations
examples: The experimental group received training on basic Math skills using this strategy while the control group was taught traditionally
key_sources: Ahmad Abdulhameed Aufan Al-Makahleh. (2011). The Effect of Direct Instruction Strategy on Math Achievement of Primary 4th and 5th Grade Students with Learning Difficulties. International Education Studies, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v4n4p199

article_title: Family-Based Training Program Improves Brain Function, Cognition, and Behavior in Lower Socioeconomic Status Preschoolers
citation: Pakulak, E., Stevens, C., Bell, T. A., Fanning, J., Klein, S., Isbell, E., & Neville, H. (2013). Family-based training program improves brain function, cognition, and behavior in lower socioeconomic status preschoolers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Differential neuroplasticity profiles of brain systems, with selective attention highly modifiable by experience
description: The article's guiding framework holds that different brain systems display markedly different profiles of neuroplasticity: some are strongly determined, others remain changeable throughout life, and some are experience-dependent only during "sensitive periods." Systems that are most modifiable show both enhancements (e.g., in deaf and blind individuals) and greater vulnerability (developmental disorders, lower SES). Sustained selective attention is presented as one such highly malleable system, central to learning, memory, and school readiness, and increasable by training.
requirements: Interventions targeting such systems should be timed with respect to sensitive periods and delivered through experience-dependent training
constraints: The framework is presented as motivation from the authors' prior basic research, not tested within this abstract itself
target_learners: Preschool children from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Selective attention as a foundation for learning, memory, and school readiness
examples: The authors cite their prior ERP studies showing selective attention deficits in lower SES children and enhancements following computerized training
key_sources: Pakulak, E., Stevens, C., Bell, T. A., Fanning, J., Klein, S., Isbell, E., & Neville, H. (2013). Family-based training program improves brain function, cognition, and behavior in lower socioeconomic status preschoolers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563293

article_title: The Effect of the Differentiated Teaching Approach in the Algebraic Learning Field on Students' Academic Achievements
citation: Bal, A. P. (2016). The effect of the differentiated teaching approach in the algebraic learning field on students’ academic achievements. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 63, 185-204. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.63.11
title: Differentiated teaching approach (Tomlinson)
description: The differentiated teaching approach, first described by Tomlinson (1999), is a framework that "accounts personal differences within a class, considers different students’ different skills and learning needs , and draws on students’ strengths". The article situates it within social constructivism, multiple intelligence, thinking styles, Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, and brain-based learning, and in mathematics it offers multiple learning environments at various levels using strategies such as stations, centers, agendas, and tiered teaching.
requirements: Teachers must diagnose students’ learning styles and readiness levels to plan suitable difficulty levels
constraints: The article notes the approach depends on the instructor’s teaching profile, skills, interests, and pre-knowledge
target_learners: sixth-grade primary school mathematics students of mixed readiness
target_learning_goals: algebraic thinking and achievement in the algebra learning field
examples: The study applied the tiered teaching technique to algebra topics new to sixth graders for four weeks (16 lesson hours)
key_sources: Bal, A. P. (2016). The effect of the differentiated teaching approach in the algebraic learning field on students’ academic achievements. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 63, 185-204. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.63.11

article_title: A Practitioner Implementation of a Tier 2 First-Grade Mathematics Intervention
citation: Strand Cary, M. G., Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Fien, H., & Baker, S. K. (2017). A practitioner implementation of a Tier 2 first grade mathematics intervention. Learning Disability Quarterly, 40(4), 211–224. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948717714715
title: Supplement formal development and efficacy studies with hands-off district-initiated implementations to observe how programs work under authentic conditions
description: The article argues that developer teams should take advantage of practitioner interest to study interventions under realistic conditions they could not arrange themselves. Such studies, the authors write, give developers the chance to see "what works (or does not work) in a wider variety of contexts and with a wider variety of students than would otherwise be possible during a typical development grant". They also let districts evaluate new practices with more rigor than typical practice changes, and feed implementation insights back into curriculum refinement and the design of later controlled efficacy studies.
requirements: District administrators willing to provide outcome data, solicit educator feedback, and supply comparison-student data
Research team able to provide training to interventionists and assessment administrators and recommendations for selection and implementation
constraints: Such studies cannot support rigorous RCT or regression discontinuity designs; the research team had little control over sample size, participant selection, or implementation, and fidelity could not be documented
target_learners: at-risk elementary students in authentic school settings
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement of at-risk students
implementation feasibility of Tier 2 interventions
examples: Educators in Hawaii implemented Fusion without external funding or ongoing support while schools administered pre/post assessments and educators completed optional surveys, informing the design of the subsequent IES Goal 3 efficacy study
key_sources: Strand Cary, M. G., Clarke, B., Doabler, C. T., Smolkowski, K., Fien, H., & Baker, S. K. (2017). A practitioner implementation of a Tier 2 first grade mathematics intervention. Learning Disability Quarterly, 40(4), 211–224. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948717714715

article_title: Digital Storytelling: A Multimodal Narrative Writing Genre
citation: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. http://www.jlls.org
title: Digital storytelling as a multimodal narrative writing genre with seven elements and three production stages
description: Digital storytelling (DS) is defined as "the newest version of the ancient storytelling", telling a story using multimedia elements such as images, music, and narrated voice. The article describes seven elements (point of view, a dramatic question, emotional content, gift of voice, the power of soundtrack, economy, and pacing) and three stages: preparation (topic selection, storyboarding, script writing), production (choosing non-verbal elements), and presentation. It positions DS as a learner-centered setting in which students construct meaning from their own experiences using multiple modes.
requirements: Script writing must be treated as the most essential part, since if the script writing is ignored the final product cannot be truly effective
constraints: DS does not negate the traditional writing process; it follows process writing steps such as drafting, editing, revising, and sharing
target_learning_goals: narrative writing skills
multimodal expression and meaning-making
examples: In the study, experimental-group students wrote scripts in three drafts, storyboarded, selected multimedia elements, recorded voice, assembled stories in WeVideo, presented in class, and shared via Facebook
key_sources: Balaman, S. (2018). Digital storytelling: A multimodal narrative writing genre. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(3), 202-212. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1193109

article_title: The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement
citation: Tongtong Zhang & Zhiwei Wu. (2017). The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement. English Language Teaching, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n1p72
title: Two validated listening tests: TEM-4-style dictation and CATTI-style summary writing
description: The study designed two tests to assess L2 listening competence: a 162-word dictation passage about flash-mob played three times with 15 pause segments (following TEM-4 design), and a 2-minute-52-second mini-lecture about kite-surfing safety rules followed by a summary under 100 words played once (following CATTI design). Piloted with 25 students from a third class, "both tests were able to separate the highest 8 performers (i.e. top 33.33%) from the lowest 8 performers (for dictation, t=4.76, p.<0.001; for summary, t=7.49, p.<0.001)". Scoring by two independent assistants showed high inter-rater reliability (dictation r=0.952; summary r=0.967, both p<0.001).
requirements: Two research assistants scored performance independently, with the average taken as the final score
constraints: Using the same tests at pre-test and post-test risks score inflation because students might remember the test contents, which the authors acknowledge
target_learning_goals: intensive listening skill
selective listening skill
examples: Dictation scored 1 point per correct word out of 162, with half points for non-hindering spelling mistakes; summary scored out of 30 across 10 minor (1 point) and 10 major (2 points) information units
key_sources: Tongtong Zhang & Zhiwei Wu. (2017). The Impact of Consecutive Interpreting Training on the L2 Listening Competence Enhancement. English Language Teaching, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n1p72

article_title: High Quality Differentiated Instruction--A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom
citation: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124
title: Differentiated instruction as a framework adapting instructional design to student characteristics
description: Differentiated instruction is a framework including a variety of teaching strategies and methods aiming at maximizing learning profit for all learners in a classroom. An essential feature is that instructional design is based not only on curriculum learning goals but also on students' characteristics such as readiness, interests and learning profile. A second essential element is that teachers invest in ongoing assessment to tailor instructional design to students' characteristics; the article operationalized both expert DI models into eight operational characteristics (A–I) including respectful tasks, growth mindset, adaptation of content, process and product, flexible grouping, and ongoing assessment and adjustment.
requirements: Teachers invest in ongoing assessment in order to be able to tailor instructional design to students' characteristics
constraints: Research on effectivity of DI is scarce and focuses on elements of the construct rather than on the construct as a whole; the concept has not been subject to academic effectivity research as a whole
target_learners: students in heterogeneous general education classrooms
target_learning_goals: maximizing learning profit for all learners
examples: The model of Hall provides a visual representation of differentiated teaching as a cyclical process of ongoing assessment and adjustment
key_sources: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124

article_title: High Quality Differentiated Instruction--A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom
citation: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124
title: Three-set structure of DI criteria: teacher-students, learning goals, lesson design
description: The checklist organizes high-quality differentiated instruction into three sets of criteria: (1) the teachers in relation to the students; (2) the teacher and the learning goals; (3) the teacher and the lesson design. The authors deliberately ordered them so that relational and goal-related themes are handled prior to instructional adaptations, stating it was "a deliberate choice to present the first characteristic of adapting instructional design only as a third theme". Each set is printed as a table of concrete teacher criteria.
requirements: Both the relational and the learning-goal themes are to be handled prior to instructional adaptations
target_learners: general education teachers in heterogeneous classrooms
target_learning_goals: implementing differentiated instruction in an evidence-informed way
examples: Table 2 lists criteria such as installing a classroom culture where failure is possible; Table 4 lists building on existing knowledge and using flexible grouping
key_sources: Wouter Smets. (2017). High Quality Differentiated Instruction – A Checklist for Teacher Professional Development on Handling Differences in the General Education Classroom. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2074-2080. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051124

article_title: The Effects of Diaries on Self-Regulation Strategies of Preservice Science Teachers
citation: Arsal, Z. (2010). The effects of diaries on self-regulation strategies of preservice science teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 5(1), 85-103. http://www.ijese.com/
title: Pair diary reporting with additional self-regulation strategy training for greater improvement
description: The study found that diaries alone improved some strategies but not others, because participants used only the self-regulation strategies they already knew. The author recommends that to achieve improvement in self-regulation strategies by using diaries, learners should not be only asked to report their learning activities daily but also some additional training program should be applied to them regarding self-regulation strategies, including specific training on cognitive strategies such as reasoning, summarizing, organizing and critical thinking.
requirements: Daily reporting of learning activities in diaries
An additional training program on self-regulation strategies beyond diary reporting
constraints: Diary keeping alone, without strategy training, showed no significant effect on cognitive strategies such as rehearsal, elaboration, organization, and critical thinking
target_learning_goals: self-regulation strategies
cognitive strategies
examples: The author recommends that additional cognitive strategy training activities such as reasoning, summarizing, organizing and critical thinking should be organized to achieve improvement in cognitive strategies by keeping diaries.
key_sources: Arsal, Z. (2010). The effects of diaries on self-regulation strategies of preservice science teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 5(1), 85-103. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ884413

article_title: The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes
citation: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274.
title: Didactic model for forming students' creative independence in foreign-language teaching
description: The authors developed a didactic model whose target is to form students' creative independence, with tasks of "formation of students' creative thinking", transferring scientific and informative knowledge, and mastering experience of creative activity. It specifies teacher didactic activity stages, pedagogical conditions, and forms and methods of student work (frontal, collective, group and individual creative tasks, creation of creative language situations). The model was realized during the formative stage of the experiment and, per the authors, "helped to increase the effectiveness of the development of students' creative independence in linguistic higher educational institutions".
requirements: Requires diagnosing students' level of creative potential, initial opportunities, cognitive activity and motivation before instruction
Requires the teacher to plan lessons in compliance with problems of formation of students' creative independence and correct the level of formation
constraints: Tested with first- and second-year university students in English language classes at one institution
target_learners: first- and second-year university students studying English
target_learning_goals: creative independence
creative thinking
transfer of acquired knowledge and skills to new language situations
examples: In the formative stage students performed differentiated actions: finding equivalents on the basis of creative tasks, finding synonyms and antonyms, translating, completing sentences, and expressing opinions on a subject
key_sources: Liya F. Shangaraeva, Alfiya A. Yarkhamova, Zubayda A. Biktagirova, Dorice Agol. (2016). The Formation of Students' Creative Independence at the English Language Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(6), 1267-1274. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1114326

article_title: Discovery Learning Strategies in English
citation: Singaravelu, G. (2012). Discovery Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 1, January - March 2012. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Discovery learning activity sequence for English grammar (diagnose, design, interactions, presentation)
description: The article describes a set of classroom activities designed to implement discovery learning for standard V English grammar: 'Diagnose the problems, Designing the Discovery learning, Face–to- Face interaction, Internet interaction, Team interaction, Team pair Table and Presentation'. The sequence begins by diagnosing learning obstacles from a pre-test, then has pupils discover grammar content through face-to-face, internet and team interaction before presenting results. Planning guidance includes selecting an activity, gathering materials, staying focused, using caution, planning extra time, recording process and results, discussing and reviewing, and trying again.
requirements: A researcher-made achievement test to diagnose problems and evaluate grammar skills
Planning steps including selecting an activity, gathering materials, and recording process and results
constraints: The study confined the sequence to 60 standard V pupils in one middle school and to the Tamilnadu state board English textbook grammar
target_learners: standard V primary school pupils learning English as a second language
target_learning_goals: functional English grammar achievement
examples: Discovery method was used in the classroom for learning grammar for one week, followed by a post-test
key_sources: Singaravelu, G. (2012). Discovery Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 2 No. 1, January - March 2012. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070208

article_title: Remedial Instruction to Enhance Mathematical Ability of Dyscalculics
citation: S. Praveen Kumar & B. William Dharma Raja. (2012). Remedial Instruction to Enhance Mathematical Ability of Dyscalculics. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 6 No. 1 May - July 2012.
title: Teach dyscalculic learners through varied techniques and materials rather than traditional methods
description: The article argues that because learners with disabilities "are wired differently and hence they have to be taught differently", teachers should match teaching style to students' learning styles, present bite-size information in sequential steps, and provide structured practice with immediate corrective feedback. It concludes remedial instruction is "an effective strategy in enhancing the performance of dyscalculic children".
requirements: Teachers willing to match their teaching style to the learning style of the student
constraints: Recommendation grounded in the authors' interpretation and a single-group study
target_learners: students with learning disabilities, including dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: numerical skills and mathematical ability
key_sources: S. Praveen Kumar & B. William Dharma Raja. (2012). Remedial Instruction to Enhance Mathematical Ability of Dyscalculics. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 6 No. 1 May - July 2012. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102291

article_title: A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students
citation: Vahdany, F., Abdollahzadeh, M., Gholami, S., & Ghanipoor, M. (2014). A Study of the Relationship between Type of Dictionary Used and Lexical Proficiency in Writings of Iranian EFL Students. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.6p.31
title: Dictionary-use skill task based on Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary exercises
description: Skill in dictionary use was measured with a four-exercise task using copied relevant parts of the Oxford Advanced Learners dictionary distributed to all participants. The exercises covered "knowledge of word labels (their usage and meaning), knowledge of word definition, knowledge of grammatical patterns, and knowledge of parts of speech". Task scores correlated .958 with lexical proficiency in writing.
requirements: Participants need access to relevant dictionary sections; the task requires answering word-usage questions using the dictionary
constraints: The authors suggest future studies use different tasks including more aspects of dictionary use skills
target_learning_goals: skill in dictionary use
examples: Twenty participants completed the task; scores were correlated with composition ratings

article_title: The Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter in Teaching the States of Matter and Their Changes
citation: Sopandi, W., Kadarohman, A., Rosbiono, M., Latip, A., & Sukardi, R. R. (2018). The Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter in Teaching the States of Matter and Their Changes. International Journal of Instruction, 11(1), 61-76. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.1115a
title: Courseware of Discontinuous Nature of Matter
description: A computer-based courseware developed by the research team to introduce the particle concept: that all matter consists of particles separated by "particle-free space" between moving particles. It presents a number of experiments with relevant animations to help students visualize the sub-microscopic level. In the study it assisted structure-oriented chemistry teaching of the particle concept before the topic of changing states of matter.
requirements: Used within structure-oriented chemistry teaching of the particle concept before teaching states of matter and their changes
constraints: The article notes the courseware alone did not maximally increase understanding, indicating other factors also influence gains
target_learning_goals: Understanding the discontinuous nature of matter (particle concept and particle-free space)
Sub-microscopic visualization of changing states of matter
examples: Guided students through experiments and animations showing particles and particle-free space before the changing-states topic
