article_title: Direct Instruction and Music Literacy: One Approach to Augmenting the Diminishing?
citation: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975621
title: Ten-minute Direct Instruction bursts at the start of regular lessons
description: The article describes a reusable lesson-level design in which a scripted 10-minute Direct Instruction segment is delivered at the commencement of each regular music lesson, following Farkota's model that 'DI is most effective when used in short 10 minute bursts at the commencement of regular lessons.' The DI component introduces and reinforces basic skills which are then applied in other contexts during the remainder of the lesson. Scripts are organised around music literacy strands arranged into levels of increasing complexity.
requirements: Carefully scripted lessons to keep teacher participants on track and minimise in-class time wastage
Student worksheets and record sheets for tracking progress on each question
constraints: Development and piloting of the scripted program took a 12-month period and many hours of deliberation and preparation, which may act as a deterrent to some teachers
target_learning_goals: Basic music literacy skills including rhythm and pitch
examples: A series of 10 minute DI scripts were developed based around five music literacy strands, later condensed to two strands (rhythm and pitch) with ten levels each, delivered over 20 lessons in one trimester.
key_sources: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1000240

article_title: Direct Instruction and Music Literacy: One Approach to Augmenting the Diminishing?
citation: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975621
title: Direct Instruction as a teacher-centred approach using explanation, modelling, practice and feedback
description: Direct Instruction (DI) is described as 'a teacher-centred teaching approach that uses teacher explanation and modelling combined with student practice and feedback to teach concepts and procedural skills.' The teacher specifies learning objectives, explains and illustrates content and models skills for students. Rosenshine and Stevens (1986) summarise six stages: revision of previous work, presentation of new material in clear and logical steps, guided practice, feedback with correctives, independent practice, and revision to consolidate learning. The model is specifically designed to teach skills and concepts with emphasis on explicit objectives, detailed instruction, and timely feedback.
requirements: Efficient and experienced teachers who rely on clear language, modelling and effective feedback
constraints: Critics describe it as rote learning, authoritarian, and failing to address individual student differences; the researchers do not advocate it as a teaching method for applied music activities such as composition or performance
target_learning_goals: Basic skills and concepts acquisition, including music literacy
examples: In Australia, DI programs have been employed in mathematics (Farkota's Elementary Maths Mastery) and in corrective reading (Carnine, Engelmann, Johnson & Meyer, 1999).
key_sources: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1000240

article_title: Direct Instruction and Music Literacy: One Approach to Augmenting the Diminishing?
citation: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ975621
title: Use Direct Instruction to build basic literacy skills before introducing student-centred applied activities
description: The article recommends that DI be used not as a total teaching approach but as a pedagogical approach suited to developing particular skills, with a DI approach used 'to develop basic literacy skill sets, leading to the introduction of more applied student-centred learning activities later in the lesson.' By building basic literacy skills, a DI program may allow more meaningful interaction in applied music activities such as composing and performing because students are better equipped technically. DI can coexist alongside student-centred teaching approaches as part of a balanced teaching approach.
requirements: A carefully scripted DI program targeting specific basic skills
Willingness to combine DI with other teaching approaches in a balanced way
constraints: The researchers do not present Direct Instruction as a 'cure-all' for music teachers and do not advocate it as a teaching method for applied music activities such as composition or performance
target_learning_goals: Basic music literacy as a foundation for applied music activities
examples: The DI intervention was created to build basic music literacy skills, and the researchers do not advocate it as a teaching method for applied music activities such as composition or performance.
key_sources: Lowe, G., & Belcher, S. (2012). Direct Instruction and music literacy: one approach to augmenting the diminishing? Australian Journal of Music Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1000240

article_title: An Investigation of the Pedagogical Impact of Using Case-Based Learning in a Undergraduate Biochemistry Course
citation: Kulak, V., & Newton, G. (2015). An Investigation of the Pedagogical Impact of Using Case-based Learning in a Undergraduate Biochemistry Course. International Journal of Higher Education, 4(4), 13. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v4n4p13
title: Directed CBL module process: case orientation, lecture, peer instruction, and case review
description: This pattern describes the four-task structure used for each course module in the directed CBL intervention. As the article states, "each module in the course involved four tasks, including orientation to the case study, a relevant lecture, peer instruction, and case review." Students had approximately four days between case orientation and peer instruction to answer directed questions in self-selected groups of five to seven, followed by a 45-minute instructor-facilitated case wrap up. This structure combines lectures with case study, suiting content-heavy courses.
requirements: Self-selected groups of five to seven students with each student assigned one to two questions to answer, with seven questions per case
constraints: The directed type of CBL uses questions with close-ended answers and allows the instructor to monitor construction of information to prevent students from diverging from the main topic
target_learners: Second-year undergraduate Kinesiology students in a biochemistry course
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge in human metabolism and biochemistry
examples: Cases included 'Baby Chloe, born with a glycogen storage disease' and 'Luiza, who went on a 28 day juice fast', each focused on one metabolic theme per module
key_sources: Kulak, V., & Newton, G. (2015). An Investigation of the Pedagogical Impact of Using Case-based Learning in a Undergraduate Biochemistry Course. International Journal of Higher Education, 4(4), 13. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v4n4p13

article_title: An Investigation of the Pedagogical Impact of Using Case-Based Learning in a Undergraduate Biochemistry Course
citation: Kulak, V., & Newton, G. (2015). An Investigation of the Pedagogical Impact of Using Case-based Learning in a Undergraduate Biochemistry Course. International Journal of Higher Education, 4(4), 13. https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v4n4p13
title: Use directed CBL as a low-resource active learning technique suitable for content-heavy courses
description: The article supports directed CBL as a versatile active learning strategy that can be implemented without major resource investment. The authors note it "does not require much investment of resources since trained facilitators are not required for each group of students" and is "a suitable technique to teach content heavy courses such as biochemistry." This principle recommends directed CBL when instructors seek active learning that combines with lectures in resource-constrained settings.
requirements: Cases accompanied by a set of questions with close-ended answers and supporting material presented with figures, tables, and texts
constraints: Each type of CBL is suitable for higher education provided that case complexity is appropriate to the knowledge base of the students and the subject taught
target_learners: Undergraduate students in content-heavy science courses
target_learning_goals: Foundational disciplinary knowledge and engagement with course content
examples: The study used the directed method across eight metabolic modules in a second-year biochemistry course, comparing outcomes to a non-CBL active learning mixture

article_title: Improving Access To, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K-12 Education
citation: Burch, P., Good, A., & Heinrich, C. (2016). Improving Access to, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K–12 Education. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373715592706
title: A taxonomy of digital tutoring defined by tutor location, synchronicity, instruction driver, and curriculum location
description: The article develops a categorization system for digital providers to enable rigorous estimation of OST tutoring program effects. It classifies programs along four dimensions: tutor location (online/phone vs face-to-face), tutor synchronicity (asynchronous vs synchronous), instruction driver (curriculum-based software, tutor with software, or tutor without software), and curriculum location (Internet-accessed, locally installed software, or nondigital resources). The taxonomy was built iteratively from provider applications to the state of Texas and cross-checked with district administrative data, defining "digital" as services in which students directly interact with digital technology at least as sophisticated as an iPod.
requirements: Provider applications and district administrative data sufficient to classify programs on all four dimensions
constraints: Classification was complicated by vague, insufficient, or conflicting information in provider responses
target_learners: low-income K–12 students in OST tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: reading and mathematics achievement
examples: Applied to 35 digital providers with the largest student market shares in Dallas ISD, 2011–2012
key_sources: Burch, P., Good, A., & Heinrich, C. (2016). Improving Access to, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K–12 Education. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373715592706

article_title: Improving Access To, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K-12 Education
citation: Burch, P., Good, A., & Heinrich, C. (2016). Improving Access to, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K–12 Education. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373715592706
title: A spectrum of tutor roles in digital tutoring: no tutor, technician, monitor/guide, and instructor
description: The article categorizes digital OST tutors into four enacted roles based on observations and interviews. "No tutor" platforms have students interact only with software; "technician" personnel provide only technical assistance; "monitor/guide" tutors respond to specific questions and call families but do not deliver instruction; "instructor" tutors interact constantly and the curriculum cannot progress without them. The authors note that in practice tutors often occupy multiple categories simultaneously, and that additional staff (case managers, curriculum teams, quality assurance testers) also interact with students' instructional processes from farther from the point of delivery.
requirements: Defining "tutor" as the provider staff most directly responsible for instruction of an individual student
constraints: Roles are distinct analytically but tutors often occupy multiple categories in practice
target_learners: low-income K–12 students in OST tutoring programs
target_learning_goals: reading and mathematics achievement
examples: A synchronous tutor used chat to explain headset reconnection when audio was lost, illustrating overlapping technical and instructional roles
key_sources: Burch, P., Good, A., & Heinrich, C. (2016). Improving Access to, Quality, and the Effectiveness of Digital Tutoring in K–12 Education. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373715592706

article_title: Effects of Scaffolds and Scientific Reasoning Ability on Web-Based Scientific Inquiry
citation: Wu, H.-L., Weng, H.-L., & She, H.-C. (2016). Effects of scaffolds and scientific reasoning ability on web-based scientific inquiry. International Journal of Contemporary Educational Research, 3(1), 12-24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102367
title: Provide direct instructional scaffolding in web-based scientific inquiry to support hypothesis generation and conclusion drawing
description: Direct scaffolding provides explicit instructional guidance, concept reiteration, and multiple-choice questions with hints during web-based inquiry activities. The study found "students who used direct scaffolding outperformed those who used indirect scaffolding in making hypotheses and drawing conclusions." This principle recommends embedding direct scaffolds at the hypothesis and conclusion phases of online inquiry programs, particularly where learners have some prior reasoning ability.
requirements: Learners engage in web-based scientific inquiry activities including hypothesis generation and evidence-based conclusion drawing
constraints: Direct scaffolding benefits were concentrated among students with high prior reasoning skills; low reasoning students showed no significant scaffolding-type differences
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry abilities including making hypotheses and drawing evidence-based conclusions
examples: The web-based program provided direct scaffolds via multiple-choice questions on main concepts and hints such as "It is still unclear what the relationships exist among the speed of transpiration, the number of leave and the rate of water transportation upwards"
key_sources: Wu, H.-L., Weng, H.-L., & She, H.-C. (2016). Effects of scaffolds and scientific reasoning ability on web-based scientific inquiry. International Journal of Contemporary Educational Research, 3(1), 12-24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1216018

title: Measure post-high school outcomes directly rather than relying on interim or indirect measures
description: The review recommends that transition research use explicit indicators of employment, postsecondary education, and independent living rather than proxies. It states "the field has not convincingly shown a connection between interim or indirect measures deemed important (for example, self-determination and locus of control) for in-school programs and these later outcomes." Researchers are encouraged to use state longitudinal data systems and administrative databases such as the National Student Clearinghouse.

article_title: The Influences of Pre-Testing Reviews and Delays on Differential-Associative Processing versus Conditions in Which Students Chose Their Learning Strategy
citation: Brenda Hannon. (2013). The Influences of Pre-testing Reviews and Delays on Differential-associative Processing versus Conditions in which Students chose their Learning Strategy. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v1i2.225
title: Differential-associative processing: a two-step strategy of identifying critical differences and associating features with concept names
description: Differential-associative processing is a learning strategy for definitions of semantically related concepts, grounded in the distinctiveness hypothesis and associative strength theory. It "includes two major steps: (i) a differential processing step that involves identifying important differences in the definitions for two related concepts, and (ii) an association step that involves each feature of an identified difference with the name of its respective concept". The article evaluates it against student-chosen strategies.
requirements: Pairs of related concept definitions presented simultaneously so differences can be identified
A facilitator or assistant to state features during the association step and record generated differences
constraints: Has been assessed only in a laboratory setting with pairs of definitions from Introductory Psychology textbooks and multiple-choice questions
target_learners: university students in introductory psychology courses
target_learning_goals: learning definitions of semantically related concepts for multiple-choice assessment

article_title: "The Joy of Reading"--An Intervention Program to Increase Reading Motivation for Pupils with Learning Disabilities
citation: Tovli, E. (2014). "The Joy of Reading" - An Intervention Program to Increase Reading Motivation for Pupils with Learning Disabilities. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 2(4). http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v2i4.496
title: Rich differentiated classroom library as a reading-motivation component
description: Each classroom maintained a library of children's newspapers, comics, poetry, story-books, fairy-tales, activity books, encyclopedias, and Bible stories, organised by topic across genres. The library was active all day long, accessible after task completion or for relaxation, with a lending system for take-home books and activity cards prompting written responses (letter to a character, alternative endings, story continuation).
requirements: Variety of genres and reading levels
Accessible throughout the school day
Lending mechanism with a borrowing form
target_learning_goals: Reading motivation
Independent reading
Written response to texts
examples: Topic-based genre clustering (e.g., 'stones': story-book 'Stone Soup', science book, science fiction book on the same topic)

article_title: Dialogic Approach to the Analysis of the Meaning-Making Process in a Blended Setting
citation: Rossana Beraldo, Silviane Barbato, M. Beatrice Ligorio. (2022). Dialogic approach to the analysis of the meaning-making process in a blended setting. Dialogic Pedagogy: An International Online Journal. https://doi.org/10.5195/dpj.2022.499
title: Dialogic thematic analysis: centripetal and centrifugal forces as an analytic framework for meaning-making
description: The article develops a dialogic-thematic analysis procedure, grounded in Bakhtinian concepts, for mapping meaning-making in blended collaborative settings. The analyst treats "centripetal forces as convergent and related to the permanence of values, ideologies, standardisation and cultural beliefs" leading to instrumental learning, while "centrifugal forces are divergent producing decentralisation, polyphonies, openness, novelty, high variability in meaning-making, and agency". Transcripts are organised in vertical turn-taking sequences and then in horizontal units of analysis, with a semantic map charting recurrent themes and a re-contextualisation box synthesising results.
requirements: Requires multimethod data: profile interview, problem-solving tasks, and an episodic interview with each dyad
constraints: The authors note the method was developed for tracking meaning-making dynamics within dyads collaborating in a blended setting
target_learning_goals: meaning-making in collaborative problem-solving
examples: Applied to one dyad's 579 turns of discussion across two tasks and an episodic interview, yielding a semantic map with twin themes, sub-themes and a re-contextualisation box
key_sources: Rossana Beraldo, Silviane Barbato, M. Beatrice Ligorio. (2022). Dialogic approach to the analysis of the meaning-making process in a blended setting. Dialogic Pedagogy: An International Online Journal. https://doi.org/10.5195/dpj.2022.499

article_title: Growth in Secondary Teachers' Content Knowledge and Practice in Discrete Mathematics
citation: James A. Middleton, Mona Toncheff, Susan Haag. (2011). Growth in Secondary Teachers' Content Knowledge and Practice in Discrete Mathematics. title: Distribute intensive professional development across the year rather than concentrating it in two-week summer workshops
description: The project's authors report that concentrating the bulk of learning in a two-week summer workshop format caused problems: "Teachers experience a high level of mental fatigue and express feelings of being overwhelmed using this format." They suggest that implementing a two-week summer workshop "may not be the most effective way to provide the bulk of the learning", implying sustained, distributed sessions (such as the project's monthly 8-hour Saturday sessions) are preferable.

constraints: The article states this as a concern about the two-week summer workshop format, not a tested comparison of formats
target_learners: Secondary mathematics teachers in sustained professional development programs
target_learning_goals: Teacher content knowledge growth
Sustained engagement in professional development
examples: The project supplemented its summer workshops with 9 additional 8-hour Saturday sessions throughout the school year

article_title: Skill-based competencies, not traits, are associated with design thinking-aligned teaching behaviours in nursing education: a cross-sectional survey.
citation: Liu Hsing-Yuan. (2026). Skill-based competencies, not traits, are associated with design thinking–aligned teaching behaviours in nursing education: a cross-sectional survey. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09830-3
title: Distal–proximal account of design thinking competence grounded in social cognitive theory
description: The article interprets its findings through a distal–proximal framework derived from social cognitive theory, in which dispositional traits are distal influences that operate through mastery experiences and skill development rather than direct correspondence with behaviour. The authors write that "dispositional characteristics exert distal influences on behaviour through mastery experiences and skill development", so DT traits such as optimism, collaboration, and experimentalism function as orientations that facilitate engagement with learning opportunities, which then translate into enactable DT process skills that proximally shape teaching behaviours.
requirements: Skill-based competencies must be measurable (here via the CSI-TW) for the mediated pathway to be modelled
constraints: Derived from a cross-sectional design; the authors state the paths are "interpreted as synchronous structures of covariation rather than definitive chronological trajectories"
target_learners: Health professions faculty involved in design thinking–integrated education
target_learning_goals: Design thinking–aligned teaching behaviours
Faculty pedagogical competency development

article_title: Why Controlling Teaching Persists in Medical Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective.
citation: Neufeld A. (2026). Why Controlling Teaching Persists in Medical Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2417
title: Distinguish necessary clinical direction from psychologically controlling pressure
description: The article argues that the relevant distinction in clinical teaching is not between authority and autonomy support, but between "authority enacted through clear, informational, and need-supportive guidance and authority enacted through unnecessary psychological pressure." Educators should ask whether direction is educationally necessary or primarily reducing their own uncertainty, and design structure so learners can act with agency within clear expectations.
requirements: Educators must be able to recognize pressure and reactance in themselves without automatically transferring them to learners
constraints: Most likely to be difficult when time is limited, stakes are high, or a learner appears disengaged
target_learners: Clinical learners in undergraduate and postgraduate medical education
target_learning_goals: Preserving learner agency and autonomy while maintaining standards and patient safety
examples: The article offers reflective prompts such as asking what pressure am I experiencing in this moment and whether the level of direction is educationally necessary or primarily reducing the educator's own uncertainty
key_sources: Neufeld A. (2026). Why Controlling Teaching Persists in Medical Education: A Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2417

title: Disaster Nursing Competency Scale (DNCS) as a self-assessment instrument for evaluating disaster nursing education
description: The DNCS developed by Hu is a self-assessment instrument theoretically grounded in the ICN/WHO core-competency framework for disaster nursing. It comprises three first-level indicators (knowledge system, professional competence, and comprehensive qualities), 11 second-level indicators, and 50 third-level indicators, using a 5-point Likert scale with total scores ranging from 50 to 250. In the original development study, the scale demonstrated a Scale-level Content Validity Index of 0.95 and Cronbach α of 0.984; in the current sample, Cronbach α was 0.927.
requirements: Requires respondents to self-assess their own disaster nursing competencies across knowledge, skills, and comprehensive qualities
constraints: The authors note it is a subjective self-assessment instrument whose sensitivity may be insufficient to capture changes in behavioral performance or subtle differences in skill mastery between two advanced teaching models

article_title: A Framework to Establish Diet and Nutrition Competencies for Oral Health Care Education.
citation: Marshall Teresa A., Crowe Michael, Touger‐Decker Riva. (2026). A Framework to Establish Diet and Nutrition Competencies for Oral Health Care Education. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70127
title: A three-question framework establishes diet and nutrition competencies for oral health care education
description: The framework defines diet and nutrition competencies for the graduating oral health care student by answering three foundational questions: identifying diet- and nutrient-related oral health domains, identifying diet and nutrition principles supporting those domains and systemic health, and identifying behavioral concepts necessary to support dietary counseling for oral health. This sequential approach ensured that competencies were grounded in disease relationships, supported by scientific principles, and operationalized through behavioral skills. Educational objectives were then organized according to Bloom's knowledge and cognitive process dimensions, followed by behavioral expectations and evaluation criteria.
requirements: Requires identification of core diet and nutrition knowledge necessary to facilitate effective dietary counseling
Requires articulation of behavioral expectations and evaluation criteria to establish competencies
constraints: The framework is proposed as a foundation to further refine competencies appropriate to guide diet-related oral health curricula
target_learning_goals: Provide dietary counseling based on nutrition science to prevent and manage oral disease
examples: The behavioral expectation for caries competency is 'Identifies and addresses diet-related caries risk factors within the context of environmental and social barriers.'

article_title: A Framework to Establish Diet and Nutrition Competencies for Oral Health Care Education.
citation: Marshall Teresa A., Crowe Michael, Touger‐Decker Riva. (2026). A Framework to Establish Diet and Nutrition Competencies for Oral Health Care Education. Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1002/jdd.70127
title: Behavioral expectations and evaluation criteria for diet-related oral health competencies across five oral health domains
description: The framework articulates behavioral expectations for oral health care practitioners and outcome evaluation criteria for five oral health domains: dental caries, dental erosion, periodontal disease, oral cancer, and oral dysfunction. For example, the caries behavioral expectation is 'Identifies and addresses diet-related caries risk factors within the context of environmental and social barriers,' with evaluation criteria including screening healthy patients, assessing diets of patients with active caries, screening for oral dysfunction and food insecurity, negotiating dietary recommendations, and referring patients to registered dietitians or community partners.
requirements: Competency documentation requires a successful demonstration of the expected behavior
constraints: Competency documentation is best performed in clinical settings during patient care
target_learning_goals: Demonstrate competent diet-related oral health behaviors including screening, assessment, negotiation of dietary recommendations, and referral
examples: Evaluation criteria for the caries competency include the ability to screen and assess diet-related caries risk factors, screen for barriers to healthy food intake, negotiate dietary recommendations to reduce caries risk, and refer patients as appropriate.

article_title: Premature closure underlies bias in medical diagnosis in students: A randomised controlled experiment.
citation: Al Essa A, Schmidt HG, Mamede S, Knežević K, Zwaan L, Magzoub M. (2026). Premature closure underlies bias in medical diagnosis in students: A randomised controlled experiment. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.70229
title: Build disease-specific discriminating knowledge to reduce susceptibility to diagnostic bias
description: The authors argue that susceptibility to bias stems partly from lack of knowledge rather than faulty reasoning strategies alone. They note that "effects of bias do not emerge when physicians have sufficient appropriate knowledge of the diseases under scrutiny, in particular knowledge of findings discriminating between look‐alike diseases", citing their prior work. This supports instructional emphasis on discriminating features between competing diagnoses.
requirements: Learners need knowledge of findings that discriminate between look-alike diseases
constraints: Based on the authors' earlier studies cited here, not directly manipulated in this experiment
target_learning_goals: diagnostic accuracy
resistance to biasing information

article_title: Screen use, health status, and self-perceived academic performance among Swedish dental and nursing students: an exploratory cross-sectional survey study.
citation: Christidis Nikolaos, Lärfars Moa, Khattar Parul, Markus Damyana, Canales Giancarlo De la Torre, Christidis Maria. (2026). Screen use, health status, and self-perceived academic performance among Swedish dental and nursing students: an exploratory cross-sectional survey study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10445-x
title: Differentiate screen use by purpose rather than measuring only total screen time when investigating screen exposure in educational research
description: The article recommends that when screen exposure is investigated as a potential risk factor in educational or public health research, researchers should disaggregate screen time by purpose (social, academic/educational, work-related) rather than treating it as an undifferentiated quantity. The article states "differentiating screen use according to its purpose appears essential rather than merely optional", because combining educational and recreational use into a single variable may obscure associations operating in opposite directions.
requirements: Screen-use measurement must capture purpose-specific categories (social, academic/educational, work-related) in addition to total duration
constraints: Findings are from first-semester Swedish dental and nursing students, limiting generalizability to other populations and educational settings
Cross-sectional self-reported data; associations rather than causal effects
target_learning_goals: self-perceived academic performance
examples: The study categorized estimated daily screen use into social, academic/educational, and work-related usage and entered purpose-specific variables as a separate regression block after total duration

article_title: Effect of an app-guided advanced cardiac life support algorithm on teamwork, non-technical skills, and workload in simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled feasibility trial.
citation: Kamphausen Anne, Pilz Maximilian, Baumgärtel Matthias, Kubitz Jens Christian, Engelen Christian. (2026). Effect of an app-guided advanced cardiac life support algorithm on teamwork, non-technical skills, and workload in simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest: a randomized controlled feasibility trial. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-026-01673-7
title: Digital decision-support effectiveness is strongly context-dependent and linked to user expertise
description: The article concludes that the benefit of digital cognitive aids depends on baseline competence: "when guideline adherence is already high, additional decision-support may offer limited benefit, with the possible exception of time-critical, high-stakes decisions such as defibrillation timing." Studies involving less experienced providers or training settings have demonstrated clearer improvements. This principle guides when to introduce decision-support tools in clinical education and practice.
requirements: Baseline assessment of target users' guideline adherence and expertise level before expecting benefit from cognitive aids
constraints: Findings should not be generalized to novice providers, mixed-experience teams, prehospital settings, or training environments
target_learners: Novice providers and trainees (as suggested future beneficiaries)
target_learning_goals: Adherence to advanced life support guidelines
Teamwork and non-technical skills in resuscitation
examples: 40 interprofessional teams of experienced clinicians showed no clear improvement with app support across TEAM, ANTS, NASA-TLX, and objective ALS metrics

article_title: When digital engagement becomes dysregulated: associations with aggression, achievement motivation, and academic performance in adolescents.
citation: Dong Minghua, He Huitao, Wei Bowen. (2026). When digital engagement becomes dysregulated: associations with aggression, achievement motivation, and academic performance in adolescents. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1896602
title: Focus on digital self-regulation rather than exposure duration alone in research and educational practice
description: The article recommends that future research and educational practice attend to digital self-regulation rather than exposure duration alone, because duration metrics "often show small effect sizes and may obscure substantial heterogeneity in usage patterns." Regulatory difficulty, the dimension reflecting impaired control, carried the incremental GPA association. The authors note the findings complement rather than directly contrast with screen-time research.
requirements: Assessment of regulatory difficulty or self-regulatory aspects of digital engagement, not solely time-based exposure metrics
constraints: Digital exposure duration was not independently assessed, so the findings complement rather than directly contrast with screen-time research
target_learning_goals: academic performance
digital self-regulation
examples: Regulatory difficulty showed a significant incremental GPA association while frequency and intensity did not in adjusted models

article_title: Effect of massed versus distributed preclinical training on subgingival instrumentation skill across the preclinical-to-clinical transition.
citation: Glevitzky, L., Cyris, M., Sutor, S., Springer, C., Kahl, M., Mekhemar, M., Sälzer, S. & Graetz, C. (2026). Effect of massed versus distributed preclinical training on subgingival instrumentation skill across the preclinical-to-clinical transition. Scientific Reports 16, 23355. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-62235-6
title: Distribute preclinical fine-motor skill practice across sessions rather than condensing it into a massed block, because distributed scheduling was associated with higher absolute performance
description: The article recommends distributed (longitudinal) scheduling of preclinical psychomotor training when the goal is robust fine-motor competence: "if the aim is robust fine-motor competence, distributed practice is superior", whereas the block format suffices for summative-threshold passing. Distributed practice here meant one 45-min session weekly over 12 weeks versus three half-days in one week, with identical 9 h total guided practice.
requirements: Both schedules must deliver the same total guided practice time (9 h) with the same supervision and calibration for the comparison to be meaningful.
constraints: The association is non-causal: schedule density could not be separated from proximity to clinical exposure, the design was non-randomised and largely cross-sectional, and the data derive from an in vitro manikin model.
target_learning_goals: subgingival instrumentation skill
retention of fine-motor clinical competence
examples: oGDLR students trained one 45-min session per week over 12 weeks of the 7th semester, overlapping with first supportive periodontal-therapy patient contacts.

article_title: Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Peer Teaching in Orthopedic Clinical Education: Historical Cohort Study.
citation: Brini Stefano, Metcalf Mary, Li Ting, Fukuzawa Fumitoshi, Yu Chengcheng, Li Fangcai, Zhang Ning, Hu Hejia, Huang Hanxu, Wang Jingkai, Tao Yiqing, Wu Yinan. (2026). Effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Peer Teaching in Orthopedic Clinical Education: Historical Cohort Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/87959
title: Distributed cognition and social constructivism as a theoretical framework for AI-augmented peer teaching
description: The article frames AI integration within peer teaching using two complementary theories. Distributed cognition theory "posits that cognitive processes are shared across individuals, tools, and the environment", with the AI tool serving as a cognitive artifact extending the collective knowledge base during peer interactions. Social constructivist learning theory suggests "knowledge is actively constructed through social interaction", with AI enriching these interactions as a shared, accessible knowledge resource. Together they predict AI enhances both individual knowledge acquisition and collaborative learning dynamics.
requirements: AI tool must be integrated within structured peer teaching rather than used as a stand-alone learning tool
constraints: Framework is theoretically motivated; the study tests its predictions observationally, not experimentally
target_learning_goals: orthopedic clinical knowledge
clinical reasoning
collaborative learning

article_title: Psychological characteristics of metacognitive strategy use and vocabulary development paths among vocational university students in a personalized english teaching environment.
citation: Zhao Xiaojuan. (2026). Psychological characteristics of metacognitive strategy use and vocabulary development paths among vocational university students in a personalized english teaching environment. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04595-2
title: Personalized English programs should target distinct psychological-strategic combinations depending on whether vocabulary breadth or depth is the goal.
description: The article proposes that vocabulary interventions should match design emphasis to the target lexical dimension. Programs aiming at breadth may benefit from confidence-building and monitoring-oriented scaffolds such as "progress dashboards, self-check prompts, success-oriented task sequencing", while programs targeting depth may benefit from curiosity-stimulating content and structured reflection protocols. This follows from the regression finding that breadth and depth had different predictor configurations.
requirements: Diagnostic profiling to identify learners' current lexical threshold and strategy baseline
An adaptive platform or task system able to adjust difficulty and review frequency to individual performance
constraints: The article states these implications remain tentative pending replication with independent observers, longer follow-up windows, and more rigorous qualitative integration
target_learners: vocational college students learning English as a foreign language
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary breadth and depth development
metacognitive strategy engagement
examples: The article's pilot model combined diagnostic profiling, tiered vocabulary tasks at three difficulty levels, an adaptive platform with automatic difficulty adjustment, and biweekly instructor-written feedback commentaries

article_title: M(1)ündlich - S(t)imulation of competency-oriented learning in physiology.
citation: Eiring Lisa, Benson Sven, Fandrey Joachim, Prost-Fingerle Katrin, Winning Sandra. (2026). M1ündlich – S(t)imulation of competency-oriented learning in physiology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09661-2
title: Wildt's didactic triangle and the didactic circle as theoretical frameworks for peer teaching
description: The article uses Wildt's didactic triangle model as a framework for theoretically classifying the peer teaching format. The triangle describes "the interdependence of teachers, learners and knowledge," with teaching promoting learning processes and requiring adopting the perspective of learners. In PT-BET, students take on both teacher and learner roles: in the teaching role they examine the structure of learners' answers and provide guidance, while in the learning role they reflect on and deepen their own knowledge. The didactic circle complements this by describing the flexibility of teaching and learning, including methods, content, social forms, and evaluations that can be adapted depending on emphasis. Together, these frameworks shaped the development and evaluation of the PT-BET intervention.
requirements: Students alternate between teacher and learner roles during the exam training
constraints: The teaching-learning process is shaped by institutional, disciplinary, and societal requirements
target_learners: Third-semester medical students preparing for oral examinations
target_learning_goals: Communication skills
Structured answering in oral exams
Exam rhetoric and structuring
key_sources: Eiring Lisa, Benson Sven, Fandrey Joachim, Prost-Fingerle Katrin, Winning Sandra. (2026). M1ündlich – S(t)imulation of competency-oriented learning in physiology. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09661-2

article_title: Closing the digital divide for hemodialysis patients: implementing technology training and support in a digital patient activation intervention.
citation: Veinot Tiffany C, et al. (2026). Closing the digital divide for hemodialysis patients: implementing technology training and support in a digital patient activation intervention. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association. https://doi.org/10.1093/jamia/ocaf226
title: Four-level digital divide framework (motivational, material, skills, usage access) guiding technology support
description: The article applies digital divide theory (van Dijk; van Deursen and van Dijk) as an organizing framework of four access levels that human technology support can address. As printed: "Motivational access describes potential users' assessment of the value and ease of use of technology. Material access concerns people's technology ownership and its reliability (eg, internet access quality). Skills access refers to people's abilities to effectively interact with technology (ie, 'digital literacy/competence')." Usage access "encompasses how people use and benefit from technologies." The study structured its support services and analysis around these levels.
requirements: Technology support services designed to target each of the four access levels simultaneously
constraints: Applied to older and chronically ill hemodialysis patients in a US multicenter trial; mentoring was in English, so language access benefits were not shown
target_learners: older adults with limited technology experience
target_learning_goals: using patient-facing digital health technologies
participating in telehealth-based peer mentoring
examples: Support targeted motivational access with explanations and rapport, material access with tablets, skills access with training calls, and usage access with on-demand and proactive engagement support
key_sources: Veinot Tiffany C, et al. (2026). Closing the digital divide for hemodialysis patients: implementing technology training and support in a digital patient activation intervention. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association. https://doi.org/10.1093/jamia/ocaf226

article_title: Closing the digital divide for hemodialysis patients: implementing technology training and support in a digital patient activation intervention.
citation: Veinot Tiffany C, et al. (2026). Closing the digital divide for hemodialysis patients: implementing technology training and support in a digital patient activation intervention. Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association. https://doi.org/10.1093/jamia/ocaf226
title: Dialysafe technology support system: preloaded tablets, training calls, and a toll-free helpline with engagement support
description: The intervention's technology support comprised "shipping preloaded tablets to mentees, technology training calls, and on-demand support via a toll-free helpline", plus proactive engagement support calls and login monitoring. A full-time technology support specialist provided most support; the helpline was available Monday to Friday, 9-5 PM, or by appointment, from October 2022 to November 2024. Training had a set curriculum with individualized supplemental assistance, and tablets were returned via prepaid packaging for reuse.
requirements: A dedicated full-time technology support specialist
IRB-approved scripts and interpersonal-skills training for staff
constraints: Helpline staffed weekdays 9-5 PM; rare unresolvable issues required family or facility staff assistance
target_learning_goals: completing technology training
connecting to and completing video-based peer mentoring sessions
examples: 93 mentees completed training; 50 mentees (69.4%) made 129 on-demand support calls; 136 engagement support calls were made to 55 mentees and 4 mentors

article_title: Skinner's programmed instruction improves diabetes knowledge and skills of undergraduate nursing students: a randomised controlled trial.
citation: Zhang Ying, Zhang Yixuan, Wang Xiaofang, Luo Baoping. (2026). Skinner's programmed instruction improves diabetes knowledge and skills of undergraduate nursing students: a randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09031-y
title: Twelve diabetes learning modules with QR-code micro-videos, Bluetooth feedback, and electronic heatmaps
description: Before the intervention, "12 diabetes-specific learning modules aligned with Skinner's five principles were developed through a four-step process": content mapping of 25 core knowledge points and 10 procedural skills, difficulty sequencing into three to five sub-modules per unit (Level 1 recall to Level 5 application), material development, and pilot testing with 15 volunteer students. Materials included a micro-video library of 45 QR-code linked videos (2–5 min each) with embedded 'pause-and-respond' checkpoints, an interactive quiz bank of 150 multiple-choice questions with immediate Bluetooth vibration feedback, and electronic progress dashboards using heatmaps (green = mastered, yellow = partial, red = needs practice).
requirements: Pilot testing to refine module difficulty and feedback timing; the final version achieved a < 15% error rate on the first attempt
Clinical instructor training before implementation
constraints: The authors report that designing effective programmed teaching materials requires considerable time, effort, and professional resources, and materials require ongoing adjustment and optimisation
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in endocrinology clinical rotations
target_learning_goals: diabetes knowledge across diagnosis, medication, diet, exercise, and complications
insulin injection and blood glucose monitoring technique
examples: Pilot testing involved three rounds with 15 volunteer students to refine module difficulty and feedback timing

citation: Xing Wenjing, Ju Huanyu, Pei Chunying, Guo Yongli, Tian Linlu, Ling Hong, Guo Tieyun, Cao Bo, Ma Jian. (2026). Research topic–driven curriculum content reform in graduate immunology to strengthen students' research and innovation competence. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08711-z
title: Replace sole reliance on closed-book exams with diversified, rubric-based assessments capturing research competence and academic expression
description: The reform's assessment principle is that evaluation should capture research thinking and academic expression, not only knowledge recall. The article states that "assessments no longer relied solely on closed-book exams but incorporated diverse and flexible evaluation methods. These included literature reviews, thematic presentations and defenses, and short papers." Rubrics were developed for each component covering knowledge integration, research design and originality, critical analysis and problem-solving, and communication and academic writing, with faculty panels scoring presentations, double-marked written work, and formative feedback enabling iterative revision.
requirements: Rubrics for each assessment component to ensure consistency and transparency
Faculty panels and double-marking to ensure rating reliability
Standardized rating forms derived from institutional graduate training manuals
constraints: The article notes faculty workload increased due to individualized supervision, iterative feedback and frequent formative assessments compared with lecture-based formats
target_learners: Graduate students in research-intensive basic science courses
target_learning_goals: Assess mastery of knowledge, research thinking, innovation and academic expression
examples: Research topic and proposal scores were derived from average anonymous ratings by expert reviewers and faculty during proposal defenses

article_title: Digitalization through the use of Ren'Py-Based interactive learning experiences in physiotherapy and rehabilitation education: a randomised, controlled, single-blind study.
citation: Koçyiğit A, Cavlak U. (2025). Digitalization through the use of Ren’Py-Based interactive learning experiences in physiotherapy and rehabilitation education: a randomised, controlled, single-blind study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08474-z
title: Use interactive digital tools like Ren'Py as a complement to face-to-face instruction rather than a replacement for practice-based fields
description: The article concludes that digital tools such as Ren'Py "may offer added value when integrated into hybrid formats" but "were not sufficient on their own to support practical performance." In practice-based fields like physiotherapy, online models should be enriched with additional methods supporting practical skill acquisition, since face-to-face and hybrid models outperformed digital-only instruction on practical exams while the hybrid model also lowered cognitive load and raised motivation.
requirements: Face-to-face sessions retained for practical skill development
Technical support resources to handle software and hardware problems during digital implementations
constraints: Evidence comes from a single one-week intervention in one course unit with a relatively small sample and no long-term follow-up
target_learners: undergraduate health-professions students in practice-based disciplines
target_learning_goals: practical clinical skills
motivation toward instructional materials
managing cognitive load
examples: The CaDEG received both the face-to-face lecture and laboratory sessions and the full Ren'Py digital module within the same week, and matched CEG on practical exam scores while reporting lower cognitive load and higher motivation than CEG

article_title: Comparison of the observer role vs. active participant role in interprofessional simulation-based education for affective skills: a randomized-controlled trial.
citation: Inam Maha, Tariq Umar, Durrani Rafia, Karim Masood Muhammad, Surani Zainish, Ismail Faisal W. (2025). Comparison of the observer role vs. active participant role in interprofessional simulation-based education for affective skills: a randomized-controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08490-z
title: Directed observer role combining vicarious observation, a checklist and debriefing participation
description: A directed observer role is a simulation participation format in which most learners watch a peer counsel the simulated patient rather than performing every scenario themselves. In this trial the directed observer role "comprised the following 3 characteristics: vicarious observation, use of a checklist and participation in the post simulation debriefing". Observer subgroups rotated through four simulated bowel-preparation counselling cases, with one member performing live at each scenario.
requirements: Observers must be directed with tools or instructions, such as a checklist, rather than observing without direction
Observers must participate in the post-simulation debriefing as active learners
constraints: In this trial each observer directly interacted with the simulated patient only once, at one scenario of the four-case circuit
target_learners: Interprofessional healthcare professionals: trainee physicians, registered nurses, endoscopy technicians and health care assistants
target_learning_goals: Delivering bowel preparation instructions and counselling patients scheduled for colonoscopy
examples: Observer subgroups rotated through four simulated cases; one participant counselled the simulated patient per scenario while the others observed as directed observers with a checklist, and all professional groups performed at least one station

title: Taxonomy of directed versus non-directed observer roles in simulation-based education
description: The article distinguishes two observer role types drawn from prior systematic review work: "Two types of observer roles have been explained: directed and non-directed". A directed observer role "involves specific instructions or tools, guiding learners on what to observe during the simulation", which may include learning objectives or checklists, whereas a non-directed role involves watching without such tools or instructions. requirements: A directed observer role requires specifying observation instructions or tools, such as learning objectives or checklists for expected actions

article_title: A Virtual Reality-Based mHealth App to Enhance Health Care Skills and Promote Health Equity by Empowering Health Care Professionals to Provide Empathetic, Compassionate, and Unbiased Patient Care Through Digital Experiential Learning: Qualitative Study.
citation: Sarvestan Javad; Aksoy Mehmet; Teaford Max; Patel Dixit Bharatkumar; Patel Mayank Bharatkumar; Wischgoll Thomas; Pei Yong; Hershberger Paul J. (2025). A Virtual Reality–Based mHealth App to Enhance Health Care Skills and Promote Health Equity by Empowering Health Care Professionals to Provide Empathetic, Compassionate, and Unbiased Patient Care Through Digital Experiential Learning: Qualitative Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/64147
title: Digital experiential learning (DEL) approach grounded in Kolb's experiential learning cycle
description: The article defines DEL as "an approach that harnesses digital technologies to create immersive and hands-on learning experiences", integrating Kolb's experiential learning principles with digital tools such as simulations, virtual environments, interactive multimedia, and web-based collaborative platforms. Kolb's experiential learning cycle comprises four stages—Concrete Experience, Reflective Observation, Abstract Conceptualization, and Active Experimentation. The mHealth app operationalizes DEL by placing learners in first-person simulated clinical encounters where they engage with real-world tasks and reflect on their experiences.
requirements: Digital tools and platforms; learners who actively engage with real-world tasks and reflect on their experiences
constraints: The article notes DEL "also presents challenges such as access to technology and the need for digital literacy"

title: Digital evaluation system with 3D deviation maps and quantitative cavity parameters
description: A software system, developed by the authors' team with a domestic company, that scans prepared teeth with an intraoral scanner, registers them to a reference cavity model, and "generated quantitative assessments includes: (1) color-coded deviation maps on 3D models indicating over-preparation (positive deviations) and under-preparation (negative deviations)" plus text of preparation parameters with grades and scores. title: Difficult endotracheal intubation scoring formula for appraising airway training manikins
description: A scoring formula adapted from the authors' clinical predictive model, computed for each manikin as "(neck circumference * 0.7 * 0.239) + (thyromental distance * -0.488) + (upper airway obstruction * 1.396) + (Mallampati grade 3/4 * 1.642)". It was applied to four simulators to quantify training difficulty, with a cut-off of 4 for difficult intubation, and proposed as a benchmark for designing new manikins.

description: The article draws recommendations from its finding that distance learning benefited knowledge and communication competencies most and technical skills least. It recommends that "distance learning can be used for transferring knowledge to residents particularly when challenges exist in the traditional offline approaches" and that "clinical skills have a crucial role in offline training, which should be noted and well used by training institutions." New technologies such as touchscreen Anatomage Table and Touch Surgery application are suggested as web-based complements for technical-skills training.

constraints: Distance learning benefited patient care and technical skills the least (β=0.14, 90% CI 0.01-0.26)

interpersonal and communication skills
patient care and technical skills

citation: Johnston Peter W., Vieira Rute, Cameron Isobel M., Kumwenda Ben, Walker Kim A., Cleland Jennifer A. (2025). Advances in Health Sciences Education 30(1), 53-68. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10406-3
title: Differential attainment as a complex, systemic problem reflecting unequal norms and practices in broader society
description: The article frames differential attainment (DA) — group-level rather than individual differences in performance — as a phenomenon that sets in early in society and persists through education into adult life, shaping which schools candidates attend and hence their educational performance indicators. The authors state that "differential attainment is a complex, systemic problem reflective of unequal norms and practices within broader society, evident throughout many different assessments and persistent over time". They use this framing to interpret why adjustment for prior attainment removed the ethnicity and gateway effects without implying ethnicity is irrelevant.
requirements: Requires linked, routinely collected educational datasets with sociodemographic variables to detect group-level patterns, as the article argues big data enables granular DA analyses.
constraints: The article states that disadvantage is set in very early in society, usually pre-school, so examination-level analysis alone cannot capture its origins.
target_learners: UK medical graduates sitting postgraduate physician examinations
target_learning_goals: Fair and equitable assessment and progression in postgraduate medical training
examples: The study found the minority-ethnic and gateway-programme pass-rate disadvantages were no longer significant once EPM and SJT prior-attainment scores entered the regression model.

title: Develop interprofessional e-learning curricula so that competencies are addressed differentially by professional group
description: Because nurses and GPs differ in prior knowledge and responsibilities in delirium care, an e-learning curriculum should contain shared core competencies plus discipline-specific ones, with each group's role made explicit. The article states: "discipline-specific competencies must be addressed, and different learning needs must be acknowledged in the development of an e-learning curriculum." The Delphi results operationalized this: pathophysiology and acute medication were removed for nurses while nonpharmacological prevention was removed for GPs.
requirements: A competence-based consensus curriculum as the basis before e-learning development
Expert panels including members of both professional groups
constraints: Differing relevance judgments between professional groups can force removal of competencies one group values

target_learning_goals: Delirium-specific knowledge and role-clarity in interprofessional delirium management

article_title: Are medical school preclinical tests biased for sex and race? A differential item functioning analysis.
citation: Dale Esther Dasari, Abulela Mohammed A. A., Jia Hao, Violato Claudio. (2025). Are medical school preclinical tests biased for sex and race? A differential item functioning analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06540-6
title: Differential item functioning as a psychometric procedure for detecting potential item bias across test-taker groups
description: Differential item functioning (DIF) is a psychometric procedure for detecting whether items function differently across groups of test-takers with equal latent ability, indicating possible construct-irrelevant variance and bias. The article defines it: "DIF occurs when test-takers with the same latent ability but from different groups have an unequal probability of correctly answering a test item." It distinguishes uniform DIF (difficulty differences) from nonuniform DIF (discrimination differences), and treats statistical flagging as a first stage followed by expert sensitivity review to conclude potential bias.
requirements: Items statistically flagged as DIF must undergo sensitivity analysis by measurement specialists and subject matter experts before bias conclusions are drawn
constraints: DIF provides statistical evidence suggesting the possibility of bias but does not itself establish that items are biased
target_learners: medical students in preclinical foundational science courses
target_learning_goals: fair and valid assessment of foundational science knowledge in anatomy, histology, and physiology
examples: The study applied DIF via the Wald test under a 2PL IRT model in IRTPRO to three preclinical course exams, flagging items at p < .05
key_sources: Dale Esther Dasari, Abulela Mohammed A. A., Jia Hao, Violato Claudio. (2025). Are medical school preclinical tests biased for sex and race? A differential item functioning analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06540-6

description: The article's methodological conclusion is "the importance of differentiating estimands and triangulating identifying strategies for the estimation of causal effects". constraints: Results rest on the assumption of no unobserved confounding; unobserved confounding was detected for the reading domain

examples: A post hoc replication of Keilow et al.'s analytic strategy reproduced a larger discontinuation effect in the Norwegian data, clarifying that the contrast estimated was not the intention-to-treat effect of initiation

Online components (50% of the grade) comprise previewing (10%), interactive discussions (10%), preview quizzes (four multiple-choice questions, 10%), classroom interactions (10%) and case analysis (10%); the closed-book unit test accounts for the remaining 50%. article_title: Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates' knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus.
citation: Mariam S, Heba I, Mohamed FHN. (2025). Diabe-teach: a randomized controlled trial of a gamified approach to enhance medical undergraduates’ knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06602-9
title: Diabe-teach board game (7×7 keyword-chain game with 49 cards)
description: Diabe-teach is a non-digital educational board game for diabetes content. It uses “49 cards, each featuring a significant keyword selected by the instructor” shuffled into a 7×7 grid; players build chains of at least four connected keywords and must “explain each chain at the end of the round,” with consensus and instructor adjudication of validity. A 15-minute trial round precedes two 30-minute rounds, with cards reshuffled each round so the board arrangement “changes each game due to shuffling.” It was evaluated in an RCT against structured self-study.
requirements: A keyword set covering the target topic, printed cards arranged in a 7×7 grid, an instructor to resolve ambiguities, and time for an orientation/trial round plus two gameplay rounds
constraints: Designing an effective educational board game for complex topics “can be time-intensive, and its implementation may require substantial facilitation”
may not resonate equally with students who prefer structured or traditional didactic teaching methods
target_learning_goals: Knowledge and comprehension of diabetes mellitus (pathophysiology, clinical features, investigations, management)
Correlation of concepts and communication of reasoning
examples: Used in a randomized controlled trial with 56 preclinical medical students at Dubai Medical College for Girls, compared with a supervised self-study hour on identical content

citation: Maier Esther C., Ödemis Veysel, Bräuer Anja U. (2025). Digitally based clinically oriented anatomy: the future of teaching. Chirurgie. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00104-024-02211-w
title: Use digital teaching methods to complement rather than replace classical anatomy teaching, linked to clinical content and designed for intuitive, time-limited use
description: The review's practice-oriented conclusion is that digital teaching methods should be integrated into anatomy curricula as supplements to dissection, not substitutes. Sessions with head-mounted displays should not be too long, tools must be intuitive and easy to handle, and digital formats should link anatomy with clinical content and be used mainly later in longitudinal curricula. The review states digital methods "können die klassischen Lehrmethoden ergänzen, aber nicht ersetzen" and should connect "die Anatomie mit klinischen Inhalten".
requirements: Digital tools must be intuitive and easy to handle
HMD-based sessions should not be designed too long
Digital formats should link anatomy with clinical content
constraints: Digital methods cannot replace classical teaching methods such as dissection
Cybersickness with VR or image-rich MR limits HMD session design
Development of clinically integrated MR approaches is complex, requiring anatomists, clinicians and computer scientists to collaborate
target_learning_goals: Anatomical knowledge with clinical relevance
Three-dimensional topographic understanding
examples: The review reports an AR glasses teaching unit on liver anatomy in which teacher and students jointly discuss case-specific features on a patient-specific 3D model, and notes images and case studies of real patients increased perceived meaningfulness of the unit

citation: Polivka L, Delcour C, Dufresne H, Bartoli S, Bataille P, Bekel L, Bonigen J, Deladrière E, Dimarcq S, Felix A, Havas C, Le Goff H, Levy M, Riback E, Welfringer-Morin A, Houdouin V, Hadj-Rabia S, Bodemer C, Faye A, Melki I. "All four steps were designed to improve the students' relational skills." The authors state that in practice "the discussion group would be followed by a formative OSCE and then an active debriefing of the group with the teachers."

title: Diversified formative-plus-summative assessment system weighting assignments, experimental operations and a final exam
description: The course adopts "a diversified assessment system combining formative assessment and summative assessment" to replace a single, one-sided final-exam-focused method. Formative components include homework (10%), experimental operations (30%) and a final closed-book written exam (60%), with evaluation points spanning seminar reports, morphological identification, self-designed experiments, bone marrow report writing and case analysis. The final exam requires "the comprehension question type is greater than the memory question type", and the authors state the system aims to "avoid the drawbacks of the traditional single assessment form of 'examination instead of evaluation'".

clinical diagnostic thinking and practical skills

title: DICE: a problem- and simulation-based learning method combining design, interpretation, computation, and estimation of a scientific investigation
description: DICE is an engaging learning method that enables students to use simple simulations to design, analyze, and interpret a realistic epidemiological study. The acronym represents the learning steps involved, but not in order, and the method combines problem-oriented learning with Monte Carlo simulations. The overall aim is to promote statistical reasoning in the health sciences by combining medical and statistical knowledge in designing epidemiological studies. The article states that "The use of DICE as a learning tool combines problem-oriented learning [10,11] with simulations [12]."
requirements: Students work in small groups to plan, generate, analyze, interpret, and communicate their own scientific investigation with simulations
Access to statistical software such as Stata or R to generate and analyze simulated data
constraints: The effectiveness of DICE in conveying statistical concepts in epidemiology has not been formally evaluated yet
The proposed simulation method is practically limited to only a few numbers of parameters, as each additional variable increases the complexity of the DGM exponentially
target_learners: Graduate students in medical sciences, including public health and epidemiology
target_learning_goals: Fundamental statistical concepts such as sampling variability, error probabilities, and the construction of statistical models
Combining substantive medical knowledge and statistical concepts
examples: Students at Karolinska Institutet worked through a simulated cohort study of physical activity and 10-year mortality, writing and presenting a structured scientific abstract

citation: de Azevedo Cardoso Taiane, Waleed Muhammad, Ogut Eren, Marques da Cruz Manuel, Thiesmeier Robert, Orsini Nicola. (2024). Rolling the DICE (Design, Interpret, Compute, Estimate): Interactive Learning of Biostatistics With Simulations. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/52679
title: Six-step DICE activity sequence from identifying a health problem to presenting an abstract
description: DICE includes 6 major steps that cover the major stages of a scientific investigation: (1) identifying the health problem, (2) designing an investigation including power and sample size calculations with simulations, (3) generating a unique sample of data, (4) analyzing the sample according to the plan, (5) interpreting the findings carefully, and (6) writing a short abstract to be presented in class. The second step is divided into three parts that can be repeated to calibrate power and sample size. The article notes that "The second step—designing an investigation including power and sample size calculations with simulations—is further divided into 3 parts, which can be repeated to calibrate the power and sample size of a study before moving on to step 3."
requirements: Sufficient time, with the first 2 steps requiring most of the time
A common seed set before generating the analytical sample so all groups replicate the study under the same conditions
constraints: Implementing DICE is resource-intensive and should not be done in a short time frame (eg, less than 1 hour)
target_learners: Graduate students in public health and epidemiology working in small groups of 3-5
target_learning_goals: Study design, power and sample size reasoning, data generation, model estimation, interpretation, and scientific communication
examples: In the worked example, groups designed an observational cohort study with a confounding effect by age, generated data under a Weibull survival model, and presented 200-250 word abstracts in presentations not exceeding 10 minutes per group
key_sources: de Azevedo Cardoso Taiane, Waleed Muhammad, Ogut Eren, Marques da Cruz Manuel, Thiesmeier Robert, Orsini Nicola. (2024). Rolling the DICE (Design, Interpret, Compute, Estimate): Interactive Learning of Biostatistics With Simulations. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/52679

article_title: The effect of simulation of sectional human anatomy using ultrasound on students' learning outcomes and satisfaction in echocardiography education: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
citation: Ding Kewen, Chen Mingjing, Li Ping, Xie Zichuan, Zhang Haorong, Kou Ruixing, Xu Jionghui, Zou Ting, Luo Zhen, Song Haibo. (2024). The effect of simulation of sectional human anatomy using ultrasound on students' learning outcomes and satisfaction in echocardiography education: a pilot randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05337-x
title: Digital human: a simulation device for sectional human anatomy using ultrasound based on Chinese visible human data
description: The digital human is a simulation device that "adopts Chinese visible human data, which is collected from complete disease-free corpses" with 3760 slices at 0.25–0.5 mm intervals and resolution up to 3072*2048 pixels. It achieves real-time display (imaging time < 0.03 s per slice), allows students to view slice images from any position and angle, provides detailed annotations, and supports highly precise 3D reconstructions of cardiac structures for interactive dissection and exploration.
requirements: Requires the digital human device and teaching venue, as provided by the West China Wismed ultrasonic simulation teaching team
constraints: The digital human remains a tool for learning a normal TTE examination only and cannot simulate pathologic conditions
The cost of digital humans is relatively high, potentially impractical for resource-limited educational settings
target_learners: first-year medical students with no prior echocardiography training
target_learning_goals: basic echocardiography knowledge including normal cardiac anatomy and four basic cross-sectional views
examples: Used for a 60-min teaching session showing cross-sectional views through the digital human model, compared against a traditional 60-min theoretical lecture
key_sources: Ding Kewen, Chen Mingjing, Li Ping, Xie Zichuan, Zhang Haorong, Kou Ruixing, Xu Jionghui, Zou Ting, Luo Zhen, Song Haibo. (2024). The effect of simulation of sectional human anatomy using ultrasound on students' learning outcomes and satisfaction in echocardiography education: a pilot randomized controlled trial. article_title: Realistic simulation in nursing education: Testing two scenario-based models.
citation: Martins, T., Santos, F., Lumini, M. J., Sousa, M. R., Peixoto, M. J., Freire, R. M., Salazar, B., Fernandes, C., & de Fátima Araújo, M. (2023). Realistic simulation in nursing education: Testing two scenario‐based models. Nursing Open, 10, 3326–3335. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1585
title: Digital scenario-based tool for standardized nursing simulation scenario writing
description: A web application developed with the computer engineering department of the Polytechnic Institute of Porto that lets teachers create, store, edit and reuse simulation scenarios. "The application allows the scenarios to be stored in a library, saved, edited and deleted", and students view scenarios on an electronic device via a link, saving them as HTML or PDF. Scenarios present patient and caregiver data in separate, pre-determined fields with photos and iconography, including a traffic-light impairment display. In the study it delivered the experimental scenario in the second simulation.
requirements: Access requires only an electronic device to open the scenario link, as the article states
constraints: The study tested it in one second-year curricular unit of a nursing degree in one Portuguese public nursing school, hindering generalizability
target_learning_goals: assessing self-care dependence, prioritizing nursing diagnoses and planning care for patients regaining independence and returning home after an acute event
examples: The digital scenario was projected on a screen during the second laboratory simulation, after a paper traditional scenario was used in the first

citation: Halliday Jennifer A., Russell-Green Sienna, Hagger Virginia, O Eric, Morris Ann, Sturt Jackie, Speight Jane, Hendrieckx Christel. (2022). title: Diabetes distress e-learning: a course for diabetes educators
description: An interactive online e-learning course for credentialled diabetes educators covering identification and support of diabetes distress. It "includes learning objectives, videos demonstrating consultation skills, and activities (e.g., opportunities to check understanding, practice skills, self-reflect, and plan actions)", with greater emphasis on skills development than the chapter active control. It was developed using intervention mapping and consists of 7 modules; median modules accessed was 6, with 47% accessing all 7.
requirements: Desktop or laptop computer access with an internet connection
About 7 hours total commitment (42–73 min per module)
constraints: A few participants experienced platform navigation and technical difficulties, to be resolved in future versions
target_learning_goals: recognising and addressing diabetes distress
consultation and communication skills
making mental health referrals
examples: In the pilot RCT, 83% of intervention participants accessed the e-learning, with a median of 6 of 7 modules accessed
All 30 intervention participants returning the 2-week survey deemed the e-learning high quality and relevant
