citation: Chuang Shu-Ting, Liao Pei-Lin, Lo Shu-Fen, Chang Ya-Ting, Hsu Hsiang-Tzu. (2022). Effectiveness of an E-Book App on the Knowledge, Attitudes and Confidence of Nurses to Prevent and Care for Pressure Injury. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192315826
title: Use direct observation of procedural skills to evaluate mobile learning outcomes beyond self-report
description: Because this trial relied on participant self-assessment, the authors recommend that future studies "use direct observation of procedural skills to evaluate and provide feedback to trainees on clinical operation techniques to ensure learning effectiveness and quality of PI care". This principle addresses the gap between improved self-reported knowledge, attitudes, and confidence and demonstrated clinical performance. The article's impact statement notes such observation "can provide feedback to trainees on techniques to ensure learning effectiveness and pressure injury care quality".
requirements: Structured observation of clinical operation techniques with feedback to trainees
constraints: The trial itself measured only self-reported scales, so this principle is a stated recommendation, not a tested result
target_learning_goals: clinical procedural skills in pressure injury prevention and wound care
examples: The authors state their study used participant self-assessment of interventional effectiveness and recommend direct observation in future research

article_title: Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population.
citation: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. (2022). Planning a Collection of Virtual Patients to Train Clinical Reasoning: A Blueprint Representative of the European Population. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph19106175
title: Design VP and case collections to represent diverse patient populations to avoid an unintended hidden curriculum
description: The article argues that the careful selection of contextual factors, key symptoms, and diagnoses in a VP collection is crucial, and that collections should represent the diversity of the patient population. It warns that "an under- or non-representation of marginalized groups holds the danger of an unintended hidden curriculum", i.e., unintended messages that can bias students toward perceiving male, heterosexual, white, cis patients as the standard. The principle motivated the blueprint's patient-related criteria, including sexual orientation, ethnicity, disability, and migration background.
requirements: Deliberate selection of contextual factors and comparison against population statistics during collection planning
constraints: The article notes suitable European data sources for comparing ethnicity were not found, limiting verification of that criterion
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning free of demographic bias, awareness of common biases
examples: The blueprint includes 1% intersexual or transgender patients and 8% homo- or bisexual VPs, checked against estimated European proportions
key_sources: Mayer Anja, Da Silva Domingues Vital, Hege Inga, Kononowicz Andrzej A., Larrosa Marcos, Martínez-Jarreta Begoña, Rodriguez-Molina Daloha, Sousa-Pinto Bernardo, Sudacka Małgorzata, Morin Luc. article_title: COVID-19 and Virtual Nutrition: A Pilot Study of Integrating Digital Food Models for Interactive Portion Size Education.
citation: Ho Dang Khanh Ngan, Lee Yu-Chieh, Chiu Wan-Chun, Shen Yi-Ta, Yao Chih-Yuan, Chu Hung-Kuo, Chu Wei-Ta, Le Nguyen Quoc Khanh, Nguyen Hung Trong, Su Hsiu-Yueh, Chang Jung-Su. (2022). COVID-19 and Virtual Nutrition: A Pilot Study of Integrating Digital Food Models for Interactive Portion Size Education. Nutrients 14(16):3313. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu14163313
title: Integrate combined 2-D and interactive 3-D digital food models into dietetic training, with tailored support for students who struggle across formats
description: The article proposes a pedagogical framework in which standardized 2-D food images and interactive, zoomable 3-D food models are embedded in an online platform and used for repeated portion size estimation practice inside a formal dietetic practicum. The authors report that "82% of students supported the educational integration of digital food models into the formal NP course" and that repeated training raised quantification accuracy to 42.9%. They conclude that "a tailored training program may be needed to master digital food viewing skills using 2-D and 3-D models."
requirements: Access to an online platform that supports both 2-D image display and rotatable, resizable 3-D models (the article used Sketchfab and LimeSurvey)
3-D food models constructed via photogrammetry from standardized 360° videos and 2-D images with fiducial markers as size reference
Training in operating the 3-D zoom/rotate functions to prevent portion distortion
constraints: Constructing high-quality 3-D food models with Agisoft Metashape is time-consuming and labor-intensive (2–8 h per model in this study)
Photogrammetry struggles with translucent, white, or textureless foods and shiny or transparent containers
3-D models did not improve vegetable estimation accuracy
Pilot evidence from a single cohort of 65 second-year students with no sample size calculation
target_learning_goals: food identification from digital images
food portion size quantification
estimated total calories of meal sets
examples: The NP course embedded standardized 2-D images (45° and 90°) and interactive 3-D models of eleven Taiwanese meal sets in LimeSurvey, and students practiced via Sketchfab throughout the second semester during the COVID-19 closure.
key_sources: Ho Dang Khanh Ngan, Lee Yu-Chieh, Chiu Wan-Chun, Shen Yi-Ta, Yao Chih-Yuan, Chu Hung-Kuo, Chu Wei-Ta, Le Nguyen Quoc Khanh, Nguyen Hung Trong, Su Hsiu-Yueh, Chang Jung-Su. (2022). article_title: Computer-assisted instruction versus inquiry-based learning: The importance of working memory capacity.
citation: Chevalère Johann, Cazenave Loreleï, Berthon Mickaël, Martinez Ruben, Mazenod Vincent, Borion Marie-Claude, Pailler Delphine, Rocher Nicolas, Cadet Rémi, Lenne Catherine, Maïonchi-Pino Norbert, Huguet Pascal. (2021). Computer-assisted instruction versus inquiry-based learning: The importance of working memory capacity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0259664
title: Diversify instructional methods rather than adopting an all-digital education system, and attend to tutoring techniques in distant learning
description: The article argues its findings legitimize CAI for preventing pandemic learning loss but should not be read as favoring an all-digitalized education system; rather, they favor a diversification of methods to better address students' heterogeneity. It suggests combining methods dynamically, for example performing CAI prior to IBL to build confidence, or the reverse to let students reflect on discussions when receiving feedback from the digital tutor. For distant learning, policy makers are urged to pay particular attention to implementing tutoring techniques in addition to providing content.
requirements: Teachers able to include CAI in their repertoires alongside other methods
constraints: Benefits of CAI do not occur whatever students' working memory capacity, so effectiveness is not guaranteed by access alone
target_learners: students in pandemic or remote learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Science and Technology achievement; mitigating learning loss
examples: The article proposes CAI before IBL for confidence, or IBL before CAI for reflection on discussions, as dynamic adjustments to individual needs

article_title: Problem-based learning for in-service training on breastfeeding in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy.
citation: Pessa Valente Emanuelle, Cattaneo Adriano, Sola Maria Vittoria, Travan Laura, Quintero Romero Sofia, Milinco Mariarosa, Decorti Cinzia, Giornelli Roberta, Braida Cinzia, Dalmin Patrizia, Giangreco Manuela, Ronfani Luca. (2021). Problem-based learning for in-service training on breastfeeding in Friuli Venezia Giulia, Italy. International Breastfeeding Journal. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13006-021-00439-4
title: Dick and Carey instructional design model combined with the PBL 7-jumps approach for curriculum development
description: The project adopted the Dick and Carey model for instructional design, in which "The output from one phase of the model provided the input for the next phase", covering analysis of learning needs, design and development of objectives and assessment instruments, participants' assessment with emphasis on formative evaluation, and evaluation of the whole strategy while being designed. Within courses, PBL tutorial groups follow the structured "7 jumps approach": clarify unfamiliar terms; define problems; brainstorm explanations; arrange tentative solutions and priorities; formulate learning objectives; undertake private study; and share and evaluate results, facilitated by trained tutors.
requirements: A working group facilitated by breastfeeding senior experts and an education expert
Input data from needs-assessment surveys and tutor focus groups
target_learners: in-service maternal and child health professionals
target_learning_goals: systematic design of inter-professional in-service training curricula and problem-based tutorial learning
examples: The 343-respondent online survey and tutor focus-group summaries were used as data input to the working group's curriculum design

article_title: Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course.
citation: Leupen, S. M., Kephart, K. L., & Hodges, L. C. (2020). Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-06-0112
title: Three-part discursive coding scheme for productive team discussion: conceptual explanations, re-evaluations, and co-construction
description: The article develops a grounded-theory coding scheme for team discourse built around three phenomena: conceptual explanations, re-evaluations, and co-construction. Conceptual explanations are "stretches of talk in which one or more students in the group produced a hypothesis of physiological functioning that was not simply fact based"; re-evaluation covers disagreement, pointing out overlooked issues, or asking for further explanation; co-construction covers turns in which speakers build on one another to create explanations. The scheme was applied to 12 transcripts of recorded team talk.
requirements: Transcribed audio recordings of team conversations so turns can be independently coded and discrepancies resolved by consensus
constraints: Definitions are discipline-specific; the authors note their definition of conceptual explanation differs from Repice et al.'s because of differences in disciplinary subject matter
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary (physiological) reasoning and conceptual understanding through team discussion
examples: Teams discussing a transposition-of-the-great-vessels question produced conceptual explanations and re-evaluations across all four recorded teams
key_sources: Leupen, S. M., Kephart, K. L., & Hodges, L. C. (2020). Factors Influencing Quality of Team Discussion: Discourse Analysis in an Undergraduate Team-Based Learning Biology Course. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(1). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.19-06-0112

article_title: Teacher Evaluation of an Experiential Vegetable Education Program for Australian Primary Schools: Does Face-to-Face Training Add Value above Digital Training?
citation: Poelman A. A. M., Cochet-Broch M., Beelen J., Wiggins B., Heffernan J. E., & Cox D. N. (2021). Teacher Evaluation of an Experiential Vegetable Education Program for Australian Primary Schools: Does Face-to-Face Training Add Value above Digital Training? Nutrients, 13(5), 1648. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu13051648
title: Provide teacher training for classroom programs digitally rather than face-to-face, as additional F2F training adds no value to acceptability
description: The article concludes that because teacher acceptability of both the digital training module and the program was independent of training intensity, "These results seem to favour the implementation of the program using a low(er) intensity training, as the program can be made available with no ongoing costs". Digital-only delivery removes ongoing costs and geographic constraints of face-to-face sessions while achieving equivalent acceptability.
requirements: A quality online training module and written implementation materials covering program objectives, theoretical background and practical implementation information
constraints: The authors note "the provision of some form of personal interaction may still be beneficial when/where possible to raise awareness of the program", suggesting combined information sessions or webinars as a lower-cost alternative
target_learners: Primary school teachers implementing classroom health education programs
target_learning_goals: Teacher capability and motivation to implement a vegetable education program
examples: In the cluster RCT, low-intensity teachers received written materials and a ~20-minute online module, while high-intensity teachers additionally received 45 minutes of face-to-face training; acceptability ratings did not differ between arms.

article_title: Exploring an e-learning community's response to the language and terminology use in autism from two massive open online courses on autism education and technology use.
citation: Lei Jiedi, Jones Lauren, Brosnan Mark. (2021). Exploring an e-learning community's response to the language and terminology use in autism from two massive open online courses on autism education and technology use. Autism. https://doi.org/10.1177/1362361320987963
title: 'Differences in terminology' discussion forum embedded in two autism-education MOOCs
description: A Week 1 discussion forum in two FutureLearn MOOCs (SMART-ASD and Good Practice in Autism Education) developed and run by the host university. Learners were first given background information and findings from Kenny et al. (2016) to establish common knowledge, then asked two questions: what names and terms they use when talking about autism, and how important the issue of different terms is. Across six runs between 2017 and 2019, "803 learners participated in this discussion forum across the MOOCs", producing 1203 comments monitored by a faculty member and a doctoral student who fostered an interactive online learning environment.
requirements: Learners need background information on terminology research to establish a common level of knowledge before discussing, since no prior knowledge could be assumed
constraints: The authors could not gather detailed demographics of forum participants because user profiles could not be traced via FutureLearn
target_learners: family and friends of autistic individuals
target_learning_goals: awareness of stakeholder differences in autism terminology preferences
reflection on how language choices convey attitudes and judgement
examples: SMART-ASD reached 6824 joiners (3210 active) from 142 countries; Good Practice reached 5015 joiners (2089 active) from 61 countries

article_title: Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping.
citation: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1
title: Distance and force visualisation concept set: colour maps, cylinders, rays and glyphs
description: The article integrates three distance visualisation concepts (a colour map on the vessel surface, a cylinder highlighting the smallest distance, and semi-transparent rays showing all distances below a threshold) and four force visualisation concepts (colour map, semi-transparent displacement rays, arrow glyphs and drop glyphs scaled and faded by strength). All concepts employ an underlying colour scale classifying values into low, mid-range and high regions, with green for non-critical and red for critical values.
requirements: An underlying colour scale; the drop glyph scales only within a certain range and is drawn semi-transparently so strong displacements do not occlude smaller ones
constraints: The green-to-red map is not usable for people with dyschromatopsia, for whom a red-to-blue scale is provided
target_learning_goals: perceiving clip-to-vessel distances
assessing force on vessel surface
examples: Figures 2 and 3 show the distance concepts (colour map, cylinder, semi-transparent rays) and force concepts (colour map, rays, arrow glyphs, drop glyphs)
key_sources: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1

article_title: Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping.
citation: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1
title: Use a diverging green-to-red colour scale to classify distance and force values into low, mid-range and high criticality
description: Although the underlying distance and force data are sequential, the visualisations aim at a classification into low, mid-range and high values rather than exact values, so "a diverging colour scale is used even if there is no zero-crossing in the data". Green represents large distances and low magnitudes, red represents low distances and high magnitudes, so critical values always appear in red, which is intuitively associated with critical situations.
requirements: Appropriate colour choice so the diverging scale conveys the three-region order; a red-to-blue alternative scale for users with dyschromatopsia
constraints: The map does not display exact values, only a classification into three regions
target_learning_goals: interpreting distance and force feedback during simulated clipping
examples: Both distance and force visualisations in the simulation use this green-to-red diverging scale
key_sources: Allgaier M, Neyazi B, Preim B, Saalfeld S. (2021). Distance and force visualisations for improved simulation of intracranial aneurysm clipping. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02413-1

title: Use structured distance wet lab mentorship where challenges such as limited faculty, poor access to training institutions, or disrupted in-person training undermine traditional wet lab delivery
description: The article proposes distance wet lab mentorship — remote interactive lectures combined with locally recorded, remotely graded wet lab assignments — as a workable substitute for in-person structured wet lab courses. The authors state the model "could provide a viable alternative method for delivering wet lab cataract surgical training" in locations facing reported challenges to wet lab training, and note it offers continuity of training respecting social distancing during disruptive events such as COVID-19.
requirements: A telemedicine platform for lecture delivery and assignment grading, a local wet lab with model or animal eyes, and a remote mentor
constraints: "Further work is needed in other settings to confirm these results."
target_learners: ophthalmology residents in low- and middle-income countries and settings with disrupted in-person surgical training
target_learning_goals: cataract surgical competency in phacoemulsification
examples: IRO and Orbis made the course a permanent part of residency training with all second- and final-year residents participating annually, and the model is being replicated at Orbis partner hospitals in Bolivia and Haiti for manual small incision cataract surgery

article_title: The Impact of Surgical Boot Camp and Subsequent Repetitive Practice on the Surgical Skills and Confidence of Residents.
citation: Wang Wei, Ma Hucheng, Ren Haozhen, Wang Zhongxia, Mao Liang, He Ningning. (2020). The Impact of Surgical Boot Camp and Subsequent Repetitive Practice on the Surgical Skills and Confidence of Residents. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00268-020-05669-x
title: Distributed practice and memory consolidation as the mechanism account for boot camp skill retention
description: The article explains boot camp skill loss and its remedy through distributed practice and consolidation. Boot camps' "effects diminish over time," and there is a delay between when skills are learned and when they are needed. Distributed practice, "referred to as a practice regime, entails periods of training that are interspersed with rest periods in order to repeat and reinforce skills." Memory consolidation is needed when learning a new skill, and repetitive practice gives more consolidation opportunities, while mental rehearsal also strengthens memory.
requirements: Training periods interspersed with rest or spacing so skills are repeated and reinforced over time
constraints: The account is the authors' interpretation, not a mechanism tested within this study
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of procedural skills
examples: The authors required the experimental cohort to complete both boot camp and a year of repetitive practice "in order to take advantage of both training models."
key_sources: Wang Wei, Ma Hucheng, Ren Haozhen, Wang Zhongxia, Mao Liang, He Ningning. (2020). The Impact of Surgical Boot Camp and Subsequent Repetitive Practice on the Surgical Skills and Confidence of Residents. World Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00268-020-05669-x

title: Digital SP seminar structure mirroring classroom SP teaching: case presentation, doctor/patient dialogue, feedback round
description: The article describes a reusable lesson-level design for simulated-conversation seminars delivered by video conference. The structure is “similar to SP-seminars in classroom teaching with a case presentation, a doctor/patient dialogue and a feedback session”. Lecturers and observing students can hear and see the conversation partners but are not visible themselves; the SP waits in Zoom's waiting room during the briefing, students are muted until the feedback round, and peer feedback follows with everyone's visual participation.
requirements: Video conferencing software with waiting-room and muting functions; a prepared SP case; a confidentiality and no-recording rule communicated before the start
constraints: Lecturers cannot see whether dialled-in students are actually present because cameras are switched off
target_learners: medical students in semester 6, 8 and 10 communication courses
target_learning_goals: history taking and communication skills with simulated patients
examples: 46 seminars with 2-3 cases and approx. 15 students per seminar were conducted in the 6th, 8th and 10th semester

article_title: Models to predict injury, physical fitness failure and attrition in recruit training: a retrospective cohort study.
citation: Orr Robin M., Cohen Bruce S., Allison Stephen C., Bulathsinhala Lakmini, Zambraski Edward J., Jaffrey Mark. (2020). Models to predict injury, physical fitness failure and attrition in recruit training: a retrospective cohort study. Military Medical Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40779-020-00260-w
title: Defence Injury Prevention Program (DIPP) injury surveillance tool for recruit training
description: The DIPP was the injury data source for this study, an injury surveillance tool documenting injuries in the 28- and 80-day recruit training courses. It recorded "the type, location, activity during injury, action, severity and mechanism (cause)" at point-of-care facilities by medical staff, physiotherapists or physical training instructors. The article reports it documented up to 10 times as many injuries as the ADF's Defence Work Health and Safety incident reporting system.
requirements: Requires documentation by trained personnel (medical staff, physiotherapists, or physical training instructors) covering all incidents leading to health care attention.
constraints: The authors note some recruits may have failed to report injuries, citing evidence that many trainees conceal musculoskeletal injury symptoms to graduate on time.
target_learners: Army recruits in basic and reserve training courses
target_learning_goals: Injury surveillance to support mitigation of training injuries and training failure
examples: Injury data retrieved from DIPP underpinned the outcome variables (any injury, overuse injury, stress fracture, neuromuscular injury, traumatic injury) used in all predictive models in this study.

article_title: Non-technical skills: a review of training and evaluation in urology.
citation: Griffin Cora, Aydın Abdullatif, Brunckhorst Oliver, Raison Nicholas, Khan Muhammad Shamim, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran. (2019). Non-technical skills: a review of training and evaluation in urology. World Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00345-019-02920-6
title: The Diamond debriefing structure: a two-sided prompt sheet for standardised, NTS-focused simulation debriefing
description: The review describes 'The Diamond', put forward by Jaye et al. as "a standardised structure … to refocus debriefing on NTS rather than TS, as well as make sure the experiences between participants are equal". It is "a two-sided prompt sheet: the first side contains the scaffolding, with a series of specifically constructed questions for each phase of the debrief; the second lays out the theory behind the questions and the process". The review positions it, alongside assessment scales like NoTSS used as reflection aids, as a way to standardise what is expected from debriefing and help debriefers deliver higher-quality sessions.
requirements: A facilitator to use the prompt sheet during the debrief session; the review notes debriefing generally should be as long as the simulation itself, with a briefing beforehand
constraints: The review states more research is needed to determine concrete benefit from one debriefing model over another; model choice should account for simulation context and debriefer confidence
target_learners: simulation course participants in surgical and healthcare training
target_learning_goals: non-technical skills reflection and learning through structured post-scenario debriefing
examples: Jaye et al. designed The Diamond so the first side contains scaffolding questions for each debrief phase and the second lays out the theory behind the questions and process

article_title: Learning and Development of Diagnostic Reasoning in Occupational Therapy Undergraduate Students.
citation: Moruno-Miralles P., Reyes-Torres A., Talavera-Valverde M.-Á., Souto-Gómez A.-I., Márquez-Álvarez L.-J. (2020). Learning and Development of Diagnostic Reasoning in Occupational Therapy Undergraduate Students. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/6934579
title: Diagnostic reasoning as a two-process information-processing model culminating in an occupational therapy diagnosis
description: The article frames diagnostic reasoning as the problem-solving process leading to an occupational therapy diagnosis, following Rogers and Holm. It involves two information-processing stages: first, to "acquire cues and recognise patterns during data collection" covering occupational performance areas, symptoms and signs, skills, performance patterns, and environment, categorized via a theoretical framework of reference; second, formulating the problem by analysing and synthesizing collected information into a diagnosis explaining occupational problems and their causes. The diagnosis comprises descriptive, explanatory, cue, and pathologic components. The article uses this framework to structure its case-based assessment of undergraduates.
requirements: A preselected theoretical framework of reference to categorize collected information
Domain-specific knowledge and organized knowledge networks, which experts develop through repeated work with similar cases
constraints: The article notes repetition with similar cases "cannot be replicated by exercises in academic environments"
target_learning_goals: diagnostic reasoning
problem formulation
occupational therapy diagnosis
examples: The study assessed undergraduates' reasoning against this framework using a clinical reasoning case with five open questions covering identification, categorization, and problem formulation

article_title: Assessment of third-year medical students' comfort and preparedness for navigating challenging clinical scenarios with patients, peers, and supervisors.
citation: Kahkoska Anna R., DeSelm Tracy M., Young Laura A. (2020). Assessment of third-year medical students’ comfort and preparedness for navigating challenging clinical scenarios with patients, peers, and supervisors. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1984-1
title: Medical students benefit from enhanced diversity-related training modules and personalized toolkits for navigating challenging clinical scenarios
description: The article recommends that curricula address gaps in students' perceived comfort with diversity-related conflict, particularly with peers and superiors. It states students "may benefit from enhanced diversity related training modules designed to address general themes and key areas of concern identified" and proposes a personalized teaching toolkit emphasizing recognition of individual vulnerabilities and biases. Toolkits could include language and professional scripts, de-escalation tools, and interpersonal skills promoting resilience in the face of conflict.
requirements: Training should target the low-comfort areas identified: peer and superior interactions and gender-, race/ethnicity-, and disability-specific conflicts
constraints: The underlying study is a single-site, cross-sectional pilot with a 67% response rate and limited generalizability
target_learning_goals: conflict management in diversity-related clinical scenarios
self-reflection on individual vulnerabilities and biases
examples: The authors propose toolkits including "language and professional scripts, tools for de-escalation, and other interpersonal skills to promote resilience in the face of conflict"

article_title: A randomized controlled trial to examine the effect of two teaching methods on preschool children's language and communication, executive functions, socioemotional comprehension, and early math skills.
citation: Gerholm T, Kallioinen P, Tonér S, Frankenberg S, Kjällander S, Palmer A, Lenz-Taguchi H. (2019). BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-019-0325-9
title: DIL: digital individual learning combining the Magical Garden adaptive math game with body-and-mind attention exercises
description: DIL (Digital Individual Learning for body-and-mind) is an individual preschool training paradigm built on the theoretical understanding of self-regulation and early math as developing interdependently. The article states that "DIL had two components: an adaptive, interactive math game and a set of attention-enhancing body-and-mind activities." The Magical Garden game, played on tablets with headphones, includes a teachable agent the child teaches early math, with adaptive difficulty and feedback; the 12 body-and-mind activities train attention, breath control, avoiding distractions, body control, and metacognition through metaphors matching the game's characters.
requirements: Educators introduce and scaffold the body-and-mind exercises at each child's level, and the game is administered online with tablets and headphones
constraints: Implemented one hour per day during the six-week intervention; the trial found no measurable effects on the targeted skills
target_learners: preschool children aged four to six
target_learning_goals: executive functions including auditory selective attention
self-regulation
early math skills
examples: Children's frequency data and play time on the Magical Garden were registered on the device, and body-and-mind sessions were logged per child for fidelity scoring.

article_title: The Relationships between High School Subjects in terms of School Satisfaction and Academic Performance in Mexican Adolescents.
citation: Baños Raúl, Baena-Extremera Antonio, Granero-Gallegos Antonio. (2019). The Relationships between High School Subjects in terms of School Satisfaction and Academic Performance in Mexican Adolescents. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16183494
title: Diener's subjective well-being framework applied to school-specific wellbeing
description: The article frames school satisfaction within Diener's subjective well-being theory, which comprises a cognitive dimension (satisfaction with life) and an affective dimension (affective balance). School-specific subjective wellbeing "is defined as the subjective and cognitive assessment of quality of life in the school environment", and school satisfaction is understood as a cognitive–affective evaluation of the student's satisfaction with their school experience and courses. The study uses this framework to justify modeling subject satisfaction as a predictor of school satisfaction and academic performance.
requirements: Measurement of both satisfaction and boredom dimensions for each school subject using validated scales
constraints: The framework is applied to secondary-school students in the Mexican context in this study
target_learners: high school students in Mexico (mean age 14.10)
target_learning_goals: school satisfaction and subjective wellbeing
academic performance across school subjects
examples: The study operationalized the framework with the Intrinsic Satisfaction Classroom scale adapted to five subjects plus a school satisfaction/boredom scale and teacher-recorded grades

article_title: Effect of simulation education and case management on glycemic control in type 2 diabetes.
citation: Ji H, Chen R, Huang Y, Li W, Shi C, Zhou J. (2019). Effect of simulation education and case management on glycemic control in type 2 diabetes. Diabetes/Metabolism Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.1002/dmrr.3112
title: Simulation education program: video viewing plus role-play sessions added to standard DSME
description: The article's simulation education (SE) component consisted of an educational video covering diabetes knowledge, diet and exercise, insulin injection and blood glucose self-monitoring. It "offered 20‐minute video watching and then let patients imitate the actor in the video by carrying out 30‐minutes role‐play", delivered 3 times in the first week and twice in the second week, with family members encouraged to attend. Role-play cast patients as, for example, a dietitian learning diet calculation and diabetic food preparation.
requirements: Delivered as an addition on top of a standard DSME program; requires patients able to attend repeated video and role-play sessions
constraints: Developed for and evaluated in a single Chinese hospital center with a tailored scale; the article notes further investigation in larger cohorts is required
target_learners: Adults with type 2 diabetes on insulin or oral hypoglycemic medication
target_learning_goals: Diabetes self-management knowledge and skills: diet calculation, exercise, insulin injection, blood glucose self-monitoring
examples: A patient who consumed 350 to 400 g of spirituous liquor per social gathering reduced consumption and controlled fasting blood glucose after role-playing diet importance

title: Digital learning portfolio of online histology resources including virtual slides, expert video demonstrations, and e-Learning modules
description: A collection of online resources forming a digital learning portfolio that did not require laboratory access, provided to supplement student learning in the histology course. The portfolio included online web-based resources and student activities (quizzes, short answer questions, annotated morphology pictures), 24-hour access to annotated moveable virtual slides, online tutorial feedback from a histology expert, interactive e-Learning modules, and expert-led video demonstrations filmed in the histology laboratory.

Annotated virtual slide resources
Expert-led video demonstrations of laboratory techniques
Online tutorial feedback capability
constraints: Access to expert videos and modules began from week 6 of the semester
The portfolio supplemented but did not replace laboratory practicals; students were still required to attend at least 80% of laboratory practicals

target_learning_goals: Tissue morphology identification
Preparation for laboratory practical sessions
Revision of histology techniques outside scheduled class time

article_title: Evaluating a dialogue-based approach to teaching about values and policy in graduate transdisciplinary environmental science programs.
citation: Hall Troy E., Piso Zachary, Engebretson Jesse, & O'Rourke Michael. (2018). Evaluating a dialogue-based approach to teaching about values and policy in graduate transdisciplinary environmental science programs. PLoS ONE 13(9): e0202948. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0202948
title: Dialogue-based values and policy curriculum module for graduate environmental science courses
description: A customizable curriculum module for graduate environmental science courses built around locally relevant case studies, student-developed discussion prompts, and a facilitated dialogue following the Toolbox dialogue protocol. Materials include instructor guidance, a customizable lecture presentation, readings, FAQs, learning objectives, and "two lesson plans–one for a 6-hour (2-week) implementation and one for a 3-hour implementation–which makes the curriculum adaptable for different situations." "The centerpiece of the curriculum is a group discussion structured around the prompts."
requirements: Documents were "sufficiently structured to alleviate the need for faculty to have deep expertise in these domains", so instructors from any discipline can use them without formal training in values and policy.
constraints: The six supplied case studies "would likely not fit perfectly for many situations"; a guidance document helps instructors select locally relevant cases.
All materials are available from the authors upon request.
target_learners: Graduate students in environmental science and related programs
Practicing K-12 science teachers in a graduate environmental education course
target_learning_goals: Awareness of and reasoning about values and policy in environmental research
Reflexivity and perspective-taking through structured dialogue
examples: Instructors across five courses implemented it over two, three, or four weeks or condensed into a single long session, adapting case studies and lecture use while all courses kept the core prompt-development and dialogue activities.

article_title: Shared reading quality assessment by parental report: preliminary validation of the DialogPR.
citation: Hutton John S, Huang Guixia, Phelan Kieran J, DeWitt Thomas, Ittenbach Richard F. (2018). Shared reading quality assessment by parental report: preliminary validation of the DialogPR. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-018-1298-1
title: DialogPR: an eight-item caregiver-report measure of shared reading quality and dialogic reading
description: The DialogPR is a brief caregiver-report questionnaire assessing shared reading quality, built on the PEER/CROWD dialogic reading model and comprising eight items on discussion before and after reading and the frequency of CROWD prompts during story sharing. Responses are ordinal (0–3 points), with CROWD items anchored to a hypothetical book. The article reports it was "pilot tested for clarity" and has an estimated 6th-grade reading level, with data captured in REDCap.
requirements: Administered by trained research coordinators following a scripted introduction referencing the past month of shared reading
A criterion measure of home reading practices (here, the StimQ-P READ subscale) for validity reference
constraints: Preliminary validation only, in a sample of 49 dyads; test-retest reliability and comparison with direct observation were not assessed
First sample was exclusively 4-year-old girls from low-SES households; girls are marginally over-represented overall
target_learners: Preschool-age children (3–5 years) and their mothers/caregivers
target_learning_goals: Assessing quality and verbal interactivity of caregiver-child shared reading and dialogic reading behaviors
examples: Administered to mothers following the child's MRI in two combined studies, one low-SES (n = 22) and one largely higher-SES (n = 27)
key_sources: Hutton John S, Huang Guixia, Phelan Kieran J, DeWitt Thomas, Ittenbach Richard F. (2018). Shared reading quality assessment by parental report: preliminary validation of the DialogPR. BMC Pediatrics. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-018-1298-1

article_title: Flipping the Classroom in Medical Student Education: Does Priming Work?
citation: Rose E, Jhun P, Baluzy M, Hauck A, Huang J, Wagner J, Kearl YL, Behar S, Claudius I. (2018). Flipping the Classroom in Medical Student Education: Does Priming Work? Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.8.35162
title: Distribute flipped-classroom preparatory materials at least three days before the in-class session
description: The article's discussion recommends that three days' notice is adequate for distributing flipped-classroom preparatory materials, since the study "found no statistical difference in completion rates between groups that received three days' vs. two weeks' notice to view the videos." This lets clerkships schedule short-notice distribution without sacrificing completion, though a trend favored two weeks.
requirements: Preparatory material must be completed prior to the in-class session for the flipped classroom to work as described
constraints: The authors state one week in advance may be ideal but a definitive answer is not yet known; viewing rates may have been higher if materials were mandatory
target_learning_goals: pre-class preparation for interactive case-based sessions
examples: In the study, links sent three days ahead yielded 60.2% viewing versus 68.7% with two weeks' notice, a non-significant difference

title: District health management fellowship training programme (11 short courses, Tabriz, Iran)
description: A training programme developed by the National Public Health Management Centre of Tabriz University of Medical Sciences to build the managerial capacity of district health managers, based on an educational needs assessment by the Ministry of Health. It comprised 11 short courses (1–3 days each) covering management and leadership, managing the district, quality improvement, planning and evaluation, health information management, health resources management and economics, community participation, epidemiology, research in health systems, human resources and creativity, and rules and ethics. The article reports that "The programme developed was used by the Ministry of Health as an applicable package for training district health managers across the country".
requirements: Delivered to heads of provincial health centres, district health managers and health deputies of district health centres, selected by the Ministry of Health
constraints: Courses were short (1–3 days each) and delivered across multiple university locations between June 2015 and February 2016
target_learners: heads of units in provincial health centres
health deputies of district health centres
target_learning_goals: health system management knowledge and skills
quality improvement
planning and evaluation
examples: Two cohorts of 89 health officials (44 and 45 participants in each cohort) completed the courses, with pretest and post-test examinations in each course and a portfolio completed in work settings

article_title: Using differential item functioning to evaluate potential bias in a high stakes postgraduate knowledge based assessment.
citation: Hope D, Adamson KA, McManus IC, Chis L, Elder A. (2018). Using differential item functioning to evaluate potential bias in a high stakes postgraduate knowledge based assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1143-0
title: Differential Item Functioning as an ability-curve-level framework for detecting item bias, with uniform, non-uniform and crossing difference types
description: Differential Item Functioning (DIF) is a psychometric framework for evaluating item-level bias that "takes into account differences at every level of candidate ability". It compares two or more groups of interest on each test question across the whole ability curve, allowing detection of no bias, "uniform differences (group A outperforms group B across the ability curve)", non-uniform differences where the gap varies, and crossing differences where the direction reverses across the curve. The article uses logistic-regression DIF with Wald tests, and uses DIF to flag questions for expert review, revision or removal in a high-stakes postgraduate examination.
requirements: Requires candidate background characteristic data (e.g. sex, ethnicity) and per-item response data across ability levels, analysed with DIF procedures such as logistic regression with correction for multiple comparisons.
constraints: The article notes simple mean-score comparisons may conceal differences at the lower and upper ends of the ability curve, and that DIF was only one of a family of DIF procedures, so other techniques such as Mantel-Haenszel may yield slightly different results.
target_learning_goals: fair and valid assessment of core clinical knowledge
examples: The authors ran a logistic-regression DIF analysis separately on each of 14 MRCP(UK) Part 1 datasets, testing 2773 questions for sex and for ethnicity, and passed the eight medium/large-effect items to a blinded expert panel.
key_sources: Hope D, Adamson KA, McManus IC, Chis L, Elder A. (2018). Using differential item functioning to evaluate potential bias in a high stakes postgraduate knowledge based assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1143-0

article_title: Using differential item functioning to evaluate potential bias in a high stakes postgraduate knowledge based assessment.
citation: Hope D, Adamson KA, McManus IC, Chis L, Elder A. (2018). Using differential item functioning to evaluate potential bias in a high stakes postgraduate knowledge based assessment. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1143-0
title: Free R packages difR and lordif for conducting DIF analyses
description: The article points readers to freely available R packages for replicating DIF analyses: "see the guidance notes provided in the package difR [19] or for an alternative see the lordif package [18]". It also notes that "many free online tools exist to test for DIF and can be used by any interested party", yet these tools had yet to be widely applied in medical education or the academic governance of high stakes postgraduate examinations in the UK. The packages provide step-by-step guidance for the logistic-regression DIF approach the authors used.
requirements: Analyses were carried out in R; users need R and the package guidance notes to replicate the analyses.
target_learners: assessment researchers and psychometric analysts in medical education
target_learning_goals: detecting differential item functioning in examinations
examples: The authors ran all analyses in R and directed readers to the difR and lordif packages for step-by-step replication guides.
